feat(deploy): seed the deployer as admin, and scope the admin list per agent (#325)

A deployed agent had no reachable admin at all. ADMIN_ADD is gated on
is_super_admin, super-admin is defined as the agent's OWN address, and that
private key is generated on the server and never leaves it. So the only
account that could grant admin was the one nobody can sign as — and promoting
anyone else requires an existing admin. Chicken and egg, with no way in.

Fix it the way ssh-copy-id does, one layer up: the deploy ships the operator's
public address, the agent finds it in its admin list, and grants the role to
whoever signs as it. Nothing secret travels, and revoking is deleting a line.

Both deploy paths, written on every deploy so the list self-heals:
  co deploy         → .co/admins.txt synthesized into the package
  co deploy --to    → written over ssh, since .co/ is excluded from the rsync

The identity is the one `co call` signs with (project .co/, then ~/.co/) and
deliberately not project_dir/.co: a --template deploy builds a throwaway
project whose address dies with it, so seeding that would name an admin
nobody can ever be.

Second defect, same area: admins.txt was the single global ~/.co/admins.txt
while the self address it is compared against came from the project's .co/.
Every agent on one machine therefore shared one set of admins — making
someone admin of one deployed agent made them admin of all of them. The list
now lives beside the identity it belongs to.

No compatibility shim for the old global file: the only writer was ADMIN_ADD,
which nobody could reach, so there is nothing out there to migrate.

Closes #305.

Publish the agent's full picture over the authenticated socket, not over /info (#323)

The unauthenticated path was handing out more than the authenticated one.

`/info` takes no auth argument at all and returned `agent_metadata["skills"]`
whole. On this machine that is 117 entries, of which 114 are `user` and
`claude-user` -- the operator's own ~/.co/skills and ~/.claude/skills. They
are not shipped with the agent and are not reachable by it once deployed, yet
any caller could read the list: personal skill names, which SaaS accounts the
operator has wired up, internal workflow names. `_build_agent_profile` already
treats exactly these locations as private and filters them out of the relay
directory, so the two answers to "what is public" disagreed.

Meanwhile the WebSocket -- which does verify an Ed25519 signature and clears
the trust gate -- carried no agent information at all. None of its 18 frame
types mentions skills. So the channel entitled to the full picture sent
nothing, and the channel entitled to nothing sent everything.

- /info now publishes the same skill subset as the relay directory, reusing
  PUBLISHED_SKILL_LOCATIONS rather than restating the rule, so the two cannot
  drift apart
- new AGENT_PROFILE frame after CONNECTED carries the complete metadata --
  every skill, tools, model, balance -- to a client that has authenticated
- establish_connection takes route_handlers optionally, so callers that only
  need the session half are unaffected

Verified live against a hosted co-ai agent:

  unauthenticated GET /info      -> 0 skills
  authenticated WS AGENT_PROFILE -> 117 skills, 24 tools, balance 25.34

Three unit tests cover the /info subset, the frame's contents and ordering
after CONNECTED, and the no-route_handlers path. Full unit suite: 2441 passed.

Note for the TypeScript SDK: fetchAgentInfo currently probes each endpoint's
/info and lets that response override the relay profile, so until it consumes
AGENT_PROFILE a browser client sees the published subset only. That is the
correct pre-auth answer, but it does mean the chat surface shows fewer skills
than before this change until the SDK follows.

feat(skills): say which tier a skill came from, and which ones will not travel (#326)

The loader searches five locations and reports nothing about where a skill came
from. Two of those five — ~/.co/skills and ~/.claude/skills — do not exist
anywhere except the machine that wrote them, and most of ours are symlinks into
a separate repo, invisible to anything that packages a project. So a skill can
look installed, work for months, and simply be absent on a deployed agent, in
CI, or on a teammate's checkout. Nothing fails; the agent just behaves
differently for a reason nothing in the output explains.

  co skills list   every tier, with a Deploys column — it used to list only
                   ~/.co/skills, i.e. exactly the tier that does NOT travel
  co doctor        counts per tier, and any broken links
  co deploy        names the skills being left behind, both deploy paths

TRAVELS_ON_DEPLOY is kept separate from PUBLISHED_SKILL_LOCATIONS even though
they nearly agree: builtin travels (it is installed with the package) but is
not published (framework noise nobody should see in a public directory).
Travelling and being publishable are different questions.

Broken links are reported rather than skipped. Only symlinks are checked — a
plain directory without a SKILL.md is somebody's notes, not a broken skill, and
flagging those produced false positives on this very repo.

The five search paths are now defined once, so discovery and the diagnosis of
it cannot end up looking in different places.

Closes #302.

feat(server): co server new provisions a server and shows what it costs (#327)

Calls the backend (openonion/oo-api#39) to create a GCE instance with the key
from co keys --ssh already in authorized_keys, then registers the result in
~/.co/servers.yaml so the operator never types an IP.

The confirmation is the point. This is the first co command that spends a
large discrete amount — everything else is free or costs fractions of a cent
invisibly. 'new' is the honest verb for what happens to the machine and says
nothing about the money, so the prompt has to:

  cost          $180.00  (12 months, charged now)
  your balance  $500.00 -> $320.00 after
  expires       2027-07-31  - the server stops unless renewed

Balance-after rather than just the price: what decides whether someone can
afford it is what is left, not what it costs.

Everything that can be checked locally is checked before the prompt, let alone
the charge: the name, a name already registered, authentication, and the SSH
key existing at all — a server created with no way in is worse than no server.
An unreachable pricing endpoint refuses rather than guessing a number it might
then charge differently.

Part of #309. Closes #313

ci: stop fork PRs failing on an empty OPENONION_API_KEY (#328)

A fork PR receives no repository secrets, so
`${{ secrets.OPENONION_API_KEY }}` expands to an empty string and the
step exports OPENONION_API_KEY="". An empty key is not the same as an
absent one: the auth CLI treats it as "not authenticated" and bails with
a help message before reaching the OAuth code the tests drive, so six
tests fail on output they never produced.

Verified on origin/main (4f289cf), tests/e2e/cli/test_cli_auth_google.py
and test_cli_auth_microsoft.py:

  unset                       20 passed
  OPENONION_API_KEY=""         6 failed, 14 passed
  OPENONION_API_KEY=test-key  20 passed

So every fork PR currently shows red CI for a reason unrelated to its
own diff — #293 failed this way while being a correct fix. That is a
false wall in front of outside contributors.

Falling back to a placeholder keeps the variable non-empty when secrets
are unavailable. The suite selected here excludes real_api, so no test
in this job ever calls out with the key.

Split out of #184, where it was bundled with the async-tool feature that
is now deferred to 1.8.0. This part shouldn't wait for a release.

fix(server): quote the price against spendable credit, not lifetime top-ups (#331)

`co server new` read credits_usd from /api/v1/auth/me, which is the sum of
every top-up and ignores everything already spent. An account that had added
$315 and spent $291 therefore reads as $315 of headroom, and the prompt tells
someone a $180 server leaves them $135. They say yes, and the backend — which
does the arithmetic correctly — refuses with 402 for a purchase they were just
told they could afford.

This is the display side of the same mistake openonion/oo-api#42 fixed inside
the balance check. `co status` and `co auth` already read balance_usd; this
one command was the odd one out, and it is the one place in the CLI where the
number decides whether someone spends $180.

co server new refuses a name it cannot use, before charging (#334)

* fix(server): refuse a server name we cannot use, rather than rewriting it

A server name becomes the machine's own name, and GCE requires those to start
with a letter. `co server new 1prod` passed the deploy-name check, showed the
confirmation prompt, took the $180 charge, and only then failed.

Checked here before the prompt, against the same rule the backend enforces
(openonion/oo-api#46). Deploy names are unchanged — they allow a leading digit
and should, being DNS labels and Docker tags.

* test: do not depend on where rich decides to wrap

The assertion looked for a phrase in console output, which rich breaks across
lines at the terminal width — so it passed on 3.10 and 3.12 and failed on 3.11
and 3.13 purely by runner width. Collapse the whitespace first.

Reproduced locally with COLUMNS=60; now passes at 40, 60, 80 and 120.

fix(server): reach the machine we just created (#354)

Three faults, each of which made a server nobody could open. All found by
running it against a real box, none by the tests, which passed throughout.

1. ssh was never told about the derived key. A machine from `co server new`
   has only that key installed, so `co server check` on a server the account
   had just been charged $180 for answered "Permission denied (publickey)".
   Offered, not forced — no IdentitiesOnly — so a box registered by hand with
   `co server add` still opens with whichever key already worked.

2. The key was derived from the nearest project's recovery phrase, so
   `co server new` in one project and `co deploy --to` from another produced
   two different keys, and the second was locked out of the machine the first
   had bought. A server belongs to the person who paid for it: the account
   charged is the global one in ~/.co, so its key is too.

3. Our copy of the key wrote each half only if that half was missing, which
   left a private key from one phrase beside a public key from another. ssh
   reports that as "contents do not match public" and refuses. Both halves are
   now written together, in ~/.co/ssh rather than ~/.ssh — a file there may be
   the operator's, and this one is overwritten by design.

`co server ssh` had its own ssh invocation and missed the fix entirely, which
is the command whose whole purpose is getting you onto the box. Every path now
goes through one _identity(); the duplicate in deploy_to_server is gone.

Verified end to end against a real server in Sydney: create, check, deploy,
write state over ssh, change the code, redeploy — the new code arrived and
`.co/` state survived.

co server ls reconciles with billing, and co server destroy (#329)

* feat(server): reconcile co server ls against billing, and add co server destroy

Two gaps from #318, both about the same thing: once a server costs money the
local ~/.co/servers.yaml stops being the truth.

co server ls now reconciles against the backend. The row that matters is the
one the local file cannot produce — billed for, not registered here. That is
somebody paying for a machine `co` would otherwise never show them: created on
another laptop, or dropped with `co server forget`. It names both ways out,
`add` to use it from here and `destroy` to stop paying for it.

The lookup is best-effort, and None is not []. None means we could not ask
(offline, unauthenticated, a 500), [] means the account owns nothing. Only the
second justifies showing a BILLING column, because only the second is an
answer. Collapsing them would let a timeout read as "you own no servers",
which is the one wrong answer that hides a machine you are paying for.

co server destroy tears the machine down and stops the billing. It asks for
the name typed back rather than y/N: a reflex "y" is exactly how someone
deletes production while meaning to tidy their config, and typing a name
cannot be done by reflex. It says the term is not refunded before asking, not
after.

The local entry is dropped only after the delete succeeds. Removing it on a
failure would hide a server that is still running and still billing — the
exact state this change exists to make visible. A 404 points at `forget`,
since a local-only entry has nothing to destroy.

Depends on openonion/oo-api#43 for DELETE /api/v1/servers/{name}.
Part of #318.

* co server destroy: state the refunded amount, not the policy

The backend now refunds the unused part of the term (openonion/oo-api#43), so
the confirmation stops warning about a forfeit that no longer happens and the
result reports the number instead.

"Prorated" tells the user nothing they can check. "$150.41 of $180.00 refunded
to your credit" does.

feat(deploy): serve a deployed agent over https on its own hostname (#355)

The last piece of the chain. A provisioned server has 22, 80 and 443 open and
the agent listens on 8000, so until now nothing a browser could reach ever
answered — no dashboard, no oo-chat over a domain.

`co deploy --to` now installs Caddy when the server has a hostname and points
that hostname at the agent over loopback. Installed by the deploy rather than
by provisioning, for the reason #318 settled: a machine registered by hand with
`co server add` never went through provisioning, so this has to exist here
anyway, and doing it in both places is two implementations of one thing.

The systemd unit gains AGENT_PUBLIC_DOMAIN, which matters as much as the proxy.
Without it announce.py publishes `http://<ip>:8000` to the relay, and 8000 is
closed — so every client probes an endpoint that can never answer and falls
back to the directory record. With it the agent announces `https://<hostname>`
and `wss://<hostname>/ws`, which is what Caddy is listening on.

`co server new` records the hostname the backend created rather than deriving
it, so the naming rule stays in one place. A server registered by hand has
none, and then no https is set up — there is no name to get a certificate for,
and inventing one would fail the challenge rather than fail honestly.

reverse_proxy passes WebSocket upgrades through unchanged, so chat, dashboard
pushes and remote exec all ride one connection with no stanza of their own.

One agent per hostname: there is one name and one :443, so a second agent
deployed to the same server takes the name. Several agents on one machine is
still open (#309); when it is answered the Caddyfile grows a stanza per agent.

Depends on openonion/oo-api#48 for the hostname in the API response, and #47
for inbound 80, without which the certificate challenge cannot complete.

test(e2e): the server lifecycle against a real machine

co server new → check → deploy with a skill → iterate → destroy, skipped unless
CO_E2E_SERVERS=1.

Every step is one that shipped broken and passed the unit tests anyway: the
preflight that answered Permission denied on a machine we had just been charged
for, the key derived from whichever directory you stood in, the pair written one
half at a time, and the skill that never left the laptop.

The second-deploy test is the one that matters most and was never covered: an
updated skill must travel, the old one must not survive it, and .co/ state
written on the server must outlive the redeploy.

docs: document co server, deploying onto it, and the AGENT_PROFILE frame (#384)

Three things shipped without documentation.

`co server` and `co deploy --to` had zero mentions anywhere in docs/ — the whole
one-server-per-agent path was undocumented, including the part that costs money.
docs/cli/server.md now covers it, deploy.md gains it as a third option beside
the cloud and self-hosting, and the CLI index lists it.

The pieces worth writing down are the ones that are surprising: why forget and
destroy are two commands rather than one, why `co server ls` reconciles against
the backend at all, what survives a deploy and what does not, and why a
hand-registered machine deliberately gets no https.

AGENT_PROFILE (#323) was merged with nothing in the protocol doc. It is easy to
mistake for an incomplete `/info`, when the point is the opposite: the public
answer is narrower on purpose, and a client that has not passed the trust gate
should render that rather than treat it as a partial version of this frame.

feat(server): lead the price with what it costs per month (#383)

`co server new` quoted only the 12-month total. "$360" is a number nobody can
compare to anything they already pay for; "$30 a month" places it immediately.
A server is a monthly thing in everybody's head — the year is only how we
charge for it, so it is still said, right next to the month and never instead
of it.

  cost   $30 / month — $360.00 for 12 months, charged now

The monthly figure comes from the backend (openonion/oo-api#52) rather than
being divided here: one price, one place, and no chance of the CLI rounding its
way to a different number than the one on the website. An older backend that
does not send it falls back to the division rather than crashing, since the
yearly price is the one actually charged.

fix(deploy): a crash loop is not a successful deploy, and a recreated server is not an attack (#385)

Both found by running the full lifecycle twice against a real machine.

A deploy reported success for an agent that was looping on an ImportError.
`Restart=always` means a unit that dies on import is "active" in the moment
right after the restart and again after every crash, so asking immediately
always says yes. The first hint the operator got was a 502 from a page they had
just been told was live. NRestarts is reset by an explicit restart and counts
only automatic ones, so anything above zero after a short grace period means it
has already died — and then the journal tail is printed, which is what they
actually need.

Separately: cloud providers reuse addresses. When one comes back attached to a
machine we just created, the key in known_hosts belongs to a machine that no
longer exists, and ssh refuses with a warning about a possible attack —
StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new covers a host never seen, not one whose key
changed. `co server check` failed this way immediately after `co server new`
succeeded. We created the machine, so we know the old key is dead; nothing else
in co removes host keys.

release: 1.5.3 (#386)

* release: 1.5.3

Servers you own. `co server new/add/ls/check/ssh/forget/destroy` and
`co deploy --to`, with an SSH key derived from the same recovery phrase you
already have. A deploy no longer reissues the agent's address, keeps its logs,
seeds the deploying key as admin so a deployed agent is administrable at all,
and serves it over https on a hostname of its own.

The agent's full picture now travels over the authenticated socket rather than
the open `/info`, which had been publishing the operator's personal skills —
117 of them on the machine where this was found — to anyone who could reach the
agent.

`co skills list` and `co doctor` say which tier each skill came from and which
ones will not survive a deploy, and both deploy paths name the ones being left
behind.

A patch, not 1.6.0. VERSIONING.md now says why: X.Y.0 is the version people sit
on, so features stabilise in patch releases first and the minor is cut once the
work has actually been exercised end to end. The file previously documented only
the mechanical roll-over rule, which reads as "features force a minor bump" —
that is semver's rule, not this project's.

* fix(server): co server --help said destroy is not refunded

It was, when #329 wrote that string. openonion/oo-api#43 then made destroy
refund the unused term, and the runtime output was updated to state the amount
— the typer help was not, so `co server --help` told the opposite of what the
command does. Caught by smoke-testing the built wheel rather than by a test,
which is what smoke tests are for.

Remote execution on a deployed server actually works (#387)

* fix: remote execution on a deployed server actually works

Five faults, all found by walking the documented path against a real machine —
`co server new`, deploy with real skills, then `co call <address> co status`,
which is the example in `co call`'s own help.

1. An admin was a stranger to their own agent. `co deploy --to` writes the
   operator's key into .co/admins.txt and prints "admin: 0x… (your key)", but
   the trust gate only ever consulted whitelisted and contact. A freshly
   deployed agent answered its owner with "agent requires onboarding", for a
   machine they had just paid for and installed their key on.

2. The agent could not find its own commands. The unit set no PATH, so the
   process inherited systemd's default and `co` — installed in the project's
   venv — was not on it: "co: command not found".

3. The agent ran as root. No User= in the unit, so `co call`, which runs
   whatever the admin sends, ran it as root — a superset of what the operator
   gets by sshing in as themselves. It also gave the process HOME=/root, which
   is where the browser looked for a cache it could never have.

4. /tmp/co is machine-global and chmod 0700, so whoever created it first owned
   it: PermissionError for every other user on the box. The docstring already
   claimed a per-user runtime dir; on POSIX without XDG_RUNTIME_DIR it was not.
   Scoped by username now, the same way the Windows pipe name is.

5. A missing browser was reported with advice for a different failure — a Linux
   server told to open a desktop Terminal, when what it needed was
   `patchright install chromium`.

Two more from the same run: pip ran from the login shell's home, so a
requirements.txt naming anything relative to itself (a local wheel, -e ., a
nested -r) failed on a file that was plainly there; and files left owned by root
by an earlier deploy stopped the now-unprivileged agent from writing its own
log, so the sync hands the tree to the user the service runs as.

2538 passed.

* test: the per-user runtime dir is a POSIX concern

Windows takes the LOCALAPPDATA branch, which is already per-user, so the new
cases asserted a scoped name against a path that is correctly unscoped.

fix(server): ready means you can log in, and the e2e deploys the working tree (#388)

Two things the repo's own end-to-end test found the moment it was run against a
real machine.

`co server new` printed "✓ ready" and suggested `co server check` next, and
that command answered "Permission denied (publickey)". The API returns as soon
as the instance has an address, which is about ten seconds before the guest
agent has copied the key into authorized_keys — the most alarming possible way
to say "wait ten seconds", on a machine just paid for. It now waits until the
machine actually lets you in, and on timeout says the server exists and is
charged for rather than pretending to have failed.

The end-to-end test installed `connectonion` from PyPI, so it exercised the
previous release while claiming to test the change in front of you — and the
template, generated by the CLI under test, can name an API that has not shipped
yet. Against PyPI that is a crash loop whose error says nothing about versions.
It now builds a wheel of the working tree and pins it.

Three more cases cover what this run's fixes were about: the agent does not run
as root, the operator can run a command on their own agent, and the remote
browser answers.

docs(e2e): how to tell 'the key is wrong' from 'you are not talking to that machine' (#390)

A run failed with Permission denied (publickey) on a machine that had our key
correctly installed. The address presented one host key to my laptop and a
different one to a GCE box, and the same private key logged in from the GCE box
first try — the connection was being answered by something else entirely.

The check is two commands and it is the first thing to run, because every other
explanation is more interesting and all of them are wrong.

docs: the relay ANNOUNCE profile is a third surface, not the AGENT_PROFILE frame (#389)

The protocol doc explains the public /info profile and the authenticated
AGENT_PROFILE frame, which reads like the complete picture. It isn't: host()
also sends a profile to the relay inside ANNOUNCE, built by a separate function
with size limits enforced on the relay side, and that is the one that decides
whether the agent is reachable at all.

Missing that costs real debugging time — an agent whose ANNOUNCE profile is
rejected starts cleanly, prints one red line, and then reads as offline
everywhere, which looks nothing like a profile problem.

fix(deploy): the marker is a claim, and a missing binary is not a traceback (#397)

Two reported deploy bugs.

#376: .co/provision.json survives every rsync by design — it is the record of
work that does not need doing again. But it records what *was* true, and the
venv it speaks for can be gone: a disk cleanup, a restored snapshot, an rm -rf
while debugging. The deploy then skipped creating one, pip short-circuited on an
unchanged requirements hash, and the restart failed naming a python that is not
there — the one cause never mentioned. The interpreter is now checked in the
same round trip that reads the marker. One test for the file the systemd unit
will execute, not a re-verification of everything the marker implies.

#377: subprocess.run raised FileNotFoundError when ssh was absent, printing a
traceback for the single problem a person can fix in one sentence.
`co server add` has always checked; this path had not, and it is the one that
runs after the server is already paid for. rsync is checked too — the sync is
rsync, so ssh alone gets you halfway and then fails.

fix(deploy): a skill is not a project (#401)

`co deploy --skills` applied the project ignore defaults to every skill
directory it bundled. A skill's `build/` is a compiled helper it shells out to;
its `todo.md` may be a document it reads; a JS tool brings `node_modules/`.
The defaults call all of that noise, so those files were dropped from the
tarball with no warning — the deploy reported success and the skill failed
later, on the server, reaching for something that was never sent.

Skills now carry only what nobody means to ship (caches, .git) plus whatever
the skill's own author put in its .gitignore.

Closes #380.

A skill still keeps its secrets (#402)

* fix(deploy): a skill still keeps its secrets

My fix for #380 dropped the project ignore defaults for skill directories
wholesale, and .env.local — which those defaults had been excluding — started
travelling to the server inside the tarball. A secret leaving the machine is a
worse bug than a build/ directory not leaving it.

The defaults were right about exactly one thing, and it is kept: .env*,
.co/keys/ and private keys never travel, whatever the skill wants. build/,
node_modules/ and todo.md still do, which is what #380 was about.

Caught by tests/e2e/cli/test_cli_deploy.py, which had asserted this since before
either change — I merged #401 without reading its CI.

* fix(browser): every failure message still names the log

My rewrite of the launch-failure advice in #387 dropped the ~/.co/browser.log
pointer from two of its three branches. Whatever else is wrong, the full log is
where the rest of it is — and a test in tests/e2e/cli had asserted exactly that
since before the rewrite.

dashboard: a Home page that survives an agent with 115 skills (#391)

The starter dashboard showed four skills. On this machine the agent publishes
115, so Home was four arbitrary buttons — whichever four discovery happened to
return first — and 111 skills the page silently pretended did not exist. The
four it did show were full-width bars stretched across the pane with an
eight-character label and no description, under a title-cased label
("Nano Banana Us") that is neither the skill's name nor what you type to run it.

Now every published skill is on the page, and the layout changes shape with the
count:

- up to a dozen: listed flat, because collapsing six items hides them behind a
  click for nothing
- past that: grouped by the family already in the names — lark-base, lark-doc,
  lark-sheets → "lark" — with a count on each group and the first one open, so
  the page opens on something to click rather than a row of shut drawers. Names
  sharing no prefix with two others land in "other".

115 skills is now one scannable screen. Each row is the skill's real name plus
its description, clamped to two lines; rows are separated by hairlines rather
than being 115 bordered cards. The header says what the agent runs on and how
much it has, omitting any part it doesn't know rather than printing "0 tools".

The markup moved out of Python, into one file: starter.html. It is a complete
page — open it in a browser and you see what a starter dashboard looks like —
then a <!--FRAGMENTS marker, then the repeated pieces as template tags. Python
splits on the marker and fills in the placeholders; it holds no HTML of its own,
and everything below the marker (including its notes) is stripped before
anything is written. One file rather than one per fragment: there is nothing to
keep in sync, and the page still previews as itself.

string.Template, not str.format — the page is mostly CSS, and every rule in it
is a pair of braces format would read as a field.

Everything here is CSS-only, and has to be: the client renders a dashboard under
a CSP that runs only its own bridge script, so an agent's script tag or inline
handler never executes. The disclosure groups are <details>/<summary>, which is
the one thing that works without scripting.

Also written down, because it was load-bearing and undocumented: dashboard.html
belongs at the project root, not in .co/ — `co deploy --to` rsyncs the tree
excluding .co/, so a dashboard there would silently not travel; the template
Dockerfile's COPY . . takes the root; and the scaffolded .gitignore leaves it
committed. And co create / co init deliberately do not scaffold one: at create
time the project has no skills yet and ensure_dashboard never overwrites, so
scaffolding then would freeze an empty Home forever.

Tests cover what actually broke: every published skill reachable, short lists not
hidden behind a disclosure, long ones grouped and opened, names verbatim,
descriptions present, no script tag, hostile names escaped, no fragment or
unsubstituted $placeholder leaking into the output, and the template file present
beside the module — a wheel that drops it would turn every host startup into a
FileNotFoundError.

dashboard: keep the Home page in .co/, and find it from the project root (#405)

Two things were wrong with where the Home page lived.

It resolved against the bare cwd. Start the agent from a subdirectory and
ensure_dashboard created a second dashboard.html there and served that one — an
agent with a Home page you had written would come up blank because you ran it
from src/. Everything else the agent is made of is found by walking up for .co/
(skills, host.yaml); the dashboard had no notion of a project at all.

And it sat in the project root while .co/skills/ sat in .co/. The line .co/ is
sorted by is not "config vs content" — deploy_to_server says it outright: skills
are *what the agent is*, not state it accumulated, which is why .co/skills/ is
rsynced while the rest of .co/ (identity, logs, evals) is excluded. A Home page
is the same kind of thing, and it was on the wrong side of that line.

So: .co/dashboard.html, located by walking up for .co/, and included in the
deploy rsync next to skills. Without that include a deploy silently drops your
Home page and the server regenerates a starter over it — the deploy succeeds and
the agent looks fine, the same failure that made skills an exception.

A dashboard.html already in the project root is still served, and is never
moved, copied or overwritten. An agent whose Home silently vanished on upgrade
would be a worse bug than an inconsistent path. If both exist, .co/ wins.

Also adds ~/.co/starter.html: write one and every agent you host starts from it
instead of the bundled template. It replaces the template, not the page — each
agent still renders its own name and its own skills, because a client validates
every button against the skills *that* agent published, so one agent's finished
Home served for another is a page of buttons that silently do nothing. An
override carries only what it changes: its fragments layer over the bundled
ones, so restyling the shell doesn't mean copying the skill-row markup with it,
or quietly losing it.

Tests were confirmed red against the current code first: written into .co/,
found from a subdirectory, a legacy root file still served and not migrated,
.co/ winning when both exist, an agent outside any project still getting a Home,
a personal starter rendering this agent's own name and skills, and the rsync
carrying .co/dashboard.html ahead of the .co/* exclude.

2572 unit + 366 cli e2e pass. Smoke-tested for real: started from src/ inside a
project, the file landed in the project's .co/ and nowhere else.

test: the suite must not be able to reach the operator's real ~/.co (#406)

A test overwrote a live Outlook session with its own fixtures.

tests/e2e/cli/test_cli_auth_microsoft.py runs `co auth microsoft` against
mocked HTTP inside CliRunner.isolated_filesystem(), which isolates the working
directory and nothing else. `co auth` also writes the global ~/.co/keys.env, so
the fake credentials the test asserts on replaced the real ones:

    MICROSOFT_ACCESS_TOKEN = 'eyJ0eXAi.test'      (13 chars)
    MICROSOFT_REFRESH_TOKEN = '0.ATcA.test'       (11 chars)
    MICROSOFT_EMAIL = test@outlook.com

It surfaces as "Microsoft session expired and refresh failed (400)", days later,
which is the last thing anyone would trace back to a test run.

Four test files use isolated_filesystem() with no HOME isolation at all, so the
fix is a global autouse fixture rather than four patches: HOME, USERPROFILE,
AGENT_CONFIG_PATH and Path.home() all point into a per-test temp directory.

Verified with a sentinel written into the real file: without the fixture the
test erases it, with the fixture it survives.

test: the dashboard suite must not render from the developer's own starter (#407)

~/.co/starter.html is a feature this file tests, so a developer who actually
uses one had every render in the suite come from their page. Measured on a real
override: a starter without a $body placeholder fails nine of these tests, one
with a script tag fails two — none of it connected to the change being made.

An autouse fixture points STARTER_OVERRIDE at a path that does not exist, and
clears the template cache either side. Tests that want an override still set it
themselves; monkeypatch applies in order, so theirs wins.

Verified by putting a real ~/.co/starter.html in place: 9 failures before, 44
passing after.

feat(skills): copy a skill into the project, which is the tier that deploys (#409)

Every deploy printed 'move one into .co/skills/ to ship it' and no command did
that. `co skills copy` writes ~/.co/skills — the operator's library, which
`co skills list` itself marks Deploys ✗ — so the two halves of the workflow
pointed at different directories and the operator was left to cp -R by hand.

`co skills copy <name> --to-project` puts it where a deploy will find it, and
the deploy's own hint now names that command instead of describing a step the
tool did not offer.

Verified end to end: after the copy, `co skills list` moves the skill from
'user ✗' to 'project ✓'.

Closes #408.

fix(skills): one unreadable skill must not stop the agent from starting (#410)

Discovery read every SKILL.md with no guard, inside a loop with no per-entry
guard, called from create_agent() before the CLI is usable. So a UnicodeDecodeError
from one file did not mean "that skill failed to load" — it meant `co ai` does
not start, and nothing said which of the user's skills caused it.

One file saved as Windows-1252, or a compiled asset copied into a skill
directory by accident, is enough. On this machine that is 1 of 121 skills
holding the whole CLI hostage.

Both loops are fixed, because both have the bug and fixing one is not a fix:
cli/co_ai/skills/loader.py and useful_plugins/skills.py.

Named rather than swallowed. Skipping silently trades a crash for a mystery —
the agent behaves differently and nothing points at the cause — so the path and
the exception type are printed.

One deliberate behaviour change: the name is claimed only after the read
succeeds. Discovery takes the first of each name and skips the rest, so a broken
higher-priority file used to claim the name on its way out and silently disable
the working lower-priority skill it was overriding. That is a harder failure to
explain than either one alone.

Closes #370.

release: 1.5.4 (#411)

Patch, not minor: everything since 1.5.3 is a fix or a small addition to an
existing command, and none of it changes an interface anyone depends on.

Also documents co skills copy --to-project, which shipped in #409 with no docs
entry, and updates docs-site/lib/version.ts — it was still on 1.5.2, having been
missed by the 1.5.3 release.

fix(llm): structured_complete() must fail the way complete() does (#413)

complete() translates 402 into InsufficientCreditsError, 503 into
ProviderServiceError, and timeouts into LLMConnectionError.
structured_complete() had no try/except at all, so an agent asking for
structured output on a depleted account got a raw openai.APIStatusError — and
every `except InsufficientCreditsError` written against the documented
behaviour, which is the pattern CLAUDE.md teaches, missed it.

Both now go through one _call() helper rather than a copied block. Two copies
of a translation table drift, and the half that drifts is the half nobody
tested — which is how these two came apart in the first place.

Scoped to OpenOnionLLM deliberately: the same request/except shape exists in
several providers, and the first version of this patch landed in GeminiLLM
instead. The tests caught it, since the fix was "applied" and three of them
were still red.

Closes #369.

fix(skills): the skill in your project must be the one that runs (#412)

load_skills() built the registry with `{s.name: s for s in skills}`, where a
later entry overwrites an earlier one — and discover_skills() appends builtin
LAST. So on every contested name the bundled skill won, the exact opposite of
the priority loader.py's own docstring states: project > user > builtin.

A team adding .co/skills/commit/SKILL.md to customise the bundled `commit`
skill got the stock one, with no error and no warning. co ai builds its system
prompt from this registry, so the agent silently followed different
instructions than the ones in the repo.

Fixed with the `seen` set useful_plugins/skills.py already uses correctly for
the same job — dropping the shadowed duplicate at discovery rather than letting
the dict comprehension pick the loser.

The duplicate is now absent from discover_skills()' list too, not merely
outranked in the registry: anything reading that list directly would otherwise
still see both, with the wrong one last.

Closes #367.

fix(llm): a model starting with "o" is not automatically an OpenAI model (#414)

`startswith("o")` routed every unprefixed name beginning with that letter to
OpenAI. orca-2-13b, olmo-7b and openchat-3.5 are real open-model families, and
each produced an OpenAI 404 about a model nobody had asked OpenAI for — an
error describing the wrong problem, since the fault was the routing rather than
the model choice.

Replaced with an explicit family allowlist, matched by prefix so o1-mini still
infers from o1 and the registry needs no entry per variant.

One existing test changed rather than added to: test_infer_openai_from_o_prefix
asserted on "o99-preview", i.e. that any name starting with the letter o is an
OpenAI model. That is the behaviour this fixes, so it now asserts on a known
family instead, with the trade written down — a new family costs one line here,
and in exchange an unknown model is named as unknown.

Closes #379.

fix(tools): the schema must keep the constraints the function has (#416)

The schema is the only thing telling the model what a tool accepts, and it was
dropping three kinds of constraint the function actually enforces. The model
then sends a plausible value, the tool rejects it at runtime, and nothing in
the schema had said it would.

Literal["fast","slow"] fell through to a bare string, so "turbo" looked legal.
An Enum class did the same. Union[str, int] collapsed to the first arm, so int
was never a legal value as far as the model could tell.

Each now carries its values, and carries them with the right type: calling
Literal[1, 2] a string would make every valid value invalid on arrival. An Enum
publishes its VALUES rather than member names — the model has to send "fast",
not "FAST".

Optional[X] deliberately stays a plain X rather than becoming a one-branch
anyOf: a nullable X is still an X, and that shape already worked.

Closes #373.

keys: SLIP-0010 derivation, so the twelve words mean something outside our code (#415)

Identity generation is standards-compliant right up to the last step:

    seed_phrase = mnemo.generate(strength=128)   # BIP-39
    seed = mnemo.to_seed(seed_phrase)            # BIP-39
    signing_key = SigningKey(seed[:32])          # ours alone

That last line is a bare slice of the seed. It corresponds to no BIP, no SLIP and
no derivation path, so a ConnectOnion recovery phrase imported into Ledger,
Trezor, Phantom or Keplr never arrives at the same address on any path any of
them offers. No hardware wallet can hold an agent identity; the signing key
exists only as a file on disk, on every machine that runs the agent. That is #400.

This adds the piece that was missing — SLIP-0010, which is BIP-32 adapted to
Ed25519 and what Solana, Brave and Trezor's own SSH/GPG features use — plus
SLIP-0013 identity paths, where the name is the path.

Nothing is rewired yet. No address changes in this commit: it adds derive.py and
its tests and stops there, because switching identity over re-keys every agent
at once and that deserves to be reviewed on its own rather than smuggled in
beside a new HMAC loop.

Hardened-only is the property, not a limitation. SLIP-0010 offers no public
derivation on Ed25519, and we do not want one: non-hardened derivation has an
inverse, so one leaked child private key plus the public tree recovers the
parent and the parent generates everything else. Agent identities and SSH keys
live on servers, which get breached and snapshotted; under SLIP-0010 that
exposes one key. The watch-only we give up answers a question nobody here asks —
balances live in a Postgres row keyed by public key and need a signature to read.
So a non-hardened index raises instead of quietly deriving something else.

Verified rather than asserted:

- the published SLIP-0010 ed25519 vectors, both seeds, every level, pinned in the
  test file rather than recorded from this implementation
- cross-checked against Trezor's slip10 package: 20 derivations across both seeds
  and every path shape used here, byte-identical. Not added as a test dependency —
  installing a crypto library to test a 40-line one is its own risk — so the
  vectors are pinned instead
- the three SLIP-0013 example paths computed in #404's design note, before this
  code existed, reproduce exactly, including LinkedIn canonicalising to linkedin

2606 unit pass.

fix(tools): passing the class instead of an instance must fail at registration (#418)

MyTools.do_thing and MyTools().do_thing are both callable, so the wrong one is
easy to pass — and in Python 3 the first is a plain function, so
inspect.ismethod() cannot tell them apart. Schema generation stripped `self`,
the schema looked correct, and every call then failed with

    TypeError: do_thing() missing 1 required positional argument: 'self'

raised inside the agent loop: the symptom, described far from the line that
registered the tool.

__qualname__ can tell them apart — a method carries its owner ("Calculator.add")
while a plain function does not, and one defined in another scope carries
"<locals>". The error now names the correction rather than the symptom.

A plain function whose first parameter happens to be named `self` is unusual
but legal and must keep working; there is a test for that, because the obvious
implementation (match on the name) would have broken it.

Closes #375.

fix(tools): say when a parameter's schema type was guessed (#419)

`type_hints.get(param_name, str)` typed anything unannotated as a string,
silently. For `def add(a, b)` the model then correctly sent "2" and "3" per
that schema, and a + b evaluated to "23" — a wrong answer with no exception
anywhere, which is the kind of defect that survives for months because nothing
ever crashes.

Warned, not refused. The issue offered both, and the project's fail-fast
instinct says refuse — but refusing breaks every agent whose tools work today,
for a defect that is about visibility. Measured before choosing: 1 of 16
shipped tool functions has an unannotated parameter, so the blast radius is
users' own code, which we cannot see. The schema is unchanged; the developer is
now told which parameters it guessed and what goes wrong if the guess is wrong.

One warning listing all of them, rather than one per parameter buried in
startup output. `self` and `agent` are excluded — both are injected rather than
sent by the model, so neither is something anyone forgot to annotate.

Closes #374.

A YAML error in a policy names the file it is in (#422)

A typo in a trust policy stops the host, and it should — a config file the
agent cannot understand is not something to guess around. What was missing is
which file: PyYAML names the stream it is given, and a bare string is named
"<unicode string>", so an operator with their own policies and the built-in
ones got a line number with nothing to open.

parse_policy hands it a named stream instead. The error is still the parser's
own, uncaught, and now reads

  in ".co/trust/custom.md", line 3, column 29
      allow: [whitelisted, contact
                                  ^

Alternative considered and rejected: catching yaml.YAMLError and re-raising a
ValueError (#403). It turns a crash into a differently worded crash, costs a
try/except this codebase deliberately avoids, and produces a worse message —
the parser already quotes the offending line and points at the column.

fix(trust): a list entry matches the whole identifier, and ignores case (#421)

* fix(trust): a list entry matches the whole identifier, and ignores case

Two defects in one function, both failing open on the whitelist.

`trusted-*` was implemented as `line.replace('*', '') in agent_id` — a plain
substring test with no anchor. An admin whitelisting `trusted-*` to grant a
prefix also granted `un-trusted-hacker`; one blocklisting `spam*` also blocked
`no-spam-here-either`. `is_whitelisted()` is built on this, so the over-grant
is a real grant.

Comparison was case-sensitive. Addresses are generated lowercase, but an admin
pastes what a UI showed them, and `block("0xABCDEF…")` then blocked nobody
while reporting success — a silent no-op on the one command whose whole purpose
is to deny.

fnmatch.fnmatchcase against a lowered pair fixes both: `*` keeps meaning "any
run of characters" wherever it sits, the pattern is anchored to the whole
string, and `*` alone still matches everything.

Fixes #362
Fixes #363

* fix(trust): keep `*` the only metacharacter

Review of the first version: fnmatch also interprets `?` and `[seq]`, which
were literal in this file before. It breaks both ways and both fail open — a
blocklist entry `agent[1]` stops matching itself, and a `?` in a whitelist
line starts matching identifiers its author never wrote. That is the same
defect class this PR exists to fix.

Escape every part and join on `.*` instead, so the vocabulary is exactly what
the docstring promises.

fix(deploy): carry the config the author wrote, delete nothing the server owns (#417)

* fix(deploy): carry the config the author wrote, delete nothing the server owns

`_sync_code` excluded `.co/*` and re-included the files worth carrying. That
default — exclude unless remembered — lost `.co/skills/` in its first version
and `.co/dashboard.html` in its second, and was still dropping `host.yaml`,
`OO.md` and `commands/`.

`host.yaml` is the worst of the three. It carries the permission whitelist that
`load_permission_patterns()` merges over the template defaults, so a project
that tightened its permissions was looser in production than on the author's
laptop, and one that widened them stalled on a headless box waiting for an
approval nobody could give. It also carries `port`, which the deploy reads
locally to configure Caddy while the server falls back to 8000 — set `port:
9000` and Caddy proxies a port nothing listens on. Every step reports success.

Invert the default. Everything ships; `.co/` gets two carve-outs, both because
the server owns that data:

  P .co/**       nothing under .co/ is deleted on the server, so identity,
                 logs, admins.txt, provision.json and whatever a future version
                 writes there survive without being listed
  --exclude ...  identity and accumulated state are never sent, so a stale
                 local copy cannot overwrite the live one

Forgetting to carry config was invisible — the deploy succeeded and a different
agent ran. Forgetting to protect state is loud.

The three tests that failed here asserted the shape of the argv, which is how
this went unnoticed: the argv was exactly as asserted and the outcome was still
wrong. They now assert what lands on the server, run against a real rsync.

Fixes #392

* fix(deploy): a local copy must not overwrite what the server owns

Review of the first version: the protect rule stops `--delete`, but it does
not stop a *transfer*. Four files are generated on the server or written there
over ssh by the deploy itself, and each had a plausible local counterpart that
would silently replace it.

The two that matter decide who is in charge. `.co/address.json` is read by
get_self_address() to decide super-admin, and `.co/admins.txt" is who may
command the agent — and add_admin() writes it into the cwd's .co when run
locally, so a stale copy is easy to have. `provision.json` and
`requirements.sha256` are cheaper: a wrong one re-runs convergence or pip.

Co-authored-by: Aaron Xie <aaronplus1996@gmail.com>

keys: retire seed[:32] — identity is derived through SLIP-0010 (#423)

seed = mnemo.to_seed(seed_phrase)
    signing_key = SigningKey(seed[:32])   # ← no BIP, no SLIP, no path

BIP-39 right up to the last step, and then a bare slice of the seed. It matches
no standard, so those twelve words could only ever be restored by ConnectOnion
itself: no hardware wallet could hold an agent identity, and no wallet ecosystem
tooling — recovery flows, multisig, watch-only, a decade of operational practice
built on BIP-32 — applied to any of it (#400).

Identity now derives at the account's SLIP-0013 path, on the tree #415 added.
This is #404's "one switch, once", taken now because the user base makes
re-keying affordable today and will not later.

**Every address derived from a phrase moves.** That is the change, not a side
effect of it.

Existing installs keep their identity: load() reads .co/keys/agent.key, and that
file still holds whatever key wrote it. What breaks is the phrase saved beside
it, which now derives a different key — so `co auth recover` with those words
lands on a new, empty agent rather than the one you have been using.

Left silent, that is discovered on a new machine, at the moment the old one is
gone. So load() compares agent.key against recovery.txt and reports
legacy_derivation, and `co status` says it in words: the identity keeps working,
the phrase no longer restores it, back up agent.key.

The two tests #310 wrote to stop exactly this refactor happening by accident are
kept and inverted rather than deleted. They were right to exist — this is that
change made on purpose, so they now fail if the derivation moves again in the
other direction, and they record the pre-switch address for what it is.

`co keys --ssh` stays on its HKDF label for now, deliberately. Its public key is
in authorized_keys on every server already provisioned, so changing it locks you
out of machines you own — folding it into the tree is a migration (add the new
key, then retire the old), not a switch. Written down in the new doc rather than
left as an inconsistency someone has to rediscover.

docs/key-derivation.md covers the tree, why hardened-only is the property we
want rather than a limitation we tolerate, and what a pre-switch agent should do.

2652 unit + 366 cli e2e pass.

fix(llm): the same failure raises the same type whichever provider handled it (#424)

An auth rejection surfaced three different ways depending on the model prefix:
openai.AuthenticationError on gpt-*, anthropic.AuthenticationError on claude-*,
and a bare ValueError("Groq API Error: ...") on groq/* — which said nothing
about what had failed, so a caller could not tell a rate limit from a bad
argument. The only handler that worked everywhere was `except Exception`, which
also swallows bugs in our own code.

LLMProviderError is now the base of every provider failure, and the three
existing exceptions inherit it, so existing `except InsufficientCreditsError`
keeps working unchanged. LLMAuthenticationError and LLMRateLimitError join
them, and all thirteen provider call sites go through one _call_provider() on
the base class.

Three deliberate limits:

- an already-translated error passes through untouched, so OpenOnionLLM's
  402 -> InsufficientCreditsError is not reburied under a vaguer type
- an unmapped status is re-raised as itself; a 400 is a bad request, and
  inventing a category for it would make the shared types mean less
- the original is always chained as __cause__ — translating must not cost the
  traceback that says what actually happened

One existing test changed rather than added to: test_complete_api_error_raises_
value_error asserted the Groq ValueError, which is the behaviour this removes.
It now asserts the shared type, that the shared base catches it, and that
__cause__ is the original — with the reason recorded where the assertion was.

Closes #372.

fix(xray): trace() can print again (#425)

It filtered the session trace for type == 'tool_execution'. Nothing has ever
written that type — tool_executor writes 'tool_result' — so the filter always
matched nothing and trace() took the "No tool execution history" branch every
time, including when called from inside a tool with xray.previous_tools
proving the history was right there.

The field names moved with the type, so correcting only the filter would have
rendered `unknown()` and `0.00ms` on every row: a fix that looks like a fix.
All four are corrected — type, name, args, timing_ms — with the old names kept
as fallbacks so a trace captured by an older build still renders.

Each field has its own test for that reason. Asserting only "it no longer says
there is no history" would pass on the half-fixed version.

Closes #303.

fix(deploy): .env is a secret on --to, the way it already is on Cloud (#420)

* fix(deploy): .env is a secret on --to, the way it already is on Cloud

`co deploy` parses `.env`, uploads the pairs as secrets, and keeps the file out
of the tarball. `co deploy --to` had no notion of a secret at all — the string
`.env` did not appear in deploy_to_server.py. It rsynced as ordinary source and
worked by accident, because systemd sets WorkingDirectory and load_dotenv()
reads the cwd.

What travelled is the problem. `co init` copies the whole of ~/.co/keys.env
into a new project's .env, so a real project here carried GOOGLE_REFRESH_TOKEN
and MICROSOFT_REFRESH_TOKEN — long-lived credentials for the operator's
personal mailboxes — onto the server in plaintext, on every deploy. Documented
behaviour said the opposite: "Local-only files such as .env are skipped."

Three changes:

- rsync excludes .env and .env.*, so secrets stop shipping as source. Anything
  else a .gitignore was holding back still ships; that is a separate question.
- _sync_env() sends them over ssh to /etc/connectonion/<agent>.env, root-owned
  at 0600. Outside the rsync root on purpose: inside /srv/<agent>/ the next
  --delete would overwrite a key rotated on the server, so production could
  never hold its own credentials.
- the unit gains EnvironmentFile=-<path>, so the process gets them from systemd
  rather than from a file that happens to sit next to it. The `-` keeps a
  project with no .env from failing to boot.

_env_for_server() also rewrites AGENT_CONFIG_PATH, which co init writes as an
absolute path to the author's own ~/.co. Shipped verbatim it names a directory
that cannot exist on Linux, and gmail.py, outlook.py, gdrive.py and
google_calendar.py all build their keys.env path from it. Cloud has done this
rewrite since it shipped; --to had not.

PROVISION_SCHEMA goes to 3 so existing servers pick up the new unit.

Fixes #393

* fix(deploy): a .env value must never become shell syntax

Review of the first version: the env file was sent in a heredoc, so a value
that happened to equal the delimiter would close it early and hand the rest of
the file to the shell — running under sudo, from input the deploy does not
control.

Send base64 and decode on the server, so no value is ever parsed as syntax.
A newline inside a value is a second problem: it ends the KEY=VALUE line and
turns the remainder into junk entries that systemd reads without complaint.
Skip those and say which, rather than write a file that looks fine.
