Co-authored-by: Aaron Xie <aaronplus1996@gmail.com>

docs: write the eleven guides the agent was already being offered (#426)

index.md is the menu the agent reads to decide what to load_guide(). Eleven rows
pointed at files that had never been written, so each was a tool call the agent
would make and that would fail, every time.

The issue proposed deleting those rows. Checking first showed why not: all
eleven name real, shipped code — bash, read_file, edit, write, glob, grep,
browser_tools, tool_approval, auto_compact, prefer_write_tool, ulw. Deleting the
rows would have turned "undocumented" into "undocumented and undiscoverable".

Each guide is written from the implementation — real signatures, real constants
(auto_compact's 90% threshold and five-message tail, grep's output modes, edit's
exactly-once matching rule) — and says what the thing is NOT for, since the
failure these prevent is reaching for the wrong tool rather than misusing the
right one.

The test is the part that lasts. Fixing today's eleven without it just resets
the clock until the next guide is listed before it is written. It also guards
itself: a menu that suddenly parses as empty would otherwise make the check pass
by having nothing to check.

Closes #297.

fix(browser): a curved path that is sometimes straight, and a test that measured it wrongly (#430)

Measured before touching anything: 134 failures in 20,000 paths, 0.67%. CI runs
eight jobs, so roughly one job in nineteen runs went red — which matches being
bitten twice in one day.

Two independent causes, and fixing either alone still leaves it flaky.

_control_points drew each offset from uniform(-0.22, 0.22), so both control
points could land near zero and the "curved" path came out ruler-straight. That
is a real defect in a module whose entire job is to not look like a machine —
it produced the exact tell-tale it exists to avoid, 0.7% of the time. The
offset now has a floor and a separately chosen side.

That left 61 failures, so the assumption was incomplete. The worst remaining
path had its first and last sampled points 3.9px apart: move() starts from a
random offset, ~3.4% of paths are under 50px end to end, and on that scale a
perfectly good bow is well under one pixel. The assertion's absolute `> 1` was
measuring curvature in units that do not survive a change of scale.

Relative to the chord instead: 61 failures becomes 0 over the same 20,000
paths. The message now carries both numbers, so a future red says what it saw
rather than needing this analysis repeated.

Closes #287.

release: 1.5.5 (#431)

Patch, not 1.6.0. The minor is reserved for the version people are meant to sit
on, and this is not it yet — the SLIP-0010 identity switch has not been
exercised end to end against a real server since it landed, and there are open
bugs. Features stabilise in patch releases; 1.6.0 gets cut once this has been
run rather than merged.

The one thing a reader needs from this release: a recovery phrase now derives a
different address than it used to. Existing installs are unaffected — they load
.co/keys/agent.key — but recovering from the phrase lands somewhere else, and
co status says so on any identity created before the switch.

fix(deploy): a server that stops answering is not a crash (#432)

subprocess.run(timeout=) raises TimeoutExpired and nothing caught it, so a hung
resolver or a box that went quiet mid-deploy printed a Python traceback. That
tells the operator we crashed, when what happened is their server did not
answer — two problems with completely different next steps.

Both _ssh helpers are fixed. deploy_to_server's alone would have left
`co server check` still crashing on the same condition, which is the command
someone runs precisely because the server is not responding.

Returned as a failed CompletedProcess rather than raised. Every caller already
treats a non-zero return as a failed step and reports it with the server name;
a new exception type would be a second shape of failure for one condition, to
be handled again at each call site. returncode 124 is the timeout convention,
so it stays distinguishable from a command that ran and failed — an exit code
alone cannot tell "the box said no" from "the box said nothing".

Tests inject TimeoutExpired directly, so none of them waits for a timeout.

Closes #399.

fix(skills): tell the agent to call skill(), instead of mentioning that it can (#433)

The injected list ended with "User can type /skill-name or you can call the
skill() tool" — a description of a capability, not an instruction. Asked in a
skill's own trigger words, the agent ran glob, then glob again, then find:
hunting for a file it could never see, because skills live under dot
directories.

It is now told that a matching description means call skill() first, before
planning and before touching files, and told explicitly that file search will
not find them and the list is the whole set.

Each entry carries its scope, and project skills are listed first. With dozens
installed — 121 on the machine where this was found — order is the signal that
breaks a tie, and the skill living in this repository is the one meant to win.

A test pins that descriptions survive: the description is what the agent
matches the user's words against, so trimming it to save tokens would remove
the trigger and reintroduce exactly this bug.

Closes #324.

fix(session): a system reminder is context about the turn, not something the user said (#440)

Two sites put reminder text into messages where nothing could tell it apart
from typed input, so the raw tags rendered as chat bubbles.

The rule is now structural. An injected reminder carries internal=True and the
renderer skips on that field, never on content. #144 proposed stripping the
tags instead; it cannot tell a system tag from one the user typed, so someone
asking "why does <system-reminder> show up in my chat?" got their own words
silently rewritten.

The bubble is suppressed; the TURN is not. user_count drives the turn index, so
skipping the increment drops every tool call that turn made from the
transcript — the regression #144's first cut shipped. There is a test for it.

agent.py was worse than the issue described: the notice was concatenated onto
`prompt`, and that one string becomes the user message, the stored user_prompt
AND the user_input trace entry. One assignment put the tags in the chat bubble,
in xray, and in the transcript. It is now its own message, and all three are
clean.

Two existing tests asserted the old shape — their comments said "system reminder
was appended to prompt". Rewritten to assert what they were actually protecting,
which is that the model still learns about the file, plus the new requirement
that the user's own message stays untouched. Strictly stronger than before.

internal messages keep role=user on purpose: the model must read them. Only the
UI skips them.

Closes #308.

fix(trust): a decision says what it decided, and to whom (#439)

The log recorded every deny twice and no allow at all, so "the log did not
grow" meant either allowed or never asked — the two states an operator
debugging a silent client has to separate. Diagnosing one such case took an
hour against a file nobody thinks to open.

Three changes, all to what gets written:

- allow paths log which condition matched (admin / whitelisted / contact),
  and onboarding logs that the client was promoted to contact
- client_id is printed whole. The next thing an operator does with it is
  paste it into admins.txt, and a 20-character prefix cannot be pasted —
  one that reads like a complete short id even less so
- the config dict is no longer dumped. It carries the agent's invite codes,
  at warning level, on every request

Tests assert on decision lines specifically: matching the whole captured
text passes on the config echo, which contains "allow" and "whitelisted"
whatever the outcome.

fix(deploy): the service runs as the user the server says we are (#443)

`co server add --ssh` takes either `user@host` or a Host alias from
~/.ssh/config. The unit's account was derived with `target.split("@")[0]`,
which only reads the first form — an alias has no "@", so the alias itself
became the username and systemd refused the unit:

  naturewill.service: Failed to determine user credentials: No such process
  Main process exited, code=exited, status=217/USER

Every deploy stage reported success first, and Restart=always turned it
into a crash loop. An alias whose Host block sets `User` cannot be read off
the target string at any rate.

Ask the server: `id -un`. Resolved once per deploy and passed down, so the
"unchanged unit costs one ssh read" property still holds. The same broken
expression in the chown fix-up is gone too — it was naming a user that does
not exist, failing quietly, and only doing no harm because rsync's ownership
happened to be right already.

Verified on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 GCE instance registered by alias: before,
217/USER crash loop; after, active with NRestarts=0 and User=changxing.

feat(deploy): a deployed agent's identity is derived, not minted on the machine (#448)

An agent minted its own key on first boot, so its address was unknowable before
the deploy and unrecoverable after the disk was gone — #306's failure mode moved
up a level, from 'changes every deploy' to 'changes every machine', which is
rarer and therefore discovered during an outage.

The derivation tree (#415) already had what this needs: the name is the path, so
agent://<name> always resolves to the same key.

  co keys --agent customer-bot     the address it will have, before it exists
  co deploy --to prod              seeds that key when the server has none

Never overwrites. An agent that already holds a key — from --own-identity, or
from an older deploy that let it mint one — keeps it, because overwriting an
identity is not something a deploy may do.

--own-identity opts out, for an agent being handed to someone else: an identity
its author can derive is an identity its author holds, whatever they intend.

Closes #396.

fix(deploy): a second agent on the same server gets its own port (#452)

co deploy --to always bound 8000, so a second agent on a machine that already
ran one died on 'address already in use'. Restart=always then kept it flapping,
which means systemctl is-active answers 'active' and the deploy reports success
for an agent that has never served a request — the operator finds out by reading
the journal of a service they have no reason to suspect.

A server can obviously host more than one agent: /srv/<agent>/ is per-agent and
so is the unit. Only the port was not.

The choice is made on the server, where the answer lives, and recorded in
.co/port so a redeploy keeps it — the Caddyfile points at that number, and a
port that moved would leave the hostname proxying to nothing. A port the project
asked for explicitly is honoured; that is the operator's own arrangement.

host() reads AGENT_PORT when neither code nor host.yaml names one, so nothing in
the author's agent.py has to know what else runs on that box.

Closes #450.

fix(deploy): a second agent no longer takes the first one's hostname (#453)

The Caddyfile held exactly one block and was replaced wholesale, so deploying a
second agent to a machine silently took the first one's name. The first agent
kept running — on its own port since #452 — and was unreachable by the name it
had been published under, with nothing said about it.

The file now holds one block per agent, tagged with a marker comment so a
redeploy replaces its own and leaves the others, including anything the operator
wrote by hand. Blocks are keyed by agent rather than by hostname: a name that
changed hands would otherwise leave two blocks claiming it and Caddy serving
whichever it read last.

A hostname keeps its owner. A second agent asking for a name that is taken is
told so — it is deployed, running and reachable over ssh, it simply has no
public name, because a server has one. That is the honest half of #309; giving
each agent a name of its own needs a DNS record per agent, which is a backend
capability the CLI does not have.

fix(server): a server you were charged for ends up in the registry (#454)

co server new read servers.yaml, spent a minute creating a machine, and wrote
the file back — so anything that registered during that minute was overwritten.
Reproduced directly: three concurrent registrations, one survivor.

The operator is charged either way, and the entry that vanishes is the one
nothing points at. co server check answers 'No server named …' for a machine
that exists, is billing, and was created by the command that just printed
✓ ready and suggested running it.

Every read-modify-write now goes through _update(), which takes an exclusive
lock and reads inside it, so a slow write picks up whatever landed while it was
waiting rather than replacing it. Writes go through a temporary file and a
rename: write_text truncates first, so a process killed mid-write left a file
that parses as an empty registry — every server forgotten at once.

The issue reported this with no other co process running. On this machine there
usually is one: several sessions drive co concurrently, which is the normal case
here rather than an exotic one.

Closes #445.

feat(server): co server fix-key — a machine that will not take your key is recoverable (#455)

The wait on a new server tells the truth when it times out: the machine exists
and is charged for. But it then said 'try co server check in a minute', and
co server check only re-probes — nothing in the product could change the
outcome. The operator was left with a $360 machine, a ✓ ready banner and no way
in except destroy and pay again.

co server fix-key <name> reinstalls the derived key through the server API
(openonion/oo-api#69), drops the stale host key for the address first — a
provider that handed the address back means the host key changed, and that is
refused before authentication is even attempted — and waits for the machine to
take it.

The timeout message now names that command instead of suggesting a wait with
nothing behind it.

Part of #449.

fix: a project is not tied to the machine that made it (#456)

AGENT_CONFIG_PATH was written as an absolute path — /Users/changxing/.co — into
the global keys.env, and co create copies that whole file into every new
project's .env. Deploy the project, clone it, or hand it to a colleague and the
variable names a home directory that does not exist there. Six tools build their
keys.env path from it, and every one then looks for credentials somewhere they
can never be.

Nothing writes it now. Every reader already defaults to ~/.co on the machine it
is running on — gmail, outlook, gdrive, synology and both calendars spell the
identical fallback — so the line only ever did harm.

Three write sites, and the one that mattered was not in the issue: co auth puts
it in the global keys.env, which is where co create picks it up. Removing only
the two in create.py and init.py left new projects carrying it anyway, which the
first real check caught.

co deploy --to still sets it in the unit's environment, where it describes the
machine it is on rather than the one that made the file.

Closes #438.

fix(co-ai): an agent is named by its project, not by its template (#446)

create_agent() passed name="oo" literally. co-ai is the only template, so
every agent anyone deploys announced itself as "oo" — three of them in one
client list during a real deployment, one of which was the one with the bug.

The author had already written the name they chose. `.co/host.yaml` opens
with it, in a field called `name`, and nothing read it.

agent_name(co_dir) reads it, falling back to "oo" when there is no
host.yaml, no name in it, or it does not parse. A name is not worth failing
a startup over, and a broken host.yaml is reported for what it is elsewhere
(#381 / #422).

Closes #436.

fix(host): an agent answers to the name you gave it (#457)

host.yaml's name: never reached the network. Metadata took the Agent object's
own name, and the co-ai template hardcodes name="oo" — so every agent built
from it introduced itself as 'oo' over /info, in the relay's directory and in
the ANNOUNCE profile, whatever the operator had called their project.

The name was already being read: load_host_config merges the whole file, so
config['name'] was sitting there unused. host() now passes it, and it wins over
the Agent's own. A library user who never wrote a host.yaml keeps exactly what
they had.

Closes #436.

fix(server): co server new declines instead of crashing without a terminal (#447)

$ co server new my-box < /dev/null
    OSError: [Errno 22] Invalid argument

questionary registers stdin with the asyncio selector, which fails on a
descriptor that cannot be polled. On the one command that spends money —
twelve months charged up front — a bare traceback also leaves the reader
unable to tell whether the charge went through, and stops CI, provisioning
scripts and any agent driving the CLI from calling it at all, even to be
told it needs --yes.

Check for a tty before prompting and say the two things that matter: what
it would cost, and that --yes is how to proceed.

    Cannot confirm: stdin is not a terminal.
      $360.00 would be charged now. Re-run with --yes to confirm without
      being asked.
    Nothing was created or charged.

Closes #437.

fix(relay): the heartbeat never sends a frame it cannot sign (#459)

The fallback re-stamped the original ANNOUNCE and sent it again. Two faults
stacked, and either alone is fatal:

The relay verifies the signature over every field, so changing the timestamp
invalidates it — the frame is rejected every time, as 'Invalid signature'.

And the value written was asyncio.get_event_loop().time(), a monotonic clock.
Measured here it sits 1785034255 seconds from epoch, against a 300-second
freshness window.

Re-signing is not possible in that branch: it exists precisely because addr_data
— and with it the private key — is absent. So nothing is sent, and the operator
is told the registration will lapse rather than being left with an agent that
reads as online and is not.

tests/unit/test_relay.py asserted the broken send as the contract: it passed no
addr_data and then required an ANNOUNCE anyway. It now asserts the opposite,
with the reason.

Closes #429.

keys: derive a per-server SSH key from the tree, beside the old one (#428)

Step 1 of #427 — the add half of add-verify-backfill-retire.

derive_ssh_key(phrase, host=...) now comes off the SLIP-0010 tree at the
SLIP-0013 path for ssh://<user>@<host>, which is what trezor-agent derives.
Without a host it is unchanged: the HKDF label, one key for every server.

Both, on purpose. The old key's public line is in authorized_keys on every
machine provisioned to date and it is the way back into them, so it stays
derivable until they are backfilled. Retiring it is 1.6 (#427 step 4).

Per-server buys what a single key cannot: a snapshot of one box no longer
yields the key that opens the others, and rotation is bumping the URI's index
rather than changing the recovery phrase and re-keying everything at once.

Nothing is wired into provisioning yet, and two findings are why.

An address is not available when the key is needed. `co server new` derives the
public line *before* the machine exists, so there is no IP and no hostname to
derive from. The durable identifier is the server's name, which the operator
chooses up front and which survives the IP changing under it — so the URI
should be ssh://<user>@<name>, not the address. Worth deciding explicitly
rather than discovering after keys are installed under one and looked up under
the other.

And the provisioning API takes one key: `ssh_public_key: str`, validated with
startswith("ssh-"). GCE's ssh-keys metadata does accept several newline-
separated entries, so two lines would pass that check and work — accidentally.
Installing both keys should be an API that says it takes several, not a field
documented as "the line co keys --ssh prints" carrying two.

Tests pin both derivations, including that the legacy line has not moved —
which is the assertion that stands between us and a locked-out server.

2722 unit pass.

fix(deploy): a released fix reaches the agent on the next deploy (#462)

connectonion in requirements.txt is an unpinned line that never changes, so the
hash deciding whether to install never changed either. A server kept whatever
version it was first deployed with, forever: 1.5.6 shipped the fix for every
agent calling itself 'oo', and redeploying from a 1.5.6 laptop left 1.5.5
running on the box.

Two halves, and either alone leaves it broken.

The stamp now carries the CLI's own version, so upgrading the CLI and
redeploying — which is what an operator does to ship a fix — reinstalls. A
code-only change with the same CLI still skips, so it still takes seconds.

And pip is told to upgrade. Measured against a real venv: one on 1.5.4 with
connectonion unpinned stayed on 1.5.4 through 'pip install -r' and moved to
1.5.6 only with -U. Without that flag the reinstall this function just decided
to do would change nothing.

Closes #460.

Install and offer the per-server SSH key (#427, step 1) (#464)

#428 made the key derivable. This installs it and starts using it, without
retiring the one it replaces.

Every server provisioned to date carries the old shared key and nothing else,
and that key is the way back into a machine we own. So this is a migration
rather than a switch:

- a deploy installs BOTH public lines, which makes every deploy the backfill —
  an existing server gets the new line appended, with the operator running
  nothing
- `_identity()` takes the server and offers both keys, per-server first. ssh
  stops at the first that works, so a box holding either is reachable
- the key is derived from the server NAME, not its address. The address does
  not exist yet at the moment the key must be chosen: it is sent in the request
  that creates the machine, and GCE only answers with an IP afterwards

Verified against a real sshd, not only in tests: the per-server key was denied
before installation, accepted after it, and the box stayed reachable by the old
key throughout.

fix(deploy): the stamp follows what was installed, not what was asked for (#466)

Follow-up to #462, which fixed the two faults it named. This is the third,
visible only once those are gone.

A deploy run minutes after 1.5.7 was published put 1.5.6 on the server. `-U`
asks the index for "newest", and newest was still the previous release at
that moment — a race with our own publish, not something the deploy can
prevent. The same server took 1.5.7 when asked for it by name a minute
later, so the resolver could see it; it just had not yet.

What makes that permanent is the stamp. It is keyed on the CLI's version and
written whenever the install exits 0, so it recorded "current for 1.5.7"
while 1.5.6 was on disk. Every later deploy matched it and skipped the
install. A transient resolution problem became a durable one, silently —
the same shape as the bug it follows: a record of intent where only a record
of outcome is safe.

Two changes:

- the runtime is installed by name and version, connectonion==<this CLI's>.
  A pin is the only form that makes "the server runs the version that
  deployed to it" true rather than likely, and it fixes the reverse skew too
  — an older CLI writing a unit that a newer runtime reads.
- the stamp goes last, after the pin. `set -e` was already there, so a
  version that cannot be installed now fails the step and leaves the stamp
  alone, and the next deploy tries again.

Verified: server put back to 1.5.5, stamp cleared, deployed from a patched
1.5.7 CLI — server came back on exactly 1.5.7, NRestarts=0, agent answering
to naturewill.

Closes #465.

test(deploy): the pin test asserts the real version, not one it hardcoded (#504)

It patched `dts.__version__` and asserted `connectonion==1.5.7`. The patch
never took effect — `_install_deps_if_changed` imports `__version__` inside
the function body, so a module attribute is not what it reads. The test
passed anyway, because the machine writing it was on 1.5.7 and the two
numbers happened to agree.

Where that surfaced is the worst place it could: the 1.5.8 release PR, whose
whole job is to bump the version. All four test jobs failed on a test that
had been green locally minutes earlier.

Now it reads connectonion.__version__ and asserts against that, so it tracks
whatever the tree says. Checked by setting the version to 1.5.8 and running
again — still green, which is the property the old test only appeared to
have.

docs(dashboard): a media query in a Home page measures the pane (#509)

The page renders inside its own iframe, so a media query inside it evaluates
against that frame's viewport — `@media (max-width: 560px)` already means "when
the Home pane is narrower than 560px", which is the question an author wanted to
ask. The isolation that locks the page down hands you a container query for free,
and nothing said so.

Measured, not assumed: with the pane at 320px the frame reports innerWidth 319
and the query matches; dragged to 900px it reports 899 and it does not.

It matters more now that the pane is resizable (oo-chat#39): one dashboard has to
hold up across 320–900px rather than at the two or three widths the client used to
pick. A four-column table needs roughly 500px — below that the column the table
exists for sits off the right edge behind a scrollbar, which is where the
naturewill contract dashboard was showing "¥4,500,0" until it got a stacked form.

Written in three places because three different readers hit it: the starter's own
CSS comment, the docs page, and the dashboard skill — the last one matters most,
since the author is usually a model that assumes media queries track the window.

Support async tool functions (#184 by @sanmaxdev, rebased onto main) (#512)

* feat: support async tool functions in tool executor

Detect coroutine functions with inspect.iscoroutinefunction and run
them via a helper that handles both bare and nested event loops.
Sync tools are unaffected. Closes #125.

* fix: preserve async tool loop affinity

* fix(tools): avoid deadlock when an async tool drives another tool execution

A nested execute_single_tool call from inside an async tool lands on the
shared loop's own thread. Submitting back to that single-threaded loop
while it is blocked waiting on the outer call hangs forever. Run the
nested coroutine on its own throwaway loop instead.

Reachable via the sub-agent pattern: an async tool calls agent.input(),
and the sub-agent runs its own async tool.

feat(host): an agent keeps its own schedule (#524)

An agent could not do anything on its own time. The obvious answer — the
operating system's scheduler — is three implementations (systemd, launchd,
Task Scheduler) of which two are ones nobody on the team runs daily, so a
capability built there works on the deploy target and nowhere else, and every
project writes its own.

The agent is already a long-lived process on all three platforms, so the clock
lives in it. One implementation.

`.co/schedule.yaml` is authored and travels with the project:

    - every: 15m
      run: "/contract-ledger check for new contracts"
    - at: "Mon 09:00"
      tz: Asia/Shanghai
      run: "/contract-ledger weekly summary"

`.co/schedule-state.json` is the server's own and is never deployed over, so
editing the schedule locally cannot reset what has already run, and a redeploy
cannot re-fire a job that fired an hour ago.

Three things the OS gave for free, given back:

- **Catch-up.** A run missed while the process was down fires on the next
  tick, once — three days of downtime is one catch-up run, not seventy-two.
- **Not blocking.** A turn takes as long as it takes; four minutes is normal.
  It runs in a thread, so the heartbeat continues and the agent stays
  reachable throughout.
- **Not running twice.** The state write holds an OS lock, POSIX flock and
  Windows msvcrt, the same shape cli/browser_agent/transport.py already uses.
  A scheduler that imports fcntl at module level does not import on Windows.

Runs go through `input_handler`, the same path as POST /input, so a scheduled
run lands in .co/session_results.jsonl beside the interactive ones with the
same fields. The state file records only the session_id — the transcript, the
result and the duration are already there, and copying them would be a second
source of truth. Background work being the one kind nobody can inspect is how
#434 happened.

The tick is not conditional on the relay: an agent reachable only on localhost
still has recurring work, and tying its clock to whether it is announced would
make "it stopped running overnight" a networking question.

Closes #521.

feat(dashboard): Home says what the agent has been doing (#525)

* feat(dashboard): Home says what the agent has been doing

The page showed a name, an address and a list of skills — everything an agent
*is*, and nothing about whether it had run today, whether the last run worked,
or what it is going to do next. All of it was already on disk beside the file
that renders the page, and none of it was read.

Two sections, both absent when there is nothing to put in them:

**Scheduled** — what #524 runs on its own, when it last ran and how that went.
Configured-but-never-fired is the state worth seeing most: it is
indistinguishable from broken until the page says otherwise.

**Recent** — the last five turns, newest first, with how long each took. The
log is append-only and a session appears twice, once as running and again as
done; the later line wins, or every finished run would be reported as still in
flight. A turn that died mid-way stays `running` forever, which makes it a free
stuck-detector — but only if something looks, and until now nothing did.

An agent with no schedule and no history renders exactly what it rendered
before. A box that is empty on every fresh agent is worse than no box: it is
the first thing a new user sees and it says nothing.

Durations are written in the unit a reader can hold. A full extraction pass is
four minutes, and "243.0s" makes you do the division to find that out.

Reads the schedule through the schedule module rather than reparsing the file,
so the page and the scheduler cannot disagree about what an entry means. A torn
line, an unreadable state file or a malformed schedule costs that section, never
the page.

Closes #522.

* perf(dashboard): five rows cost five rows, not the whole history

Found reviewing the section this PR adds, against the deployed agent rather
than a fixture. Fourteen turns had already produced a 322 KB log — each record
embeds the turn's whole message list, 23 KB on average and 85 KB at the top
end — and recent_runs() read all of it, parsed every line, to render five.

The snapshot is rebuilt on connect and after every run, so that was a per-turn
cost on an append-only file nothing trims. A year of hourly scheduled work,
which #524 has just made easy, is roughly 400 MB read and parsed on every
message. Nothing about it looks like a bug; the agent just gets slower to
answer, in a path nobody associates with chatting.

Now it walks backwards from the end, bounded by the answer instead of the
history. On a 44 MB log: 190.9 ms → 1.1 ms.

The chunk size is a starting point rather than a window — one record can be
larger than it — so the walk continues until enough lines are found or the file
is exhausted. Reading newest-first also removes a subtlety: a session appears
twice, running then done, and from this end the later line is simply the one
seen first.

Closes #526.

fix(dashboard): Recent does not say the same sentence three times (#529)

A schedule entry's prompt is one fixed sentence sent verbatim on every firing,
and Recent rendered the prompt. On the deployed agent that meant three
indistinguishable rows plus a fourth copy of the same string one section above:

    SCHEDULED
      /contract-ledger 检查云盘里有没有新合同。有新增…     done · just now
    RECENT
      /contract-ledger 检查云盘里有没有新合同。有…    42.8s · 7m ago
      /contract-ledger 检查云盘里有没有新合同。…     2m 35s · 23m ago
      /contract-ledger 检查云盘里有没有新合同。有…    9m 2s · 38m ago

The more useful the schedule, the worse it got — and the rows that differ, the
typed ones, were the first pushed out of a five-row list.

Two changes, one code path:

A run whose prompt matches a schedule entry is labelled with that entry's
name, so an entry can be called "检查新合同" while its instruction stays a
paragraph. Both sections use the name; Entry.name already falls back to the
run text when none is given, so nothing changes for entries without one.

Consecutive firings of one entry fold into a row with a count. Only
consecutive: a typed turn between two firings keeps them apart, because it did
happen between them. The duration shown is the newest of the group.

    RECENT
      检查新合同 ×3                              42.8s · 11m ago

Found by rendering a real deployed agent's Home at the width it renders in,
not by a test — on a fixture with distinct prompts it read fine, and distinct
prompts are exactly what a scheduled agent does not have.

Closes #528.

fix(schedule): a schedule that will never fire says so (#532)

Four faults, one shape: the file is hand-written and deployed, and every way
of getting it wrong was silent. Found testing #524 against what a real file
produces rather than what it was built against — before 1.6.0 went out.

**A clock entry missed during downtime was skipped for good.** An agent down
through Monday did not run its weekly summary late; it did not run it at all,
and the next chance was a week away. Interval entries caught up, so the two
forms of one feature disagreed about the property #521 exists to preserve.
Due is now "the most recent scheduled moment has not been served", which fires
once for any number of missed occurrences.

A new entry is deliberately not caught up: last Monday happened before it
existed, so there is nothing to make up for. Writing that rule down resolved
two tests of mine that contradicted each other, both of which I had written.

**`every: 0m` parsed and busy-looped** — always due, so a full agent turn every
tick, forever, on a typo that looks like a working schedule and shows up as an
LLM bill.

**Two entries could share a name.** State is keyed by name, so each overwrote
the other's last_run and both ran half as often as written. Only reachable with
an explicit `name:`, which #529 has just made worth using.

**A malformed `at:` and an unknown timezone failed silently** — one never fires,
the other fires eight hours off. The timezone still falls back to UTC, because
refusing to run is worse; it just says so now.

All four are reported rather than swallowed: once at startup, and on Home,
where a dropped entry otherwise renders as nothing — which is also what a
schedule that is merely not due yet renders as.

Closes #531.

fix(dashboard): "done" claimed the work succeeded, and it does not know that (#536)

A scheduled run on a deployed agent answered:

    卡在哪一步: fetch.py (阶段一：遍历云盘目录)
    错误信息: lark-cli 未配置或授权无效 (not_configured)

That is a good failure report. It was recorded `done`, and Home rendered
`检查新合同  done · just now`. Three consecutive runs, all failing, all
displayed as a healthy job.

The turn did return, so `done` is accurate at the level the scheduler works
at — an agent that says "I could not reach the drive" returns exactly as
successfully as one that did the work. The framework cannot read the prose to
tell them apart. What it can stop doing is implying it can: `ran · 2m ago`
claims only what happened.

`failed` still says failed, because there the turn raised and the scheduler
genuinely knows.

Found by leaving the scheduler running unattended against a broken
dependency. The rest of #535 — a deadlock I reported from a single in-flight
snapshot — turned out not to exist; approval is skipped when there is no
client, and every scheduled run had completed. Corrected in a comment there.

fix(schedule): an entry does not start a second copy of itself (#538)

record_run only happens after the turn returns, so last_run is stale for the
whole duration of a run. An entry configured `every: 15m` whose work takes
twenty minutes is therefore due again at minute fifteen, while the first copy
is still working, and again at thirty.

Not only wasted compute. Two copies of the contract pipeline this was built
for download, extract and write to one shared table — racing each other into
the same rows, through an extraction cache both are writing into.

Measured on a deployed agent, five consecutive runs of one entry took 7m14s,
2m21s, 3m34s, 3m53s, 3m52s. None overlapped — but those are runs that failed
at stage one because a dependency was unconfigured. The work they were meant
to do is documented at four minutes for a full pass, longer for long
contracts, and the first run or a batch of twenty new files lands squarely on
fifteen.

The tick now keeps the names it has in flight and skips them, releasing in a
finally so a crash cannot leave an entry marked busy forever — that would be
worse than the overlap it prevents.

Skipping is said out loud rather than silently: an entry that overruns every
interval is a misconfiguration, and the schedule claiming fifteen minutes
while the truth is twenty-five is worth hearing about.

Closes #537.

fix(dashboard): an entry that is running right now says so (#540)

Rendered from a live deployed agent:

    SCHEDULED
      检查新合同 (every 15m)          ran · 23m ago
    RECENT
      检查新合同 ×2                  running · 3m ago

Fifteen-minute entry, last run twenty-three minutes ago. At a glance, eight
minutes late. It was not — a new run had started three minutes earlier and
was still going, which only Recent said.

Scheduled is the row someone reads to answer "is this healthy", and it was
silent about the run happening right now. Getting the truth meant reading two
sections and subtracting.

The state is not an edge case: `ran · Nm ago` where N exceeds the interval is
exactly what an entry looks like *while it works*, because record_run only
lands after the turn returns. The longer a run takes the longer its row
misreports it, and long runs are the ones worth watching. #538 makes it more
common still — a long run now legitimately holds its slot across ticks.

The scheduler already knew: #538's in-flight set is this fact. It is now a
module-level registry the page can read, rather than a closure variable.

The fallback is what the row is really for: an entry whose last run was long
ago *and* which is not running is genuinely stuck, and stays visible as
"ran · Nm ago" rather than being hidden behind an optimistic "running".

Closes #539.

fix(dashboard): a failed entry says why (#542)

* fix(dashboard): a failed entry says why

A deployed agent had been failing every fifteen minutes for an hour. Home:

    检查新合同 (every 15m)          failed · 5m ago

That was the whole of it. The cause took an ssh session to find:

    ❌ Insufficient ConnectOnion Credits
    Balance: $0.0018   Required: $0.0878

One line, entirely actionable, and the scheduler had already caught it —
record_run was called with status="failed" at that moment. It threw the
exception away and wrote it to the console instead, and on a deployed agent
nobody is reading the console. That is what deployed means.

The failures this row exists for are the ones nobody watched happen. A
failure you see you can diagnose from the log; a failure you find on Home
later is the one whose log line has scrolled past, or is on a machine you
have to ssh into. And session_id is null for these — the run died before a
session existed — so the page cannot even offer a transcript to click.

record_run now takes the reason, keeps it in the state file, and the row
renders its first line:

    检查新合同 (every 15m)   failed · 5m ago · Insufficient ConnectOnion Credits

First line and sixty characters: naming the failure is the job, and the row
now tells the reader which log to open and roughly when.

The state entry is rebuilt rather than updated, so a later success drops a
previous failure's reason — a stale cause on a healthy entry would be worse
than none. State written by an older version has no reason key and still
renders.

Closes #541.

* fix(dashboard): take the first line that carries information

The first deployed failure this shipped against rendered as punctuation.
Providers format refusals as banners:

    ======================================================================
    ❌ Insufficient ConnectOnion Credits
    ======================================================================

Literally the first line is the separator, so the row said `failed · 5m ago ·
======================` — strictly worse than the `failed` it replaced,
because it looks like the reason is there.

Skip lines with no letters or digits. The test uses the real state file
written by the deployed agent, not an invented one.

fix(eval): scoring the work is not the work (#544)

* fix(eval): scoring the work is not the work

A deployed agent checking a drive for new contracts every fifteen minutes
failed every single time for over an hour:

    03:58:43  running 检查新合同
    03:58:48  检查新合同 failed:
    ❌ Insufficient ConnectOnion Credits
    Balance: $0.0018   Required: $0.0025

Five seconds in, before the first tool call. Two defects that only bite
together.

The account was out of credits, so the agent was pointed at Gemini directly
— same model, a funded key already on the box. It kept failing, identically,
because the call that fails is not the agent's: _generate_expected passed a
literal "co/gemini-3.6-flash" and ignored agent.model entirely. Configuring
a provider is rarely cosmetic; here the override existed precisely because
the co/ account was empty.

And that call runs @after_user_input, before any tool, so its failure took
the turn with it. What it produces is a one-to-two-sentence guess at what
success would look like, used to score the run afterwards. $0.0025 for a
sentence describing work that then never happened.

Both halves fixed: the scoring calls follow agent.model, and neither handler
can stop the run. Losing the expectation costs the score and nothing else,
which is why these two calls earn a catch that most do not.

evaluate_completion gets the same treatment. It is less dangerous — the work
is already done — but an exception there turns a run that succeeded into a
run that reports failure, the same lie in the other direction.

The Required figure was the tell. $0.0025 is far too small to be the turn,
which is the only reason this was found rather than concluded to be a
deployment that had not landed.

Closes #543.

* fix(system_reminder): acknowledging the request is not doing the request

Third instance of the same shape, and the one that was still killing the
deployed agent after the eval fix landed:

    04:14:27  /expected unavailable (…)          ← eval fix working
    04:14:31  检查新合同 failed: Insufficient Credits

detect_intent is @after_user_input, calls a hardcoded co/ model, and what it
produces is a sentence telling the user they were understood — "user feels
seen", per the comment above the io.send. Being unable to say "I understand"
is not a reason to refuse to do the work.

Follows agent.model and returns quietly on failure, same as eval. This one
is in the `co ai` default plugin list, which is why it fired in production.

fix(session): a turn that died with its process is not running (#547)

Home on a deployed agent, four of the five most recent rows:

    检查新合同 ×2                     running · 12m ago
    /contract-ledger 检查云盘…         running · 43m ago
    /contract-ledger 检查云盘…         running · 59m ago
    /contract-ledger 检查云盘…         running · 1h ago

None were running. The process had been restarted three times mid-turn.

A turn writes two records — one when it starts, one when it returns. A
process that dies between them never writes the second, and nothing on the
next boot contradicts the first. Worse, `running` is exempt from TTL in both
get() and list(), so these rows are not merely wrong until they age out;
they never age out.

Restarting mid-turn is not an edge case. It is what deploying does.

Startup is the one moment the answer is certain: this process has just begun
and owns no sessions, so anything still marked running belongs to a process
that is gone. One pass over the file the page already reads.

`interrupted`, not `failed`. The turn may well have finished its work before
the process went away, and for a scheduled entry that writes to a shared
ledger, "failed" invites a rerun that duplicates. `interrupted` says what is
known: it stopped, and how far it got is recorded nowhere.

Append-only, so the history stays intact, and idempotent, so a boot that
finds nothing to fix writes nothing. Once reconciled the record expires like
any other, which is what makes the phantoms finally clearable.

Closes #545.

fix(relay): a reconnect does not leak a socket (#549)

Deployed agent, twenty-five minutes and two disconnects after boot:

    ESTAB       0   0  …:58944  35.197.139.111:443  fd=6
    CLOSE-WAIT  25  0  …:52190  35.197.139.111:443  fd=8

CLOSE-WAIT means the relay sent FIN and this side never called close().
Twenty-five bytes sitting unread in a socket nobody will read again.

The supervisor opened the connection itself and dropped it on both exits —
serve_loop returning on a clean disconnect, and any exception mid-serve.
Neither closed it. The object became garbage, but websockets keeps internal
task references, and a file descriptor is not something to leave to the
collector.

Two disconnects in twenty-five minutes reaches the default 1024 limit in
about two to three weeks of uptime, and an agent meant to run for weeks is
exactly what this is. There is no symptom before the limit, and at the limit
the failure appears somewhere else entirely — a file that will not open —
with the relay nowhere in the message.

serve_once owns the socket from open to close, so both exits go through the
same finally. Errors still propagate: the backoff and its escalation after
five consecutive failures depend on seeing them. A close that itself fails
is suppressed, since the socket is already gone and the serve failure is the
one worth reporting.

The announce message is now built by callback rather than passed in. Moving
its construction before the connect was a regression: a bad signing key
would spin the supervisor without ever attempting a connection, reporting
the wrong failure — which the existing resilience test caught.

Also: say when it comes back. The log printed `Relay disconnected` and then
nothing on recovery, so a journal read as a permanent outage when the truth
was a three-second blip. Telling those apart meant inspecting sockets on the
box, which is how this leak was found at all.

Closes #548.

fix(session): a question nobody can answer is dead too, and a killed turn is not done (#554)

Found by reading a deployed agent nine hours after 1.5.11 landed:

    Counter({'done': 82, 'waiting_approval': 5, 'interrupted': 5})

interrupted: 5 is the reconcile working. waiting_approval: 5 is it being
incomplete.

`running` means a turn had work in flight; `waiting_approval` means a turn
stopped and asked. After a restart both are equally dead — the thread that
would receive the answer is gone — and only the first was closed out. It is
the worse of the two: an unfinished run merely looks unfinished, while a
session that asked renders as *waiting for you*, inviting a reader to answer
something no thread is listening for. The oldest on that agent was 52 hours
old, and three of the five had another 9–14 hours of TTL left to keep
claiming it.

The second defect only became reachable because of the first fix. Recent
branched on `running` and sent everything else to a duration — and a turn
that never finished has none, so it fell through to the word "done". Marking
those sessions `interrupted` in 1.5.11 meant a turn killed by a deploy began
rendering as one that completed. That is the lie #536 removed from the
Scheduled row, arriving through the other door.

Recent now has branches for both: "waiting on you" for a live question,
"interrupted" for a turn killed with its process.

Closes #553.

fix(session): a torn line costs itself, not the boot (#556)

>>> open('.co/session_results.jsonl','w').write('{"session_id": "a", "sta')
    >>> SessionStorage(path).reconcile_interrupted()
    JSONDecodeError

get(), list() and reconcile_interrupted() each called json.loads on every
line with nothing around it, so one malformed record raised out of all three.
reconcile_interrupted runs at startup — which makes a single torn line a
refusal to boot, not a display bug. That is new in 1.5.11, where reconcile
started running at startup.

The file is appended from more than one thread. A crash, a full disk, or an
interleaved write is all it takes.

This was already settled twice elsewhere. schedule.py, on its own state file:
"Refusing to boot over it costs the agent, so a truncated write or a hand
edit is not allowed to be fatal." And dashboard.py, reading this very file:
"a torn write must not cost the whole page." Same shape, two places that got
it right and one that did not.

One tolerant reader now backs all three: blank lines skipped, unparseable
records skipped, everything else kept — including the good records on either
side of the tear.

Closes #555.

fix(schedule): two writers no longer destroy each other's state (#560)

Twelve threads, 240 writes:

    FileNotFoundError: …/schedule-state.json.tmp -> …/schedule-state.json
    entries: 3 -> ['entry0', 'entry2', 'entry3']     # entry1 simply gone

Two defects that compound.

The lock was a single non-blocking attempt, and every caller treated a
refusal as permission to proceed — so under contention nobody held it and
every writer did its own read-modify-write of the whole file. Last writer
wins, and the entry another writer added in between is lost. That is not
cosmetic: last_run is what is_due reads, so an entry the scheduler forgets
about runs again.

And every writer used the same schedule-state.json.tmp. They overwrote each
other's file and raced to rename it: the first os.replace consumed it, the
second raised FileNotFoundError out of the scheduler's own tick.

The lock now retries briefly instead of giving up at the first refusal —
bounded, because blocking forever on a lock held by a process the OS never
noticed dying is worse than proceeding. Each writer gets its own temp name,
removed if the replace never happens, so a crash between write and rename
does not leave one temp file per incident in the directory the agent reads
at boot.

Not the common path: one process runs entries in sequence. It is the restart
path — a deploy starting while the old process finishes a turn — which is the
case the lock beside the file was there for, and the case where a lost
last_run reruns something that writes to a shared ledger.

Closes #559.

fix(trust): an invite code per agent, not one published in this repo (#563)

A stock `co init -t co-ai` + `co deploy` printed this on startup:

    Invite: OpenOnion

which is trust/policies/careful.md line 16, in this repository, on the public
internet. Verified end to end: a fresh browser context with no keys and no
prior session typed that word into the deployed agent's public chat URL and
was admitted in five seconds with a working composer.

It is not a read-only peek. `contact` is in the default allow list, so it is
a session — and the approval prompt does not know who is asking (#551), so
the stranger is offered "Trust bash for this session" and their answer counts.
A published constant therefore reached arbitrary commands on the operator's
machine.

The policy now declares `invite_code: [$CO_INVITE_CODE]`, resolved from the
environment. `.env` because that is already the secret channel: git ignores
it, `co deploy`'s rsync excludes it, and deploy delivers it separately as a
root-owned 0600 file that a later deploy will not overwrite.

An unset variable resolves to nothing — never to the placeholder text, never
to a default. That is the whole point. Falling back is how one constant
became every agent's password.

`co init` mints the code once and writes it to .env, and leaves it alone if
it is already there: regenerating would silently lock out everyone holding
the old one. The alphabet omits O/0 and I/1 because this gets typed by hand
on a phone.

Two paths needed it, and only one was obvious. evaluate_request goes through
fast_rules; the real door — ONBOARD_SUBMIT — calls TrustAgent.verify_invite,
which read the raw config. An existing test caught that the second one was
still open.

The test that asserted `verify_invite("new-user", "OpenOnion") is True` now
asserts the opposite, and says why.

Closes #561.

test(e2e): the multi-turn test now tests the system, and is proven to (#565)

Three versions of this test, and the first two could not see the bug they
existed to catch.

It began by asking the model to remember a number and asserting the number
came back. That is a model behaviour, not a system property. It had been red
for three releases because gemini-3.6-flash answers "I am an LLM and I do not
have memory of past conversations" to being asked to remember something — on
the FIRST turn, before any session round-trip exists. The red test pointed at
the session layer, which was working the whole time, and cost a full
investigation to clear.

The second version asserted on agent.current_session after two turns. It
passed — and kept passing with server-side restoration deliberately
sabotaged, because RemoteAgent accumulates history on the client. It was
testing the client's own bookkeeping.

This version runs turn one on one client and turn two on a fresh client that
knows only the session id. Any history it sees can only have come from the
server.

Proven, not assumed:

    both restoration paths sabotaged  → messages=2, red:
      "the first turn is missing — the server did not restore the session"
    restored                          → messages=4, green

"Both", because the investigation turned up something worth knowing: session
restoration has two independent paths — the merge into conn['session'] at
CONNECT, and input_handler's own storage.get. Either one alone carries the
history, which is why breaking one at a time left the test green and made it
look powerless. It is not; it needs both gone, which is the correct
sensitivity for a test of "the server remembers".

Relates to #564.

fix(host): the startup line says which door this is, and never the key (#567)

Three problems in one line, found reviewing #563 rather than by it failing.

Upgrading closed the door silently. An existing deployment on the default
careful policy, with no CO_INVITE_CODE in its .env, now refuses every invite
code — correct, since the old constant was a published password, but the
operator saw only that nobody could get in, with nothing connecting it to an
unset variable.

The line printed the code. That is stdout, which on a deployed agent is
journalctl: readable by anyone with the box, kept as long as logs are, and
copied into every pasted startup dump. A unique code per agent does not make
publishing it acceptable.

And with the placeholder it printed `Invite: $CO_INVITE_CODE`, which reads as
the code to anyone who has not seen the policy file.

Now one line for whichever of the three states holds, naming where the code
lives and never what it is:

    Invite: set — CO_INVITE_CODE in .env, not printed here
    Invite: set — in the trust policy, not printed here
    Invite: no one can onboard — CO_INVITE_CODE is not set. Add it to .env,
            or run `co init` to mint one.

The first draft of this said "share the code from .env" for every configured
agent, which is wrong for anyone whose code is a literal in trust.md and would
have sent them looking in a file that does not contain it. A declared but
unset variable is still mentioned when another code works, because whoever
holds that half of the door still cannot open it.

Closes #566.

fix(session): a paused turn remembers what it was (#569) Read off the deployed agent minutes after installing the release candidate: Recent interrupted · 13h ago interrupted · 13h ago interrupted · 17h ago Five rows, no labels — `` in the HTML. The operator learns that five things were interrupted and nothing about what. checkpoint() writes the record a turn leaves behind when it pauses for approval, and it hardcoded prompt="" — while holding a session dict that has carried user_prompt the whole time. prompt is exactly what Home renders as the row's label. created had the same shape of problem: it is what Recent turns into "13h ago", and stamping it when a turn *pauses* makes one that began this morning look like it began when it stopped. Now taken from the earlier record when there is one. Neither was visible before. These records used to sit as waiting_approval forever and nobody looked at them; reconciling them into interrupted put them on the page, where the missing label became obvious. Also restores the label collapse from #546. I closed that issue claiming it shipped with #542 — it did not. The _why() fallback existed only in a working branch and never reached the PR, so main still pasted a whole instruction paragraph into a one-line row for any scheduled run whose entry text had since changed. Closes #568.

perf(session): finding one session no longer parses the whole log (#571)

The live agent's .co/session_results.jsonl is 17 MB across 222 sessions after
thirteen hours. It is append-only and never shrinks.

get() parsed all of it, and so did checkpoint(), which calls get(). Measured
on a 4 MB log: ten checkpoints took 0.9 seconds. At 17 MB that is roughly
380ms each, growing for as long as the agent stays up.

Both callers are hot. input_handler calls get() on every turn to restore the
session; checkpoint() runs before every blocking operation — every approval,
every ask_user. And each record carries its full message list, so a Session
was being constructed from megabytes of history to find one session_id.

Self-inflicted in two steps. get() used to read backwards and stop at the
first match; #555 replaced that with a shared tolerant reader so a torn line
could not stop the agent booting — correct, and it made every lookup a full
forward parse. #568 then put a get() inside checkpoint(), moving the full
parse onto the pause path too. Neither showed up in tests, because a fixture
writes five sessions and the cost is invisible under a megabyte.

Now reads backwards in chunks and stops at the first matching record, keeping
the tolerance from #555 — a torn line is skipped, not fatal, and the test
pins that a tear near the end still leaves the good record readable.

    10 checkpoints:  0.9s → 0.007s
    50 gets:               0.022s

Pinned by counting json.loads calls rather than by timing, so the assertion
is deterministic rather than machine-dependent: finding the newest session
must parse about one record, not sixty.

Closes #570.

fix(schedule): a write that gave up on the lock says so (#572)

_lock retries for about a second and then returns None, and record_run
proceeds regardless. That is the deliberate choice — blocking forever on a
lock held by a process the OS never noticed dying is worse than proceeding —
but it was silent, and the consequence is not.

The write is a read-modify-write of the whole state file. Without the lock it
can drop another writer's entry, and a lost last_run makes the scheduler run
that entry a second time. On an agent whose schedule writes to a shared
ledger, that is a duplicate row someone has to find and explain.

Now it prints one line naming the entry. The duplicate run becomes findable
in the log instead of being inferred from the ledger weeks later.

Two tests: one that the warning appears when the lock is unavailable, and one
that a normal write stays quiet — a warning nobody sees is useless and one
everybody sees is noise.

Found reviewing #560, not by it failing.

fix(trust): one place decides how open a host is, and it is not the environment (#573)

The docs promised `CONNECTONION_ENV=development` sets trust to "open", and
shipped two functions implementing it — get_default_trust_level() and
get_default_trust() — that nothing ever called. host() reads
`config.get('trust', 'careful')` and always has. The promise was in five
places, including the prompt `co ai` reads, so the agent would confidently
teach a variable that does nothing.

#366 asks to wire it up. I think that is the wrong fix and this does the
opposite: the promise and the dead code are both gone.

An environment variable that can *widen* trust is a bad mechanism no matter
how carefully it is implemented. CONNECTONION_ENV=development is exactly the
kind of thing that sits in a shell profile for months, and the person running
`co host` on their laptop is not reading the trust docs at that moment. The
failure is silent and total: a host open to everyone, with a host.yaml that
says careful.

How open a host is now lives in one file the operator owns and can read back.
Different machines get different files; `co deploy` copies the one you mean.

Worth noting how this hid for so long: five unit tests covered
get_default_trust() in isolation and passed the entire time. A green test on a
function nothing invokes reads exactly like a working feature. The replacement
tests pin the *system* behaviour — trust does not change across six values of
CONNECTONION_ENV — plus one that fails if the deleted helpers come back.

3072 unit tests pass. Closes #366.

fix(trust): a whitelist belongs to one agent, not to the machine (#575)

* fix(trust): a whitelist belongs to one agent, not to the machine

admins.txt was moved out of ~/.co/ and beside the agent's own identity, because
one box hosting two agents meant making someone an admin of one made them an
admin of both. whitelist, contacts and blocklist were left on the old global
path — the same bug, in the file that grants.

is_whitelisted() is a real allow. Promoting an address while poking at a
throwaway agent promoted it on the production agent running on the same box,
and nothing in either agent's directory recorded that it happened. Four tests
put two agents in two directories and prove what one grants the other has never
heard of; all four were red.

Upgrading moves where these live, and nobody should learn that from a lockout.
The old entries are not read — reading them is the bug — so the read path says
once, per list, per process, where they went and which file to copy them into.

The test fixtures are the tell. Eight of them monkeypatched a module-level
CO_DIR to keep tests from seeing each other's lists, which is exactly the shape
of the defect: isolation required reaching into a process global. They now
chdir into an agent directory instead, which is also what a second agent on the
same machine does.

3078 unit tests pass. Closes #507.

* test(deploy): pin the WorkingDirectory the trust lists depend on

Scoping the lists to the agent means resolving them from the working
directory. On a deployed agent that only holds because the unit file says so —
verified against the live one, cwd is /srv/naturewill as intended.

Drop that line and every list resolves under /, quietly empty: the whitelist
stops granting, the blocklist stops blocking, and nothing anywhere says why.
It was one uncommented line in a unit template with no test on it.

* fix(cli): four empty lists and no agent are not the same thing

Now that the lists belong to one agent, running `co trust list` from the wrong
directory printed four "Empty" sections and a path. That reads as "my whitelist
was wiped" — the opposite of what happened, and exactly the ambiguity this
release is supposed to be removing.

It now says there is no agent here, names the directory it looked in, and stops.

fix(trust): the party being judged does not write the question (#576)

`careful` is the default policy. A stranger with no invite code and no payment
falls through the fast rules to `default: ask`, and the prompt that decided
their admission interpolated the whole request:

    - request: {request}

That text is composed by the party being judged. An authorization decision was
taking the subject's own testimony as evidence.

Seven tests, red before the fix, put four injections through the real path and
check that none of them reach the model — including one nested two levels deep
in the request dict, because whatever the transport puts there is still
caller-controlled.

The decision now gets only what this agent established for itself: the Ed25519
address, verified against the signature at the request boundary, and the level
held in its own files. Not because a model would probably see through the
trick — that is a defence whose strength cannot be reasoned about, sitting in
front of an agent that runs shell commands and writes files.

careful.md had to change with it. It told the model to approve if the "agent
responds appropriately to tests" and there are "no suspicious patterns", both
of which describe content it can no longer see. Asking for evidence you do not
provide is how a policy becomes a coin flip. It now says what is shown, why the
message is withheld, and that refusing costs the stranger one message — the
agent answers with how to onboard, and a code or a payment settles it without
the model.

3089 unit tests pass. Closes #508.

test: the release gate does not depend on four funded provider accounts (#578)

`make test-e2e` was `pytest -m e2e`, and tests/conftest.py auto-marks by
folder: everything under tests/e2e/ gets `e2e`, everything under
tests/e2e/real_api/ also gets `real_api`. So the gate pulled in 140 tests that
call Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and Codex for real.

Running it today:

    52 failed, 492 passed, 59 skipped in 427.53s

Every failure a 401 from a provider; none about our code. The system tests
underneath were green the whole time and nobody could see it.

There is a guard in conftest, and it is the wrong shape: real_api tests are
skipped only when *no* provider key is present at all. One key — here
OPENONION_API_KEY — and everything runs, including the tests needing the three
keys this machine does not have. All-or-nothing where the requirement is
per-provider.

Narrowing the gate to `e2e and not real_api`:

    445 passed, 18 skipped, 3229 deselected in 325.06s

The paid tests are not deleted, they are opt-in through `make test-real`. Four
tests cover the split, including one that reads the Makefile — the gate is only
as good as what it actually invokes, and the marker expression is the kind of
thing that gets widened back in a hurry.

A check that answers "is this laptop funded" instead of "is this release sound"
teaches people to read red as normal. That is not a state a long-term-support
release should ship in.

Part of #577; the per-provider skip is the rest and is filed there.

fix(approval): the approval dialog belongs to the operator (#579)

The host knows exactly who is on the socket — CONNECT is signed and the trust
layer classifies the caller before the session exists. That answer was computed
and dropped: approval.py had zero references to the requester, so the dialog
went to whoever was connected. A contact, meaning anyone who typed the invite
code, saw the owner's "Allow" button. An invite code carried command execution.

Now the requester's address and level ride from CONNECT to the approval point,
and only an admin is shown the prompt. Everyone else gets a refusal naming the
host.yaml entry the operator would have to add, which is something they can
paste into a message and ask for.

Three things this got wrong first, each caught by a test rather than by review:

The gate sat above the mode logic, so it refused `read_file` for a contact.
That gates access, not approval, and makes the agent useless to the people it
was shared with. It now sits at the one line that is about to prompt.

The level was read from the session dict. That dict round-trips through the
client, so claiming to be the operator would have been a matter of editing one
JSON field — a worse hole than the one being closed. It is recomputed from the
signed address every turn and overwrites whatever arrived.

And the gate compared against `get_level(...) == 'admin'`, which nothing can
ever produce: get_level returns stranger / contact / whitelist / blocked. Every
test passed because every test wrote `level: 'admin'` by hand — the tests
agreed with the implementation and both were wrong about the system. The owner
would have been refused as loudly as everyone else. Admin is admins.txt, a
separate question, and there is now a test that goes through the resolver the
host uses so agreeing with the implementation is not enough to pass it.

3104 unit tests pass. Closes #551.

fix(skills): a turn's permissions end where the turn began (#580)

Two faults in the same two functions.

_grant_skill_permissions wrote its snapshot into one slot, and a second skill
in the same turn overwrote it — with a state that already held the first
skill's grants. Restore then returned to "after skill A", so A's patterns were
permanent for the rest of the session. Skills reference other skills; two in a
turn is ordinary.

#371 proposes a stack. A stack is the answer if restore runs per skill, and it
does not: cleanup_scope is @on_complete and fires once, at the end of the turn.
The only snapshot worth having is the first, so the first write wins.

_restore_permissions replaced the whole permissions dict with the snapshot,
which discarded anything approved *during* the skill. The operator answered a
dialog with "trust this for the session", and it silently did not stick (#204).
User-sourced entries now survive the restore; skill-sourced ones still go.

Making the first write win removed an accidental safety net, which is the third
thing here. `on_complete` is not in a finally block:

    result = self._run_iteration_loop(...)
    ...
    self._invoke_events('on_complete')

A turn that raises — a rejected approval does exactly that — never restores and
leaves its snapshot behind. That used to be overwritten by whoever granted
next; with first-write-wins it would survive and send the following turn back
two turns. The snapshot now records which turn it describes, and one from an
older turn is replaced rather than trusted. A test covers it.

Three existing tests asserted the snapshot's internal shape and were updated.
Worth noting what they were worth: all three passed while permissions leaked
across nested skills, because they checked the structure rather than what a
turn leaves behind.

3111 unit tests pass. Closes #371 and #204.

fix(session): a restored session keeps what plugins put in it (#581)

Agent.input(session=…) rebuilt current_session from four keys — session_id,
messages, trace, turn — and dropped the rest. Plugins keep their state there,
so ULW lost mode and skip_tool_approval every turn and fell back to Safe: the
web client visibly stepped back after a turn or two, and over HTTP, where
mode_change does not exist, ULW never worked at all.

The same drop had silently disabled #579, merged two hours ago. The host writes
session['requester'], input() threw it away, and the approval gate saw every
requester as unknown — which is the branch that behaves as before. A contact
could still click Allow. The tests passed because they used a fake agent that
kept what it was given; the real one did not. Verified now against the real
Agent rather than a stand-in.

Keeping everything is not the fix on its own. merge_sessions picks the client's
session or the server's wholesale, so a client that wins the merge would hand
the agent its own skip_tool_approval: True and skip every approval check. So
input_handler strips a defined set of keys from whatever arrives and re-applies
them from what the server stored — mode, the ULW budget, permissions, approval
state, requester. The client carries them for continuity; it does not author
them.

Three tests cover that half: a bypass in the incoming session is dropped, a
permissions grant in the incoming session is dropped, and the server's own ULW
state is restored.

3117 unit tests pass. Closes #191.

fix(trace): the agent is plumbing, not an argument (#582)

Tools that declare `agent` got the live Agent injected by mutating the caller's
dict, and the trace entry holds that dict by reference:

    "args": tool_args              # by reference
    tool_args['agent'] = agent     # the trace now holds an Agent
    agent._record_trace(entry)     # forwarded over the socket
    finally:
        tool_args.pop('agent')     # after the window that mattered

In host mode the agent runs on its own thread while the forwarder drains and
encodes those entries, so the existing pop was a race, not a fix. Its own
comment says it exists to prevent "Non-JSON-serializable object: Agent"
warnings — the hazard was known and the mitigation was timing.

The agent now goes into a call-only copy. Nothing is put into tool_args, so
there is nothing to take out and no window to lose. It is not something the
model asked for and does not belong in the record of what was called.

Two things this got wrong on the way, both worth naming:

The first fake agent had no `_invoke_events`. The real path calls it between
recording the trace and injecting, so the fake raised, the except swallowed it,
and four of five tests passed having exercised nothing. Third time this session
a fake diverged from the real object and turned a test green.

And only the sync call site was updated. An async tool declaring `agent` would
have been called without it — a TypeError where the tool runs, in the path no
test covered. Both call sites now, both covered.

3124 unit tests pass. Closes #382.

test: the version cannot drift without a test saying so (#583)

A release updates the version in four places by hand and nothing checked them.
During 1.5.1 the docs site still said 1.4.0 — the whole 1.5.0 cycle advertised
a version two behind, and nobody noticed because nothing looked.

It had drifted again, further:

    pyproject.toml            1.5.11
    connectonion/__init__.py  1.5.11
    VERSIONING.md             1.5.10
    docs-site/lib/version.ts  1.5.5     ← what docs.connectonion.com served

Six releases, on the page where people decide whether to install. That file's
own header called it "Single source of truth", which is what stopped anyone
comparing it to the original; it is a copy, in another repo. Both are corrected
here and in wu-changxing/connectonion-docs-site#26.

#299 suggests deriving __version__ from installed distribution metadata to
remove one of the four. That is worse here, and measurably: in this checkout
the metadata says 1.5.10 while the source says 1.5.11, because the installed
dist lags the working tree. Deriving would make connectonion.__version__ report
the wrong number in exactly the setup developers use. Four literals that are
checked beat three that can lie.

The docs-site check finds the sibling repo through the git common dir, not
through REPO.parent. The first version used the parent, which in a worktree is
a scratch directory — so the check skipped silently in the setup the work
happens in, which is the same failure as the drift it exists to catch.

It skips when the sibling repo is absent, which includes CI. That is the honest
limit of a cross-repo check living in one repo: it catches drift locally and in
the release runbook, not on every push.

3127 unit tests pass. Closes #299.

fix(trust): an unreadable list is not an empty one (#585)

_check_list wrapped its read in `except Exception: return False`. For whitelist
and contacts that is the safe direction — an unreadable grant grants nothing.
For the blocklist it is fail-open: is_blocked() answers False and everyone on
the list is admitted.

Getting there is ordinary. An operator opens blocklist.txt in a Windows editor
and saves it as GBK, and the next read raises UnicodeDecodeError. Or a deploy
leaves it root-owned and the agent cannot read it. Either way the deny list
stops denying and nothing says so.

Same swallow, safe one way and dangerous the other, which is why it lasted: the
direction that matters is the one nobody tests.

load_admins swallowed the same way, and the cost went up in #579. The approval
dialog is admins-only now, so an admins.txt that cannot be read does not merely
lose a permission — every approval the owner attempts comes back "you are
stranger", naming the wrong reason, about a file nothing mentions.

Absent is still an answer and still returns False; a fresh project has no
blocklist and must start. Unreadable is a question this agent cannot answer, so
it names the file and stops — and for the encoding case says what to do about
it, since "not UTF-8" is not obvious when your editor did it silently.

3135 unit tests pass.

fix(auth): a trust list the agent cannot read still answers the client (#586)

#585 made an unreadable trust list raise instead of quietly answering "not
blocked". That was right — a blocklist that could not be read was admitting
everyone on it — and it moved the failure somewhere with no exit.

auth.py documents its contract as returning error strings and never raising,
and the WebSocket session loop documents the other half: "other exceptions
propagate out". So a GBK-saved blocklist.txt closed the socket with nothing
sent, and the client saw a connection that died and no reason — #434 arriving
by a new route, introduced by the fix for a different silent failure.

The auth boundary keeps its contract: refuse, name the file, and let the ERROR
frame carry it to whoever is holding the other end. Fail closed, and say why.
The SDK change in connectonion-react#8 is what makes that frame land as a
message instead of a timeout, so the two halves meet.

Checked the other two paths that reach these reads rather than assuming they
were fine: the scheduler already catches per-entry and records `failed` with
the reason (that is what produces the "<entry> failed:" lines in a live agent's
log), and the WS input thread stores the exception and the forwarder emits it
as ERROR. Both have exits. This one did not.

_sync_code chowns the deployed tree to the user the service runs as, and the

    PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '.co/logs/oo.log'

Then it discarded whether the chown worked. On a box where sudo wants a

`_mark_provisioned` is the third unchecked write and stays unchecked on

3145 unit tests pass.

`co init` in an empty directory wrote ~/.co/keys.env into the project's .env.

    GOOGLE_ACCESS_TOKEN      MICROSOFT_ACCESS_TOKEN
