   token and (now) its invite code. Written unconditionally: an unused
   .gitignore costs a few bytes, a missing one costs a published token.

Verified by running the real commands: co create writes .env with exactly
one code and a .gitignore beside it, the project starts, prints
"Invite: set — CO_INVITE_CODE in .env", and answers /health.

fix(create): a new project carries no bytecode from the installer (#611)

pip byte-compiles every .py in the wheel, and cli/templates/co-ai/agent.py
is a .py under the package even though nothing imports it. So an installed
copy holds templates/co-ai/__pycache__/agent.cpython-3xx.pyc, compiled by
whichever interpreter did the installing — and co create copies the
directory as it finds it:

    $ co create wheeltest --template co-ai
    $ ls -a wheeltest
    .co  .env  .gitignore  Dockerfile  __pycache__  agent.py  ...

Found by installing the built wheel into a fresh venv and running create
from it, which is the only place this appears — a checkout has no such
file.

Nothing breaks: a mismatched magic number is ignored and .gitignore covers
the directory. But compiled output for code the user has not run is a
question their first project should not raise.

The copy loop moved into copy_template_files() so it can be tested, and
co init's own loop got the same guard.

Closes nothing — no issue for this; found while checking the wheel.

docs(events): the examples describe the trace the agent writes (#612)

core/events.py is where someone learns to hook into a run, and three of
its docstrings — the code people copy — filter on 'tool_execution' and
read trace['tool_name'] / trace['timing']. Nothing writes that type; the
entries are tool_call and tool_result, the name field is 'name', and the
timing field is 'timing_ms'.

A handler written from those examples never fires. The if is never true,
the comprehension is always empty, and nothing errors — the run finishes
and the hook simply had nothing to say.

'tool_execution' came from tool_executor.py's module note, which claimed
to write it and did not. That note was corrected when co eval's copy of
the same mistake was fixed; these examples had not been.

Same shape in README.md and docs/README.md, also fixed. The design note
in docs/design-decisions/019 is left as written — it is a dated record of
what was proposed, not instructions.

A test now holds the docstrings to the trace: every type they compare
against must be one something writes, and every field they read must
exist on that entry.

Verified with a real Agent: handlers written exactly like the corrected
examples fire — after_each_tool saw 'add in 0ms', on_complete saw ['add'].

co browser status starts a browser to find out whether a browser is running (#610)

* fix(browser): asking whether the browser runs does not start it

co browser status went through the same cold-start path as every other
verb, so with no daemon listening it called _spawn_daemon — which creates
~/.co/ and opens ~/.co/browser.log before launching a detached Chrome.
The answer to "is the browser running?" was obtained by making it run.

In a managed sandbox ($HOME readable, writes only in the workspace and
temp) the mkdir raises PermissionError, send() catches only RuntimeError,
and the CLI printed a Typer traceback instead of a status. Reproduced
with HOME pointed at a 0500 directory and the socket path pointed at
nothing:

  before:  PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '.../.co'
           (under a full traceback)
  after:   Browser daemon: not running — the next page command starts one

With nobody listening the answer needs no process, no home directory and
no log.

status only. tab/use/close read a registry that lives inside the daemon,
so they have a reason to want one — a test pins that they still spawn.

Closes #356

* test: the warm-daemon fake ends, so the test can too

CI killed the job at five minutes on this test (exit 143). The fake
socket's recv returned the same bytes on every call, so send()'s
read-to-EOF loop never ended. It was green locally, which is the whole
problem with a fake that cannot do the one thing the real object does:
stop.

docs: the real-world examples in docs/README.md can be run (#613)

Both lines of the customer-support example raise before doing anything:

    agent = Agent("customer_support", tools=[send_email],
                  instructions="You help users …")
    response = agent("Send a welcome email to alice@example.com")

Agent.__init__ takes system_prompt, not instructions, and has no **kwargs
to absorb the difference — TypeError. Agent defines no __call__, so the
second line raises too; the method is agent.input(...). The monitoring
example below it repeats both.

This is the section that promises real-world usage, so these are the
first lines a reader runs, and neither survives.

The test is the general rule, not these two fixes: every keyword a
documented call passes must exist on the callable (skipped where the
callable takes **kwargs — llm_do forwards temperature to the provider,
which is fine), and no example may call an agent instance.

fix(create): the person who made the agent can command it (#615)

co deploy writes the deployer's address into the agent's .co/admins.txt
and says why: admins.txt is who may command the agent, and without it
nobody can — ADMIN_ADD is gated on super-admin, super-admin is the
agent's own address, and that private key lives only with the agent.

co create and co init never did it, so an agent run from the machine
that made it treated its own author as a stranger:

    $ co call 0x900d7723... "co status"
    agent requires onboarding — run input() once to onboard, then call() works

which is advice a CLI user cannot follow: input() is the Python API and
co call has no way to submit an invite code (#614, second half — left
open, it is a decision about the CLI's shape).

The address comes from the keypair, not from keys.env's AGENT_ADDRESS.
The file has to name the key that will actually be presented at CONNECT,
and on this machine those two values disagree.

Appended and only when absent: the file may already name other admins,
and a second co init must not add the same line twice.

Does not touch the server: .co/admins.txt is in the rsync exclude list,
with a comment saying a stale local copy would silently change who is in
charge. Deploy still writes its own.

Verified end to end, not only in tests — co create, python agent.py,
then a real co call returning the agent's own directory listing.

fix(status): say which list is empty, and where the other one is (#617)

On a machine with four registered servers and two agents running on one
of them, the whole of what co status says about deployment is:

    Deployed Agents: none

_fetch_deployments() asks ConnectOnion Cloud. An agent put on your own
box with `co deploy --to` lives in ~/.co/servers.yaml and is never in
that list; `co server ls` shows it and status never mentions either.

Status is the command people run to find out what they have, so this is
not a small imprecision — it is that question answered wrongly.

Nothing changes about what is fetched or shown. The empty line names its
scope and points at the other list; the populated table is untouched, and
does not carry the pointer — it is there to answer "where is mine?"

fix(identity): keys.env names the key the machine actually has (#618)

AGENT_ADDRESS in ~/.co/keys.env is a copy of the keypair, written once at
first setup. ensure_global_config() does contain the reconcile — it
rewrites the line from the key — but only inside the branch that
regenerates a *missing* key, and a key that merely *changed* returns
above it:

    if key_file.exists():
        return

So after a co reset, or a restore from a different recovery phrase, the
file keeps naming the previous identity. From a clean HOME:

    keypair  0x8a6c70b01453   stated  0x8a6c70b01453   fresh: agree
    keypair  0x2cc36d08f71a   stated  0x8a6c70b01453   after the change

Every project made afterwards copies that line into its .env and every
deploy ships it. Found on three of this operator's machines, two of them
naming an address whose key signs nothing they hold.

An address is what other agents whitelist, what goes in admins.txt, and
what someone pastes to a colleague. One whose private key nobody holds is
worse than none.

Written every time rather than once — the same self-healing rule deploy
applies to authorized_keys and admins.txt — and a no-op when they agree.

Closes #616

fix(deploy): the container package keeps the admins the project names (#619)

_build_tarball packs the project — .co/admins.txt included, since only
parts of .co/ are excluded — and then _add_deployer_as_admin appended a
second member with the same path holding only the deployer. Extraction
takes the last one, so anyone the operator had added was dropped.

Measured on a real tarball with a colleague in the project's file:

    entries named .co/admins.txt   2
    winning content                ['0x10e6…']   the deployer alone

Silent, and the loss surfaces much later as a colleague who cannot
command an agent they were given access to.

The deployer must always end up in the file — that is what this function
is for, and #614 is what happens without it — but "always present" and
"the only one" are different guarantees and only the first was intended.
The two lists are merged, the project's copy is left out of the file walk,
and the archive carries one entry for the path.

The function's docstring claimed .co/ was excluded from the package. It
is not, and has not been since host.yaml started travelling; corrected.

fix(doctor): say when the project names a model 1.6.0 no longer prices (#620)

#603 dropped thirty pre-2025 models and deliberately left routing alone,
so a project that still says MODEL=gpt-4o-mini keeps working. Its price
table entry is gone though, so every figure shown for it is
DEFAULT_PRICING:

    MODEL from .env      gpt-4o-mini
    is_estimated_price   True
    cost for 1M/100k     $1.30        the real price is $0.21

Six times too high, on a project that upgraded and changed nothing. The
~ says the number is a guess; nothing says why.

co doctor is what people run after an upgrade when something looks off,
and on a 1.5-era project it reported one unrelated broken symlink and
said nothing about the model — the one thing that had changed under them.

An ○ rather than a ✗: the agent runs, only the accounting is approximate.
A test pins that the note does not claim otherwise, and that supported
models — including dated variants that resolve by prefix — say nothing.

fix(trust): the agent counts as its own admin, so ADMIN_ADD is reachable (#621)

load_admins said 'Self address is always admin (from project's
.co/address.json)' and read address.json — a file nothing has written
since identity moved to .co/keys/. get_self_address was corrected for
exactly this (oo-chat#28, where paid onboarding could not succeed because
the payment address came back None); load_admins was not, so the two
disagreed about who the agent is.

On a project that has been run once:

    self address    0x530c85d3641cff867d
    is_super_admin  True
    is_admin        False

ws_admin gates on is_admin first and the super-admin check second, so the
only super-admin was refused at the outer gate — ADMIN_ADD and
ADMIN_REMOVE were unreachable by anyone, including the account they were
written for.

Third time this shape has appeared in this release: a gate compared
against a value the resolver never produces for that identity (#579 for
the approval dialog, #614 for CONNECT). Fixed the same way — ask the
resolver everyone else asks.

No access widens: signing as the agent's own address needs its private
key, which lives with the agent.

The unauthenticated /info publishes the operator's account balance (#622)

* fix(host): /info stops publishing the operator's balance

/info needs no credentials. Its own comment reasons carefully about that
for skills — 'anyone who can reach the agent can read it, and on a
deployed agent that is the whole internet' — and twenty lines below the
same response carried balance_usd. Against a live agent here:

    $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8477/info
    "balance_usd": 1207.1999

The operator's real account balance, readable by anyone who can reach the
agent. Commercially revealing on its own, and a targeting signal: credits
are money, and an agent holding a lot of them is worth more effort than
one holding none.

The boundary was already written down on the client side —
connectonion-react documents the authenticated profile as carrying
'name, model, tools, every skill, balance' and says 'the public /info
answer is deliberately narrower'. /info was not keeping it.

Authenticated clients are unaffected: AGENT_PROFILE and the CONNECTED
frame still carry it, which is where oo-chat reads it from (its e2e
mocks feed it through PROFILE, not /info).

* test: the /info balance assertion follows the change

test_includes_balance_when_present pinned the behaviour this PR removes.
Same shape as #604's AGENT_CONFIG_PATH tests: an assertion that recorded
what the code did rather than what it should do. It now asserts the
absence, and says why in its docstring.

Caught by CI, not locally — I had run only the new file and the ones I
expected to interact.

fix(host): an image counts against the upload limit, like a file (#623)

host.yaml says 'max_file_size: 10  # MB per file (both WebSocket and
HTTP)' and validate_files enforces it — for files. The same two handlers
take images beside it, a list of base64 strings that goes straight to
agent.input() and on to the model, and nothing measured it. uvicorn sets
no request-size cap of its own.

Smaller than it first looks: /input is authenticated, so this sits behind
the trust gate exactly where the existing file check does. But
'authenticated' includes contact level, which an invite code grants, and
on the 1-2GB VPS co server new provisions one large image is enough to
end the process — leaving an operator with an agent that died and nothing
explaining why.

Not a new limit: the one already advertised in /info as max_file_size_mb.
Size is read from the base64 string rather than by decoding it, so an
oversized image is refused without first allocating it.

fix(ws): a frame the agent does not understand is answered (#624)

Probed a live agent with malformed frames. Everything got a reply except
two, which got nothing at all:

    garbage text            ERROR: Invalid JSON …
    CONNECT, no signature   ERROR: unauthorized …
    INPUT before CONNECT    ERROR: authenticate first …
    empty object            (silence, socket still open)
    {"type": "NOPE"}        (silence, socket still open)

The dispatch chain ends at `elif active_io:`, which forwards unrecognised
frames to a running agent's mailbox. With no agent running there is no
active_io, so the frame falls off the end: no reply, no log, nothing. The
client waits until its own timeout and then reports something unrelated
to the cause.

Silence is the answer #434 was about, and every other branch in this same
dispatch sends an ERROR frame.

It matters most for a long-term release: an agent from this version will
meet clients of many versions, and the first symptom of version skew
should be "I do not know that message", not a connection that looks fine
and never answers.

The forwarding branch is above the new one and untouched — a running
agent still gets ASK_USER_RESPONSE and the rest.

fix(host): relay_url in host.yaml decides which relay the agent uses (#626)

Every project's .co/host.yaml carries the line, under a header that says
'edit these values'. Editing it did nothing.

load_host_config applies code parameters over the file 'only if not None',
and relay_url alone among them defaulted to a real string:

    port: int = None                     file wins
    trust: … = None                      file wins
    workers: int = None                  file wins
    relay_url: str = DEFAULT_RELAY_URL    file never wins

Every generated agent.py calls host(agent) without naming a relay, so that
default was passed as an explicit override on every start.

Measured with host.yaml saying wss://127.0.0.1:9/ws — a port that refuses
instantly, confirmed by a direct connect (ConnectionRefusedError in 0.0s):

    banner              ✓ relay
    relay errors        none, over 75 seconds
    co call <address>   returned the agent's pwd

It was announcing on the public relay, and nothing said so, because as far
as the process was concerned nothing had gone wrong. Anyone pointing an
agent at their own relay was on the public one instead, and the first
symptom would be whatever they were keeping off it.

UNSET as the default rather than None: None already means 'no relay at
all' here, and collapsing the two would turn 'off' into 'use the public
one'. resolve_relay_url keeps them apart — explicit wins, then the file,
then the default; an empty value in the file means off.

After the fix, the same project reports the refusal and retries with
backoff, which is what the loop below was written to do.

fix(host): the startup banner says what is configured, not what worked (#627)

Two lines asserted more than the process knew at the moment they printed.

  ✓ relay   was "✓ relay" if relay_url else "no relay" — a green tick for
            "a URL is set", printed before any connection was attempted.
            Against a relay that refuses instantly it still showed the tick,
            and the operator had been told their agent was reachable.

  ↳ chat.openonion.ai ↗   was printed unconditionally, whichever relay the
            agent announced on. Accidentally true while every agent was on
            the public relay; #626 made a private relay_url work, so it can
            now point at a site that has never heard of this agent.

Neither is something the banner could have known: it prints during startup,
before the relay loop has connected to anything. So it states the relay it
is about to use, and leaves success to the lines that do know — the
"relay connection error" and "relay reconnected" lines, and the heartbeat
a terminal gets.

    relay: oo.openonion.ai        public, with the chat link
    relay: relay.example.internal private, without it
    no relay                      unchanged

Verified live on both, rebased onto #626 so the private case is reachable.

co init dies with a JSONDecodeError when the backend has a blip (#628)

* fix(auth): a non-JSON error from the backend is reported, not raised

On a non-200, authenticate() read the reason with

    error_msg = response.json().get("detail", "Registration failed")

A gateway in front of the backend does not answer in JSON. Its 502 page
made .json() raise out of `co init` and `co auth` as a traceback, and init
stopped before writing the project's .env — half a project, and a stack
trace where an explanation belongs.

Seen for real during this release loop. At 22:00 on 2026-08-03 the relay
returned 502 for about twenty seconds — the deployed agent logged
"[host] relay still unreachable after 5 attempts" — and in the same
window every test that runs a real `co init` failed with

    json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1

That is also why CI went red on an unrelated branch: those tests reach the
network, and the network was briefly unwell.

A backend blip is ordinary operation for something meant to run for years.
The status code is what the operator needs; the shape of the reply this
code hoped for is not.

* fix(email): the same non-JSON error, in send_email

A sweep for the pattern found 34 places that call .json() on a response.
Most are on the success path, where a 200 that is not JSON is the
backend's own bug. Four are on error branches, where a gateway's HTML
lands — and two of those already guard it: deploy_commands._error_text
and server_commands._report_failure both wrap the call. So somebody met
this before; auth (above) and send_email were the two that were missed.

In a tool the crash is worse than in a CLI. send_email returns
{"success": False, "error": …} for every other failure, and the model
reads that and tells the user. An exception unwinds the turn instead.

A SKILL.md that cannot be read is reported instead of swallowed (#629)

_parse_skill_content catches yaml.YAMLError and carries on with an empty
frontmatter, so a skill with a typo in its frontmatter loads anyway: no
description, no tools: patterns, no warning. It reaches the model looking
like a working skill that nobody can say the purpose of.

find_skill_problems already exists for exactly this shape of thing, and its
docstring gives the rule: a symlink is a claim that a skill lives somewhere,
and that claim can be false. A SKILL.md is the same claim. It now checks the
content of any SKILL.md it finds, not just links, and names the line -- the
same thing #422 settled for policy files.

Loading stays forgiving; this is reported, not raised.

Found by running it over the 117 skills installed on this machine: 7 were
genuinely broken, from two ordinary typos --

  argument-hint: [analyze <person/org>] | [dig messages]
  description: ...frontmatter outline: field...

Neither looks wrong to a human, which is why swallowing the error is the
wrong thing to do with it. A SKILL.md with no frontmatter at all is still
accepted -- that is a legitimate way to write a simple skill.

co --version: 3.4s -> 0.9s, by not importing the whole framework to print it (#631)

#588 removed the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs from the startup path and stopped
there. The remaining 3.4s was the same bug one level up: connectonion/__init__.py
imported every subsystem eagerly to re-export its names, and importing
connectonion.cli.main runs the package __init__ first -- Python offers no way
around that -- so printing a version string paid for Gmail's Google credentials,
the TUI and the whole network stack.

    connectonion.cli.main       3.36s
      connectonion              3.30s
        connectonion.core         1.39s
        connectonion.useful_tools 1.16s   (gmail -> google.auth, google.oauth2)
        connectonion.tui          0.59s
        connectonion.network      0.54s

The names are now resolved on first use (PEP 562). Only the lookup moves.

Two things this had to get right, both found by running the suite rather than
by reading the code:

llm_do and transcribe each name a module *and* the function inside it. Importing
connectonion.llm_do makes the import system bind the module onto the package,
shadowing the function, and connectonion.llm_do(...) then raises "'module' object
is not callable". The eager version won that race by accident -- __init__ ran
first and rebound the function last. Ordinary code loses it: docs/README.md,
web_fetch.py and gmail.py all import that submodule. Settled in __getattribute__,
where it does not depend on import order.

The old guard could not have caught any of this: it asserted 'google' not in
sys.modules, and a .pth file in site-packages puts the google namespace package
there before user code runs. It now measures what importing connectonion *adds*.

  co --version   3.5s -> 0.92s
  test suite     616s -> 358s
  3884 passed

Lazy package keeps every submodule attribute that used to resolve (#632)

#631 made the package resolve names on first use, and two names stopped
resolving with it: connectonion.tui and connectonion.useful_plugins. Neither
is re-exported by anything -- they were bound onto the package as a side
effect of the eager imports, and nothing put them back.

Checked against the commit before #631 rather than assumed:

    connectonion.tui             module          -> restored
    connectonion.useful_plugins  module          -> restored
    connectonion.cli             AttributeError  -> unchanged, nothing to keep

Nothing in this repo reads them that way -- every internal user goes through
importlib.import_module('connectonion.useful_plugins.X'), a module path, which
never depended on the parent attribute. That is the reason to fix it rather
than the reason not to: an undocumented attribute that quietly stops resolving
is found by somebody else's code, after the release.

Listing a name in _SUBMODULES does not import it. co --version is unchanged.

One reader for SKILL.md frontmatter (#633)

* One reader for SKILL.md frontmatter

Closes #630. SKILL.md had two parsers and they disagreed in both directions.
co_ai/skills/loader.py split each line on the first colon; useful_plugins/skills.py
parses YAML. Measured on real skills installed on this machine:

  feishu-data-analysis   YAML {}                 line-split: 4 keys
  outline-plan           YAML {}                 line-split: 3 keys
  tools: [read_file, write_file]
                         YAML ['read_file', 'write_file']
                         line-split '[read_file, write_file]'   (a string)

So a skill behaved differently depending on whether the skills plugin or co ai
loaded it, and neither said anything. YAML is the documented format and the one
all 9 bundled skills are written in, so it is the reader that stays. #629 made
co doctor name the file and line of a frontmatter that does not parse, which is
what makes converging on the stricter reader safe: a skill that was being read
wrongly in silence is now one that gets reported loudly.

Second half of the issue: tools: went straight into a "for pattern in patterns"
loop, and YAML returns a string for a scalar "tools: read_file" -- so it walked
the characters and registered r, e, a, d as permission patterns. Fail-safe, but
the declaration did nothing. _tool_patterns() normalises it.

And the bug this change introduced, found by probing it rather than reading it:
YAML types its values, so "name: 123" became an int and "name: no" a bool (YAML
reads no/on/yes/off as booleans). The registry is keyed by name, so a skill keyed
by False cannot be looked up by anything a user can type. The two human-facing
labels are coerced back to str; tools: keeps its real type.

* A tools: key with nothing after it is no patterns, not a crash

Found reviewing the change above, and pre-existing -- it crashed the same way
before the readers were unified. `tools:` with an empty value is a null in YAML,
and the caller does `for pattern in patterns`, so it raised

    TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not iterable

when the skill was invoked. _grant_skill_permissions is not in a try block, so
that took the user's turn with it. It belongs in the function that now owns
reading that key.

co call can answer the onboarding it is asked for (#634)

Part 2 of #614. call() refused with "run input() once to onboard" -- the Python
API, which is no help to whoever typed `co call`. There is no way to submit an
invite code from the CLI at all.

input() already does the whole exchange over the same socket and the same
frames, and the host finishes the handshake itself: ws_router/session.py pops
the stashed pending_connect on a successful ONBOARD_SUBMIT and calls
establish_connection, which sends CONNECTED. So call()'s existing wait loop
receives it with no new machinery -- it submits and keeps waiting.

Not unconditional: with no terminal to ask, prompting would hang a script on
stdin, so it still fails there, but says what the agent asked for and what to do.

A wrong code was checked rather than assumed: handle_onboard_submit answers it
with ERROR "Invalid invite code", which the loop already ends on -- one prompt,
a clear reason, no command run.

Also worth recording: the first red run was partly spurious. The fake websocket
did not echo exec_id, and the client skips any EXEC_RESULT that does not carry
the id it sent, so a test that should have passed was failing for a reason that
had nothing to do with the product. The fake now echoes it the way the host
does, and red-then-green was re-proven against the corrected fake.

Declining an invite code is an error result, not a traceback (#635)

Found by probing #634 against a real host through a pty: pressing Enter at the
prompt printed a stack trace.

    Enter invite code:
    Traceback (most recent call last):
      ...
    ValueError: No valid onboard credentials provided

_prompt_onboard raises when nothing is entered. call() never reached it before
#634, and every other refusal it can meet -- a blacklist, a bad invite code, a
tool that is not whitelisted -- comes back as ExecResult(status="error"). This
puts declining on that same channel; it is the function's error contract, not a
swallowed exception. input() keeps raising, as its docstring says it does.

A docstring example is a call somebody will make (#636)

test_the_documented_calls_are_real_calls.py checks README.md and docs/README.md.
Docstring examples were never in its scope, and one of them does not run:

    connectonion/network/relay.py:58
        >>> addr = address.load()
    TypeError: load() missing 1 required positional argument: 'co_dir'

That is what help(send_announce) prints and what an IDE shows on hover -- the
place a reader is most likely to copy from without checking. The whole example
is now copy-pasteable: the relative `from . import announce, address` is a real
import too, and it is not one a reader can use.

The guard resolves conservatively, because a careless version of it reports
mostly noise. A first pass flagged five examples and four were its own fault:

    relay.py       await connect()                  relay's own connect() takes no
                                                    required args, not connectonion.connect
    llm_do.py      llm_do("John, 30 years old", …)  the comma is inside a string,
    transcribe.py  transcribe("meeting.mp3", …)     not between two arguments

So arguments come from ast, never from splitting on commas, and a name resolves
against the module the docstring lives in first. Three tests pin those, so the
check cannot quietly become one that passes by resolving nothing.

Across 209 source files it now reports exactly the one real defect, and the
corrected example was run for real: address.load() returns the keypair and
create_announce_message() builds an ANNOUNCE.

An agent on a schedule fills its own disk with eval runs (#637)

Every turn writes .co/evals/{slug}/run_{n}.yaml holding the whole message array,
and nothing removed them. Measured on the deployed naturewill agent:

    evals                  17 MB      171 run files
    session_results.jsonl  504 KB     compacted, so it stays small
    oldest run             2026-08-01 09:30
    newest run             2026-08-03 04:30

17 MB in 43 hours is about 9.5 MB a day, or 3.5 GB a year, on the 1-2 GB VPS
`co server new` provisions. The agent fills its own disk in a couple of months
and what dies is the agent.

What reads a run file, checked rather than assumed: nothing does during a run --
co eval globs evals/*.yaml, the per-eval file beside the directory, not the runs
inside it. Logger.load_messages(run=N) can open one and no caller in this
codebase does, only its tests. So the readers are a human looking at what went
wrong and anyone calling that method, and for both the recent runs are the ones
worth having. Older runs really are deleted; that is the trade.

run_*.jsonl is a read-only legacy format nothing writes any more (the deployed
agent has zero) and is left alone.

The easy mistake, pinned by a test: sorted as text "run_10" comes before
"run_9", so a trim that sorts by name deletes the newest run and keeps the
oldest. Run numbers are numbers.

Verified with one real agent turn against a directory seeded with 30 runs:
30 -> 20, keeping 11..30.

workers or reload in host.yaml stops the agent from starting (#639)

Two of the nine keys in every generated .co/host.yaml, under a header that says
to edit them, turn the agent off:

    workers: 1     -> 2
    reload: false  -> true

host() ends at uvicorn.run(app, ...), and uvicorn can only fork workers or watch
files when given an import string. Handed an app object it refuses both and
returns without serving. Measured, through the code parameter and through
host.yaml:

    [host] ───────────────────────────────
           http://localhost:8794
           0xe8eab6d…
    WARNING:  You must pass the application as an import string ...
    $ curl http://localhost:8794/info      (nothing -- the process is gone)

So the banner announces an address that answers nothing.

Not made to work, because that is a design question rather than a fix: each
worker would run its own scheduler loop and its own in_flight set, and
record_run writes last_run only after the turn returns -- so a schedule that
overruns its interval gets one copy per worker, the race #537 is about.

Until that is answered the agent keeps running and says what it did not honour.
Silently running one worker is a smaller lie than dying behind a banner that
says otherwise.

Verified on a real server with workers: 4 and reload: true --
processes 0 -> 2, GET /info no answer -> 200.

Three of the twelve tests drive host() itself and assert what reaches
uvicorn.run: a helper nothing calls is the bug, not the fix.

open trust allows everyone in; it does not let anyone in unsigned (#641)

The shipped policy said the second thing:

    connectonion/network/trust/policies/open.md
        # Open Trust (Development)
        # Allow everyone - no verification needed

Verification is exactly what is still needed. extract_and_authenticate refuses
an unsigned request before any trust level is read:

    # Protocol requirement: ALL requests must be signed

Measured against a real agent started with trust: open in host.yaml:

    GET  /info                     {"trust": "open"}
    POST /input   unsigned    ->   401 unauthorized: signed request required
    POST /input   signed      ->   200  (brand-new address.generate() identity)

The levels decide authorisation -- which signed identity may act. open means
any, careful means admin/whitelisted/contact, strict means the whitelist. None
of them decides authentication. careful.md and strict.md already describe
themselves in those terms; open.md was the one that conflated the two, and it
is the level a developer picks precisely when they want to curl the thing.

The behavioural tests matter more than the wording: an open that skipped
signatures would let an unauthenticated caller run the agent's tools while
looking like it did what its own documentation said. Ten of the eleven assert
that, across all three levels.

Everything the file now claims was run first, including that a freshly
generated identity is enough to be let in.

Every call went through the relay, because the gate was on a field nobody sends (#643)

resolve_endpoint picks the best way to reach an agent -- localhost, then LAN,
then public -- and falls back to the relay when it finds nothing. It had never
found anything:

    if not agent_info.get("online") or not agent_info.get("endpoints"):
        return None

The relay does not send `online`. Measured against a live agent announced on
wss://oo.openonion.ai, the reply is endpoints / relay / last_seen / profile --
no such key. So this returned None for every agent that has ever existed,
_sort_endpoints and its localhost-first ordering never ran, and an agent on the
same machine as its caller was reached over the public relay.

    resolve_endpoint(0xe8eab6d…)   ->  None
    GET http://10.5.27.133:8797/info -> {"address": "0xe8eab6d…"}   (answering)

after:

    resolve_endpoint(0xe8eab6d…)   ->  ws://10.5.27.133:8797/ws     (1.0s)

An explicit `online: False` is still honoured -- the relay knowing an agent is
gone is worth more than rediscovering that at one timeout per endpoint. Absent
means no opinion. Liveness was never what the flag established anyway: each
candidate is fetched and its /info address must match the agent being looked
for, which is stronger and current, and stays.

Verified against the live agent through the path this switches on: `co call`
reached it (and was refused by the host's own permission whitelist, which is
the gate working), and connect().input() ran the tool and returned its marker.

Filed #642 for what this surfaced: one address announced by two different
agents resolves to whichever is nearest. That collision predates this.

A browser daemon that is shutting down exits; it does not abort the process (#644)

* A browser daemon that is shutting down exits; it does not abort the process

Closing the listener is how the daemon is told to stop, and _accept's docstring
says the raise is the mechanism:

    A dead listener still raises out on both platforms so a dying daemon exits.

Raising is intended. Escaping as an unhandled thread exception is not. Each
serve() thread printed a full traceback on the way out, and several doing that
at once while the interpreter finalised took the process with them:

    ConnectionAbortedError: [Errno 53] Software caused connection abort
      File ".../browser_agent/daemon.py", line 694, in _accept
    ...
    Fatal Python error: _enter_buffered_busy: could not acquire lock for
    <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stderr>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due
    to daemon threads

Seen at the end of a full local run: 4181 tests passed, then exit 134. An abort
at shutdown discards whatever was still buffered, and what a user stopping
`co browser` sees is a wall of tracebacks under a fatal error.

_cleanup now marks the daemon as closing before it closes the socket, and the
accept loop returns quietly only in that case. A listener that breaks while the
daemon is supposed to be serving still raises -- that is a real failure and must
not be swallowed, and two of the five tests are about exactly that.

* Wake the accept loop on Linux too

CI caught what macOS could not: closing the listener raises out of accept() on
macOS, and on Linux it simply keeps blocking, so serve() never reached the flag
and never returned. This file's own test failed on all four Linux jobs and
passed on macOS and Windows.

_cleanup now makes one throwaway connection to the socket before closing it, so
a thread already inside accept() comes back and sees the flag. connect_ex
reports failure as a return value rather than an exception, and a failure there
means the socket is already gone -- the outcome that was wanted.

A direct endpoint that stops answering falls back to the relay (#645)

* A direct endpoint that stops answering falls back to the relay

#643 made resolve_endpoint work for the first time, and a resolved endpoint is
cached for the life of the RemoteAgent with no way back:

    if self._resolved_endpoint:
        ws_url = self._resolved_endpoint
    else:
        ws_url = f"{self._relay_url}/ws/input"

So an agent that restarts on another port, or a caller that moves off that
network, breaks every later call on that object -- over a path that worked
before #643, when resolution never succeeded and everything went through the
relay. That is the regression the change brought with it, and step 7 of the
loop assumes exactly this.

_open_best_connection tries the agent first and the relay behind it, and only
the connection attempt is retried: once a socket is open, an error on it is the
agent's answer and belongs to the caller. Retrying a refused tool call
somewhere else would run it twice.

The dead endpoint is forgotten at the same time, so the next call resolves
again instead of paying for the same refusal every turn.

Proven against a real agent, not only the fake -- the fake could not have shown
this, since the change is to how the connection is opened:

    turn 1                      ws://10.5.27.133:8798/ws   answered
    agent killed, moved to 8799
    turn 2, same client object  relay                      answered
    endpoint after turn 2       None                       (re-resolves next time)

Before this, turn 2 raised ConnectionRefusedError.

* Make the websocket stand-ins awaitable, like the thing they stand in for

connect.py now awaits websockets.connect(url) so a refused connection can be
retried elsewhere. The real Connect object is both awaitable and an async
context manager; three fakes modelled only the second half, so 22 tests failed
with

    TypeError: object FakeWebSocket can't be used in 'await' expression

which is the fake being wrong about the API, not the product. Each gains the
five lines that make it true.

The release checklist names files that are not there (#646)

VERSIONING.md's "Files to Update When Versioning" and "Version Update Checklist"
are what someone follows on the day a release is cut, and every entry was wrong:

    /connectonion/__init__.py  __version__ variable   reads `from ._version import
                                                      __version__` -- no literal
    /setup.py                  version parameter      does not exist
    /docs-site/app/page.tsx    version badge          does not exist; the real one
                                                      is docs-site/lib/version.ts
    /pyproject.toml            "(if exists)"          it exists, and must change
    connectonion/_version.py   --                     the only literal, named nowhere

and the build step could not run: `python setup.py sdist bdist_wheel`.

Version *consistency* was already guarded -- test_the_version_agrees_with_itself.py
compares pyproject, the package, this file and the docs site -- so a release that
edited the wrong things would be caught. The instructions for getting there were
guarded by nothing.

Now checked, in the same shape as #636: every file the procedure names must exist,
the file the version actually lives in must be named, and the build command must be
the one this project is set up for.

Verified by following it on a copy: bump the three files to 9.9.9, guards pass,
`python -m build` produces connectonion-9.9.9-py3-none-any.whl, and the installed
`co --version` says 9.9.9. The old procedure could not have produced that.

The host serves the address you were told, instead of inventing one (#647)

A project with no key of its own got two different answers. co status falls back
to the machine's identity:

    co_dir = Path(".co")
    if not (co_dir.exists() and (co_dir / "keys" / "agent.key").exists()):
        co_dir = Path.home() / ".co"

host() did not fall back. It looked in cwd/.co, found nothing, and minted:

    addr_data = address.load(co_dir)
    if addr_data is None:
        addr_data = address.generate()
        address.save(addr_data, co_dir)

Measured in a project created by 1.5.x -- the co init that pointed at the global
~/.co and wrote no local key of its own:

    co status says   0x10e68f6dff39ab1c50cc48ea…
    host served as   0x3910103910d99954443e42a3…

So the operator reads one address, hands it out, and nothing reaches the agent:
it is answering as somebody else. The project's identity changes on the way past
too, silently -- whatever was whitelisted or announced under the configured
address is now a different agent.

Generating stays for a machine with no identity at all; an agent has to have an
address. What goes is inventing one while a configured identity sits unused.

Projects made by today's co create and co init write their own key, so nothing
changes for them -- this only reaches the ones that predate that, which are the
ones most likely to be running unattended somewhere.

After, on the same project:

    co status says   0x10e68f6dff39ab1c50cc48ea…
    host serves as   0x10e68f6dff39ab1c50cc48ea…
    key written      none

A skill's permissions do not outlive a turn that ended by raising (#648)

The module docstring states the guarantee: "Auto-clears when turn ends
(security) — only affects current turn (no permission escalation)".

cleanup_scope is @on_complete, and on_complete is a plain statement after the
loop in Agent.input -- no finally. A turn that raises never reaches it, and the
ordinary way to make a turn raise is the operator refusing an approval. They say
no, and the skill's grants survive their refusal.

Measured on a real agent, sampled at after_user_input -- during the turn, which
is when a permission decides anything:

    at the start of turn 2      permissions                        snapshot
    before                      ['Bash(git status)','read_file']   turn=1
    after                       []                                 none

So the whole of turn 2 ran with the previous turn's grants active: a tool
matching those patterns is auto-approved and the operator is never asked. They
were cleared only at the END of turn 2, when the stale snapshot was finally
restored. The permission record even carries expires={'type':'turn_end'};
nothing was enforcing it.

Restoring at the start of a turn is the fix. The plugin's own @after_user_input
runs every turn before anything is granted, and a snapshot tagged with an
earlier turn is exactly the evidence that its restore never ran. Not
try/finally around the turn: that would make on_complete fire on failures, and
the logger and the eval writer both read it as "the turn finished".

Worth recording: the first real-agent probe sampled after input() returned, saw
[] on unfixed code, and looked clean -- the leak is only visible while turn 2 is
running, which is the only time it matters.

Prefer a TLS endpoint over a plaintext one at the same distance (#650)

_sort_endpoints ordered by closeness and nothing else, so an agent announcing
both schemes on one host was reached over whichever the relay listed first --
and it lists plaintext first:

    >>> _sort_endpoints(['http://agent.example.com:8000',
    ...                  'https://agent.example.com:8000'])
    ['http://agent.example.com:8000', 'https://agent.example.com:8000']

The connection then went in the clear to an agent that had offered TLS.

What travels on it is a signed CONNECT, and #649 measured what a captured one is
worth: EXEC carries no signature of its own, so within the five-minute freshness
window a replayed CONNECT opens a session on which any whitelisted tool runs with
any arguments -- measured, three times, on a tool with a side effect. Before #643
this never came up: resolution always failed and every client went through the
relay over wss://.

Closeness still decides first. A plaintext loopback connection has no network to
be observed on, and reaching an agent on this machine is the case direct
resolution exists for. This only chooses between endpoints that are equally close.

Not the whole of #649. An agent that offers no TLS at all still speaks plaintext
across a LAN; what to do about that is the trade filed there, along with the
protocol question of signing each command. This is the part with no trade in it.

The WebSocket path runs the prompt that was signed, not the one beside it (#651)

_build_input_message signs the prompt into `payload`, and start_agent read the
unsigned top-level field, checking only that the connection had authenticated:

    if not conn["authenticated"]: ...
    prompt = data.get("prompt")

Measured against a live agent, with the signature covering one prompt and the
top-level field saying another:

    POST /input            signed: SIGNED   top-level: UNSIGNED  ->  ran SIGNED
    INPUT over WebSocket   signed: SIGNED   top-level: UNSIGNED  ->  ran UNSIGNED

Same protocol, same client, two different guarantees -- and the client signs on
both paths, which is what made this one look authenticated while the signature
decided nothing.

Reading the signed field is not enough on its own: an unverified payload can say
anything. So a frame that carries a signature now goes through the same verifier
the HTTP path uses, which is the one the admin messages already use a few lines
away in session.py. "open" there is about authentication, not authorisation --
who may act was settled at CONNECT.

After, on the same agent:

    substituted top-level prompt  ->  SIGNED-PROMPT
    forged signature              ->  refused

A frame with no signature keeps using the top-level field: a client built with
no keys sends none, and its connection was authenticated by its CONNECT.
Whether a signature should be REQUIRED is the decision in #649, along with
single-use CONNECT and what to do about plaintext LAN endpoints.

co reset says what it deletes (#655)

The warning shown before the prompt claimed everything:

    ⚠️  WARNING: This will DELETE ALL your ConnectOnion data
    You will lose:
      • Your account and balance
      • All transaction history
      • Your Ed25519 keypair
      • All configurations and credentials

The code removes two paths:

    shutil.rmtree(global_dir / "keys")
    (global_dir / "keys.env").unlink()

Everything else in ~/.co survives -- skills/, subs/, backups/, browser_context/,
blocklist.txt, agent.json, the logs.

The file described its own blast radius three ways and only one was right: the
header said both "deletes ~/.co/keys/, ~/.co/keys.env" and "deletes entire ~/.co/
directory contents", and the comment above the two removals read
"# Delete everything".

Overstating destruction is the safe direction to be wrong in, and it is still
wrong -- someone reading it cannot tell whether their skills and subscriptions
survive a reset, and they do. For a command whose whole job is to destroy
things, what it destroys is the one thing its description has to get right.

The tests pin the blast radius rather than the wording: a ~/.co holding skills,
subs, backups, a blocklist and agent.json keeps all of them, and loses the
keypair and keys.env. So the wording cannot drift away from the behaviour again.

Checked while here and left alone: the prompt is real (Prompt.ask, cancels on
anything but Y) and it raises EOFError with no terminal, so the Bash(co *)
remote path cannot reach it.

Every "tested by" pointer names a file that is there (#656)

The LLM-Note headers exist to orient whoever reads a module next. Across the
package, 48 of their 106 test pointers pointed at nothing.

Two causes, treated differently:

  25   the tests moved into tests/unit/ and the headers stayed
       tests/test_address.py  ->  tests/unit/test_address.py
       tests/test_llm.py      ->  tests/unit/test_llm.py

  23   no file of that name anywhere -- dropped, not guessed at

The second group cannot be resolved by matching. Name similarity paired
tests/tui/test_divider.py with tests/unit/test_gdrive.py and
tests/tui/test_dropdown.py with tests/e2e/test_deploy.py. Matching by "which
test imports this module" is no better for the purpose: core/llm.py is imported
by 42 test files, so naming one as THE test is as arbitrary as the wrong pointer
already there. Replacing a dead pointer with a confident wrong one is worse than
removing it, so those say "no direct test file" instead.

Docs only -- every changed line is a `tested by [...]` segment, and the diff
shows nothing else.

The test walks the package and fails on any pointer that does not resolve, so
this cannot rot again the next time tests move. Three more tests pin the parser
itself, so a later "fix" cannot make it pass by matching nothing.

A copied skill leaves its secrets behind (#657)

VERSIONING.md said so in the entry that introduced the command:

    skills carry their own files but never their secrets, and
    `co skills copy --to-project` puts one where a deploy will find it

Nothing implemented it. _copy_entry took the directory whole, and measured on a
skill that kept a credential beside itself:

    src/leaky/.env              -> copied
    src/leaky/credentials.json  -> copied
    src/leaky/keys/id_rsa       -> copied

Nothing in skills_commands.py, useful_plugins/skills.py, the co_ai loader or the
fanout mentions .env or a secret at all, so the sentence was never true of any
skills path.

It matters most where the command points: --to-project puts the skill where
co deploy will find it, and a deploy rsyncs the project tree to a server, so a
credential that lived beside a skill on a laptop lands on the box.

Matched on the name rather than the contents -- guessing at contents gets both
kinds of wrong, and `.env` or `id_rsa` is what people actually use.
`.env.example` is deliberately not caught; it is the file you commit.

Nothing is dropped silently: each skipped file is named. A skill that really did
keep something here would otherwise lose it without a word. A directory left
empty because everything in it was a secret is removed too, since an empty
`keys/` arriving reads as "the keys came along".

After, on the same skill: only SKILL.md arrives, and the three secrets are named
as skipped.

The secret filter covers the shapes the first pass missed (#658)

Step 7 on #657: assume the fix was incomplete. It was. Run against a list of
things people actually keep:

    token.json  auth.json  service_account.json  .git-credentials  secrets.yaml
        names that were simply not in the list

    .ssh/id_ecdsa   .aws/credentials
        a credential DIRECTORY, where naming each file inside is the wrong shape
        of rule -- the first pass named id_rsa and id_ed25519, and id_ecdsa
        walked straight past

So directories that exist to hold credentials are now skipped whole: .ssh, .aws,
.gnupg, .kube, .docker, .azure. Nothing inside one travels, and nobody has to
have thought of the filenames.

An SSH private key is `id_<type>`, so that is the rule rather than two examples.
`id_rsa.pub` is not a secret and still travels.

What must not be caught still is not: config.json, package.json, data.yaml,
README.md, tokens.md, secrets.md -- documentation about secrets is not a secret,
and a rule that eats it is a rule nobody keeps.

The trust lists belong to the agent, not to the directory it was started from (#660)

list_file resolved against the bare cwd:

    return Path.cwd() / ".co" / f"{list_name}.txt"

so running the agent one directory down looked for subdir/.co/contacts.txt.
Measured on a project with a real contact and a real block in its lists:

    from the project root       -> contact
    from a subdirectory of it   -> stranger

The directions are not symmetric. A contact or a whitelisted address demoted to
stranger is refused, which is annoying and safe. A blocked address demoted to
stranger is NO LONGER BLOCKED -- is_blocked() reads the same list -- so someone
who was blocked gets back in, silently, because of where the process was started.

The project fixed this exact shape once already, for the Home page, and left the
rule in dashboard.py: "The directory that owns .co/ -- the project, not wherever
you ran from. Walks up from start. Everything else the agent is made of is found
this way (.co/skills, .co/host.yaml)". The trust lists were the outlier;
_admins_file had been given a co_dir parameter for a related reason, and its
default was the same bare cwd.

Walking up also closes the other half of the hazard that comment names -- a tool
or a plugin calling os.chdir mid-run. Nothing in the codebase does today, but a
user's tool can, and every trust check after it would have read somewhere else.

An agent hosted where there is no .co/ above it still has lists; they live where
it was started, which is what the Home page does too.

An agent started one directory down is still the agent host.yaml describes (#661)

load_host_config resolved against the bare cwd, so starting the agent from a
subdirectory found no host.yaml and every value fell back to a default. Measured
on a project whose file says port 8806, trust careful, 88 permission entries:

    from the project root       port 8806   trust careful   permissions 88
    from a subdirectory of it   port None   trust None      permissions 0

They fall back in different directions. The port lands on 8000, so the agent
listens somewhere else. Permissions land on none, so everything asks -- safe.
Trust lands on "careful", so a project that says `strict` runs as `careful`:
it admits contacts and accepts an invite code while its configuration says
whitelist only.

Two things had to change, and finding the second is why this is not a one-liner.

host() computed `co_dir = Path.cwd() / '.co'` itself before calling
load_host_config, so fixing only the loader would have left the real path
untouched. Two of the tests drive host() and assert what reaches uvicorn and the
banner, because a resolver the real path does not reach is the bug rather than
the fix.

And Logger defaulted to `Path(".co")`, which CREATES a `.co/logs/` wherever the
Agent is constructed. The scaffold builds the Agent before calling host(), so in
a subdirectory the scatter happened first and the walk-up then found that new
`.co` -- the fix defeating itself. Measured: constructing an Agent in a
subdirectory created `.co/logs/` there; it now writes to the project's.

Same rule as #660 and as dashboard.py before it: the directory that owns `.co/`
is the project, not wherever the process was started.

Two assertions in test_logger.py compared a relative path. Same location,
resolved -- and resolved is the point: a chdir after construction can no longer
move where the logs go.

A stray .co/ one directory down quietly replaces the project's own (#663)

#660 and #661 made the rule: the directory that owns `.co/` is the project,
and everything walks up to find it. The walk stops at the *nearest* `.co/`,
which makes any code that creates one wherever it is standing far more
dangerous than it was before those fixes — it plants a decoy that every later
lookup finds first.

Measured on a real scaffolded project (`co init`, `trust: strict`, one
permission), from `deep/nested/`:

  on main                          after this change
  trust      : strict              trust      : strict
  my_tool ok : False               my_tool ok : True
  plan file  : nested/.co/PLAN     plan file  : <project>/.co/PLAN
  -> plan mode planted .co/        -> no decoy
  trust      : None                trust      : strict

Two creators and six readers:

  plan_mode.get_plan_file_path   mkdir'd .co wherever `co ai` was started
  co skills copy --to-project    same, and its SOURCES table resolved the cwd
                                 at *import* time, so nothing could change it
  project skills, subagents, the co_ai loader, the permission whitelist,
  load_admins, get_self_address, the trust agent's own keys

The whitelist is the sharpest of the readers: #661 taught host() to walk up
for host.yaml, and the approval plugin reads permissions out of that same
file — so one half of it was found from a subdirectory and the other was not.
trust/tools.py had the same split inside one file, list_file walking up while
load_admins did not.

The walk itself had been written five times, once per bug that needed it. It
now has one home in connectonion/project.py and the four existing copies point
at it.

from connectonion.logger import Logger raises ImportError (#664)

A regression from #631, which stopped `__init__.py` importing the framework
eagerly. The eager imports had been hiding a cycle:

    connectonion.logger
      -> from .core.usage import totals_from_trace     (line 22)
      -> connectonion.core.__init__ -> from .agent import Agent
      -> from ..logger import Logger                   -- logger is on line 22

Nothing pulls core in first any more, so importing logger from a fresh process
dies. Measured at 6863e45~1 (before #631) against main, one interpreter per
case, because accessing any one attribute imports the others and hides it:

    import connectonion.logger                worked -> ImportError
    from connectonion.logger import Logger    worked -> ImportError
    connectonion.logger                       worked -> ImportError
    connectonion.console                      worked -> AttributeError
    connectonion.derive                       worked -> AttributeError
    connectonion.useful_events_handlers       worked -> AttributeError

The last three are #632's own claim -- "keeps every submodule attribute that
used to resolve" -- and it missed them. They were named from a measured list of
what resolved before, not from reading the imports.

The cycle is closed by importing `.core.usage` inside the one function that
counts tokens, rather than at module level. `co --version` stays at 0.45s.

Hosting from a subdirectory plants a .co/ and loses the session history (#666)

SessionStorage defaulted to a bare relative path and its constructor creates
the directory:

    def __init__(self, path: str = ".co/session_results.jsonl"):
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

host() builds it with no argument, so this is the hosting path. Measured on a
project whose host.yaml says trust: strict, from a subdirectory, on main after
#663:

    storage path      : .co/session_results.jsonl   (sub/.co, not the project's)
    decoy .co created : True
    trust now reads   : None

Two costs. The history goes where no later run looks, so a restart from the
project root cannot see the turns just served. And the created .co/ is a decoy:
the walk-up stops at the nearest one, so the project's own host.yaml and trust
lists stop being found -- a whitelist-only project runs as careful.

#663 fixed the same shape in plan mode and in `co skills copy --to-project`
and missed this one: every test built SessionStorage with an explicit path, so
nothing exercised the default. This PR adds the guard that catches the next
one -- each entry point a hosted agent touches, run in a subdirectory of a real
project in its own interpreter, asserting no .co/ appears. It was checked
against a reverted fix, and against the mistake of probing the *installed*
package instead of this repo, which reported three false creators.

The path is now resolved rather than relative, so a tool calling os.chdir can
no longer move the history mid-run.

What the agent serves comes from the directory it was started in (#667)

Four readers left on a bare relative path after #660, #661, #663 and #666:

    http_router.admin_logs_handler       Path(f".co/logs/{agent_name}.log")
    http_router.admin_sessions_handler   Path(".co/evals")
    slash_command.SlashCommand           Path(".co/commands"), Path("commands")
    send_email.get_agent_email           Path(".co") or Path("../.co")

Measured on a project holding one of each, at two depths:

                    root    sub     sub/deeper
    /admin/sessions 1       0       0
    logs found      True    False   False
    agent email     set     set     None
    slash cmd found True    False   False

The first two are served over HTTP by the hosted agent, so an operator looking
at Home sees no sessions and "No logs found" for an agent that has both.

get_agent_email is the reason the table measures two depths. Someone already
knew the walk was needed and wrote one level of it by hand -- Path("../.co") --
so it survives one subdirectory and returns None from two.

Preserved, not redefined: `commands/` for built-ins. No commands/ directory
ships in the package and there is none at the repo root, so "built-in" here
means a directory in the project. That reading stays; only the resolution
changes.

GET /admin/logs looks for a file the agent never writes (#669)

The endpoint rebuilt the path from the agent's *display* name:

    agent_name = agent_metadata["name"]
    log_path = project_co_dir() / "logs" / f"{agent_name}.log"

agent_metadata["name"] is host.yaml's name, deliberately -- the comment above
it explains why, and for the relay, the directory and /info it is right. The
log file is named by the Logger after the *Agent*. `co init` makes the two
differ by default: host.yaml gets the directory name, the Agent is named in
code.

Measured against a real hosted agent over HTTP, Agent("a-different-agent-name")
in a project whose host.yaml says name: e2e4:

    before                              after
    ls .co/logs/  a-different-agent-name.log      (same)
    /info name    e2e4                            e2e4      (unchanged)
    /admin/logs   {"error": "No logs found"}      the log

Nothing surfaced it because every test passed a name and created a file with
that name, so both sides of the mismatch were the test's own string. Only a
real agent writes under one name and serves under another.

The handler takes the path now, asked of the logger that writes it, which also
reaches `Logger(log=...)` -- an operator with an explicit log file was
unreachable whatever the names matched.

The path stays out of agent_metadata: that dict is published to /info and the
relay directory, and an operator's filesystem layout is not part of an agent's
public profile.

Two existing tests asserted the old signature, including one of #667's own.
Both were updated rather than deleted -- #667's moves to the route, where the
logger's walk-up and the endpoint actually meet.

An agent offers doors that cannot open, and one that opens for a single letter (#671)

* An agent offers doors that cannot open, and one that opens for a single letter

Two problems on the onboarding path, found by driving a real hosted agent over
the relay with `co call`.

1. The advertiser was never compared against the resolver.

   get_onboard_requirements lists a method whenever the policy *mentions* it:

       if "invite_code" in onboard:
           result["methods"].append("invite_code")

   verify_invite does not use that list directly -- it resolves it, and the
   resolver is explicit about an unset variable (#561): "a missing code is a
   closed door, not an open one". So every agent without CO_INVITE_CODE set --
   the default -- offers strangers an invite code that no value satisfies:

       GET /info          "onboard": {"invite_code": true, "payment": 10}
       co call <address>  agent requires onboarding (invite_code, payment)
       verify_invite('anything')  -> False

   This is #561's third path. That fix changed evaluate_request and
   verify_invite, and the comment on the second says why both were needed.

   Payment had the same shape for a different reason: the amount was advertised
   whether or not get_self_address() gave anywhere to send it -- told to pay,
   not told where.

2. A scalar invite code opens for any one of its letters, and refuses itself.

   _resolve_codes iterates what it is given. The shipped policies write a list,
   so a bare string never showed. `invite_code: mycode` -- the natural way to
   write one value in YAML -- iterates the string. Measured:

       _resolve_codes("mycode")        -> ['m','y','c','o','d','e']
       verify_invite(addr, "m")        -> True    (promoted to contact)
       verify_invite(addr, "mycode")   -> False   (the real code refused)

   A scalar `$CO_INVITE_CODE` splits the same way.

Not changed here: `payment: 10` in the shipped careful policy, which every
agent gets without configuring anything. Filed separately -- that is a product
decision, not a bug fix.

* /info reached the opposite conclusion, to the whole internet

There was a fourth place deciding what onboarding exists, and it is the one
without credentials:

    onboard = trust_config.get("onboard", {})
    if onboard:
        result["onboard"] = {"invite_code": "invite_code" in onboard, ...}

trust_config is the *raw* policy, so with no code set this holds the unexpanded
placeholder and the test is still true. Measured with CO_INVITE_CODE absent:

    /info path   (_parse_trust_config)   {'invite_code': ['$CO_INVITE_CODE'], 'payment': 10}
    CONNECT path (get_onboard_requirements)   None

Both now apply one rule, doors_that_open(onboard, self_address), each on its
own input -- so trust_config stays the handler's data rather than becoming a
flag, and a fifth caller cannot reach a different verdict by accident.

Also corrects this branch's own claim. `co init` DOES mint a CO_INVITE_CODE
into the project's .env and importing connectonion loads it, so a laptop
project usually has a working code -- the earlier wording said "every agent
without a code set, which is the default", and that is wrong. Where the code is
missing is the deployed agent: the resolver's docstring notes the env file is
"the one thing co deploy neither rsyncs nor overwrites", so a server whose env
file was never populated runs without one, as does any host() in a project that
never ran co init.

The two Mock-based /info tests keep passing without being touched, which is the
point of passing each caller its own input: a Mock trust that never had a real
config is exactly why neither of them caught this.

connect(address).input(...) cannot talk to a default agent (#673)

`connect` took keys=None and passed it straight through, so the documented
one-liner sent unsigned frames. Measured against a real hosted agent on
trust: careful -- what `co init` writes -- using the example from connect's own
docstring:

    >>> agent = connect("0x3d4017c3...")
    >>> response = agent.input("Book a flight")
    ConnectionError: Auth error: unauthorized: signed request required

The parameter doc said signing was "required for strict trust agents". It is
required by careful too. What careful adds over strict is a way *in* for a
signed stranger, not permission to stay anonymous.

`co call` never hit this because it loaded the keys itself -- a second copy of
the resolver, with a bare Path(".co") that reads the wrong project from a
subdirectory. The host side had already settled the question
(resolve_agent_identity: the project's key, else the machine's ~/.co), so a
client now gets the same answer with the walk-up #661 gave the project half,
and _load_keys is one call into it.

Verified end to end after the change: the documented one-liner reaches a live
agent and returns its answer, over the direct LAN endpoint and over the relay.

keys= still wins when passed, and keys=False still connects anonymously, which
trust: open accepts and people use in development.

The identity prints its own recovery phrase (#674)

address.load() returns a plain dict and puts the 12-word recovery phrase in it,
so printing the object prints the phrase. The object is held in ordinary
places -- it is what load() hands to connect(keys=...), and since #673 every
client stores one by default -- so `print(keys)`, a logger call, a crash
reporter that renders locals, or repr(agent.__dict__) all emit twelve words
that reconstruct the private key.

That is not hypothetical. It happened during review of #673, to a real machine
identity, from a five-line probe that printed the loaded dict.

The phrase stays in the dict, because things need it after loading: `co server`
derives the deploy SSH key from it and `co keys` shows it on request. What
changes is that reading it is something you ask for -- keys["seed_phrase"] --
rather than something that falls out of printing the object.

Identity is a dict subclass whose repr replaces seed_phrase, signing_key and
private_key with <hidden>. Everything else about it is unchanged: isinstance
dict, item access, .get, .keys/.items, deepcopy, equality with a plain dict,
and signing all behave as before. derive_ssh_key's private_key is covered too --
same hazard, different name.

Verified that the deliberate displays still work: `co keys` still shows the
recovery phrase (behind its own masking), because it reads the field.

Check what we ship, not only what we have (#675)

Nothing looks at the artifact that goes to PyPI. The suite runs against the
source tree, where every file is present whether or not it is packaged, and it
cannot be pointed at an install: much of it audits the repository -- VERSIONING.md,
the Makefile, Path(__file__).parents[2] / "connectonion" -- so running it against
a wheel produces failures that are all harness, not package. Measured on a wheel
built from bb67f19:

    51 failed, 4113 passed          against the installed wheel
     0 failed, 4440 passed          against the source tree

Every one of the 51 was the repo not being there. That is not a fault in those
tests, but it leaves the packaged artifact unchecked, and the failures that live
there are invisible from a source checkout: a data file that is not packaged, a
loader that resolves a path from the working directory, an entry point that is
not registered.

This repo has shipped one already. pyproject.toml records it: every wheel went
out without the documentation while `co init` reported ".co/docs/ (full
documentation)" over an empty folder.

So: build a wheel, install it into a throwaway venv, and run the checks from
outside the repo -- the trust policies, the co_ai prompts, the project template,
the docs, the `co` entry point, and `co init` filling .co/docs/.

Two things this had to get right about itself:

  - which connectonion it imports. A subprocess started in the repo has '' on
    sys.path and the source tree wins silently; the first draft did exactly that
    and reported the venv was fine when it had never been consulted. Every check
    runs from a scratch cwd, and one test asserts the import came from this
    venv's directory -- not merely from "some site-packages", which the outer
    environment would also satisfy.

  - that it fails when it should. Verified by excluding the trust policies from
    the wheel in pyproject.toml: one test failed, the rest passed.

Marked slow, so CI's "not slow" selection skips it, and VERSIONING.md's checklist
now says to run it between `python -m build` and `twine upload`. The checklist
guard from #646 caught the first draft of that note naming a path that only
exists inside the built wheel.

It is cheap: --no-isolation build, --system-site-packages venv, --no-deps
install. 8 checks in 14s.

The agent asks a question and the client is handed an empty string (#676)

ask_user sends the question under `question`:

    event = {"type": "ask_user", "question": question, "options": options,
             "multi_select": multi_select}

connect.py read it under `text`. No producer sends `text` -- both
useful_tools/ask_user.py and diff_writer.py send `question` -- so every
multi-turn conversation over the network arrived with the question missing.

Measured against a real hosted agent holding the ask_user tool, from a client
with its own identity:

    before                          after
    done      False                 False
    status    waiting               waiting
    text      ''                    'Which colour do you prefer?'
    ui text   None                  'Which colour do you prefer?'
    options   ['Red','Blue', …]     unchanged

The options arrived all along because that is the one field both sides spell
alike. So a client following the documented contract -- done=False means the
agent asked something, and `.text` is what it asked -- renders buttons under a
blank prompt. multi_select and fields were dropped entirely, so a form asked for
over the network could not be rendered at all; both are carried now.

The suite certified the broken contract. tests/unit/test_connect.py built the
event by hand as {"type": "ask_user", "text": "Which date?"} and asserted the
text came back -- a fake sending a key the real tool has never sent. Corrected
here rather than left agreeing with itself.

`text` is still accepted on the way in: one `or`, and anything built against the
old shape keeps working.

Every tool spins forever in a live client (#677)

tool_call and tool_result are two events, each with its own event `id`. What
they share is `tool_id` -- the LLM's call id, which is what correlates them, and
the producer says so: "tool_id": tool_id,  # LLM's tool call ID for client-side
matching.

The client correlated on `id`, so the match never succeeded. Captured off the
wire from a real hosted agent running a real tool:

    tool_call    id='cce032b5-8037…'  tool_id='function-call-…'  status=None
    tool_result  id='dac9873f-9ee8…'  tool_id='function-call-…'  status=success  result='42'

    ui tool_call entries: [('cce032b5-…', 'running')]

The tool returned 42 and its entry still said `running`. Nothing moves it off
that, so a client rendering the live stream shows every tool spinning for the
rest of the session and never shows a result.

The replayed path already gets this right -- session/ui.py keys on
entry.get('tool_id') -- so reloading the page shows the finished state that the
live view of the same turn does not.

Same shape as #676 and found by the sweep #676 prompted: the client reads a
field the producer fills with something else. The frames in the test are the
ones captured above rather than invented, because a fake that agrees with the
reader is what let both of these live this long. There is also a check that the
replayed half still keys on tool_id, so the two cannot diverge silently again.

`id` stays as the fallback, and the UI event keeps its own `id` -- that is what
a client keys its rendering on.

Verified end to end after the change: status done, result '42'.

A project skill is loadable by name and never listed, one directory down (#678)

#663 gave the loader (`_get_skill_paths`) the walk-up that #660/#661
established, and left `_skill_search_paths` -- the other half of the same
module -- on the bare cwd:

    base = project_dir or (co_dir.parent if co_dir else Path.cwd())

So the two disagree. Measured on a project holding .co/skills/secret-handshake,
from a subdirectory of it:

    _discover_all_skills() sees it : False
    _load_skill() finds it         : True
    project path searched          : <project>/sub/.co/skills

The loader walks up and the discoverer does not. A skill that exists and can be

`.claude/skills` came along with it: same `base`, same bare cwd.

This is my own half-fix. #663 changed the function I was looking at rather than

co deploy one directory down tells you to break your project (#679)

Deploy resolved the project against the bare cwd, so from a subdirectory
_read_project found no .co/host.yaml and said:

    Not a ConnectOnion project. Run 'co init' first.

You are in one. load_host_config(None) from the same directory returns the
project's trust: strict, because #661 taught it to walk up. Only deploy could
not see it.

Following the advice is what makes this a bug rather than a wrong message.
Measured end to end in a subdirectory of a project configured trust: strict:

    co init here
    a decoy .co now exists here : True
    trust now reads             : careful      (was strict)
    _read_project               : name=sub, entrypoint=agent.py

Three things at once. The project's trust is silently downgraded -- a
whitelist-only agent now admits contacts and accepts an invite code -- because
the decoy shadows the real .co, which is the hazard #663 removed. Deploy then

Fixed the way the rest of the codebase already settled: the project is the
directory that owns .co/, found by walking up. Both entry points -- the server

After: from a subdirectory the project is found (name deploy2, entrypoint

_find_co_dir looked in the bare cwd and fell back to the machine's, so one

Measured on a project with its own keypair:

    from the project root   Address 0xd72fbbd5…   Source .co (project)
    from a subdirectory     Address 0x10e68f6d…   Source ~/.co (global)

visible direction, saying they found nothing rather than silently acting on the
wrong thing". True of co status and co doctor; not true here, because the ~/.co
fallback always finds something.

the project's key is found by walking up, as everything else has since #660.

Step 7 caught two things this introduced. The Source label interpolated co_dir

Three lookups in doctor_commands.py resolved the project against the bare cwd,

    project      Keys ✓ .co/keys/agent.key
    project/sub  Keys ✓ <home>/.co/keys/agent.key

#427 step 4: retire the HKDF SSH key and the single global key (#684)

SSH access was a second construction — HKDF over the label
connectonion:ssh:v1 — producing one key for every server, installed into
