  - connectonion:ssh:v1 appears nowhere in the shipped package
  - _hkdf_sha512 is gone from address.py
  - ~/.co/ssh/ holds a key per server; derive_ssh_key requires a host
  - co keys --ssh prints the set, one line per registered server

The precondition was checked against the real fleet first, because #427 says
there is no undo — the way back into a server is a key it already trusts. Each

    nw-runner (claude-runner)    NEW_KEY_WORKS
    nw-prod   (naturewill-test)  NEW_KEY_WORKS
    naturewill-prod              NEW_KEY_WORKS
    test      (co-test-deploy)   unreachable — the box no longer exists

So no reachable machine was left holding only the retired line.

line is kept the way PRE_SLIP10_ADDRESS is kept — as the thing that must not be

TestThePerServerKeyMigration asserted the transitional two-key contract and now
asserts the retirement, with the fleet check recorded in it.

Step 7: co keys --ssh printed each key folded at the terminal width, which is a
broken line once pasted into authorized_keys, and pasting it is the only reason

The deploy already knows .env is not source, and says so:

    # _sync_env(), as a root-owned 0600 file systemd reads — not as a
    # world-readable file that happens to land in the working directory.

RSYNC_FILTERS stopped there. It did not exclude the other shapes a credential
takes — credentials.json, token.json, service_account.json, secrets.yaml,
*.pem, *.key, or an .ssh/ .aws/ .gnupg/ directory in the project. Those went up
as ordinary source, to land at 644 in a 755 tree.

This project already decided what a credential looks like: #657 and #658 built

Verified with rsync itself, not by reading the list:

    transferred      agent.py  config.json  requirements.txt
    not transferred  credentials.json  server.pem  token.json  .env
                     id_rsa  .aws/credentials

A scheduled entry runs once, not once per uvicorn worker (#687)

* A scheduled entry runs once, not once per uvicorn worker

create_app's docstring tells people to run

    uvicorn myagent:app --workers 4

That is a real import string, so uvicorn forks four processes and each one
runs the lifespan, including the scheduler loop. The overlap guard does not
reach across them -- in_flight is a module-level set, so it is per process --
and the state file cannot close the gap either, because record_run does not
write last_run until the turn returns. So all four workers saw the same due
entry and each started its own copy.

Measured, four real interpreters ticking one .co/ together:

    before   4 workers ran it: ['do the thing'] x4
    after    ['do the thing']

The fix is one lock, taken per tick. Whichever worker gets it runs that tick;
the others return without a word -- under --workers 4 a skip is the normal
case three times a minute, and saying so would bury what the running worker
says. Nothing is elected for the life of the process, so a worker that dies
holding it costs one tick rather than stopping the schedule until someone
notices.

Refusal, not retry: the existing _lock() waits and then proceeds anyway,
which is right for a short write to the state file and exactly wrong here,
where proceeding is the duplicate run.

Closes #640. Splits out of #639, which fixed the other half -- workers: 2 in
host.yaml killing the agent. This is the path where forking does work.

* Say why workers is not honoured, without the reason this change removed

usable_uvicorn_options gave two reasons: uvicorn needs an import string,
and the scheduler is per process. The second one is what this branch fixes,
so the operator-facing line now names a limitation that is larger than the
real one.

Say so when two agents answer to one address (#688)

#642, measured on this laptop: 0x10e68f6dff39ab... was announced by two
different agents at once -- `oo` here with bash, write and 22 more, and
`naturewill` on the deployed box with the contract-ledger tools -- because
both loaded the same keypair. Every 1.5.x project's `co init` wrote
AGENT_CONFIG_PATH=~/.co, and a project with no key of its own inherits the
global one deliberately (that fallback fixed a worse bug: the host used to
mint a third address and serve under it while co status reported the
configured one).

Since #643 a client resolves an endpoint directly and picks by proximity, so
a call meant for the deployed agent lands on the local coding agent instead
-- one holding bash and write on the caller's own machine. /info
verification cannot catch it, and cannot in principle: the address genuinely
matches.

The identity directory now records which project and name serves under it,
and a different agent starting on the same keypair is told, by name and
directory, rather than silently joining. The record lives beside the key,
because the whole problem is several projects sharing one identity
directory.

A warning, not a refusal. The agent whose address this is may be the one
restarting, and nothing today mints a local identity for a project that
already exists, so refusing would strand every 1.5.x project with no way
forward. That missing piece is filed separately.

Also: excluded from the deploy. It names a directory on the operator's
machine, so shipping it would put a local path on the server and make the
deployed agent read the laptop's claim as a collision on every start.

The operator sets the price, and only if they set one (#691)

Two halves of the same gate.

#672 -- the shipped careful policy carried `payment: 10` as a bare literal,
so every agent `co init` created advertised a price its operator never
chose, and admitted whoever paid it. `invite_code` next to it reads
$CO_INVITE_CODE specifically so a shipped literal is not one password for
every deployment (#561); payment had no such switch. It has one now, with
the same contract: unset resolves to nothing, never to a default.

#690 -- verify_payment took the minimum from the client's own frame:

    min_amount = amount if amount > 0 else required

The only caller reaches that line when amount > 0, so the operator's price
was never the minimum. An agent advertising 10 was opened by a transfer of
0.01 from anyone who sent {"payment": 0.01}; oo-api confirmed it honestly,
having been asked about 0.01. Both prices now come from one resolver, so
what /info advertises is what the transfer is checked against.

Measured against a real host, its own identity, no relay:

    CO_PAYMENT unset   GET /info -> "onboard": null
    CO_PAYMENT=25      GET /info -> {"invite_code": false, "payment": 25.0}

Zero and below are not prices: `payment: 0` admits a stranger who sends
nothing, which is `open`, and an operator who means that should say so.

Docs: CO_INVITE_CODE was never documented and CO_PAYMENT would have been a
switch nobody could find, so both are now written down with what each does
when unset. Also corrected the trust-level table, which said `careful`
accepts unsigned requests -- no level does; extract_and_authenticate refuses
an unsigned request before it reads the level.

Closes #672. Closes #690.

EXEC asks who is calling, not only what they ask for (#692)

#653 measured the chain on default settings, no attack on the protocol:

    1. connect                  -> ONBOARD_REQUIRED ['invite_code']
    2. submit the invite code   -> CONNECTED       (a stranger is now a contact)
    3. the contact ran  whoami  -> changxing       (the operator's account)

Step 3 worked because the two handlers were not written to the same
standard:

    def handle_ws_input(..., requester_address=None):
        requester = {'address': requester_address, 'level': level}

    def handle_ws_exec(tool_name, args):
        return exec_handler(create_agent, exec_permissions, tool_name, args)

INPUT resolved the caller's level and carried it down. EXEC was handed
neither the address nor the level, so the permission whitelist was the whole
gate and any authenticated connection could run any whitelisted tool. The
session loop said "Auth is the same gate as INPUT" -- the authentication
was; the authorisation was not. conn["agent_address"] had held the caller
since CONNECT and nothing asked it.

EXEC now requires admin or whitelist. It is the terminal-style fast path: no
LLM, no session, no approval hook -- before_each_tool does not fire, so a
tool invoked this way skips everything that normally sits between the model
deciding to call something and it running. A contact can still talk to the
agent through INPUT, where those checks are in the way.

Behaviour change: a caller who is a contact rather than whitelisted stops
being able to drive tools directly over remote.call / co call.

Two existing fakes declared ws_exec(tool, args) -- the signature without the
caller. Updated to the real one; a fake that keeps the old shape is a fake
that certifies the gap.

Part of #653. The other half is the scope of what is whitelisted --
Bash(co *) is auto-approved and co is not a read-only tool -- which is #652.

The trust gate stops crashing on every stranger, and stops selling on credit (#693)

* The trust gate stops crashing on every stranger, and stops selling on credit

Two things on one line, both mine.

#691 made the shipped price opt-in (`payment: $CO_PAYMENT`). Three places
read onboard.payment; that change routed two through a resolver and missed
this one:

    required_payment = onboard.get('payment')
    request_payment = request.get('payment', 0)
    if required_payment and request_payment >= required_payment:

A non-empty string passes the guard, so `0 >= "$CO_PAYMENT"` raised
TypeError on every stranger CONNECT -- the first contact any agent ever has.
Measured against a real host on default trust:

    fast_rules.py:226: TypeError: '>=' not supported between int and str
    client: websockets.exceptions.ConnectionClosedError

The suite was green: nothing drove the CONNECT path with the shipped policy.
Found by starting a real host, not by reading the code.

The older half is worse. `request_payment` is a number the client wrote in
its own request, and nothing on this path verifies a transfer --
verify_payment and its oo-api call are on ONBOARD_SUBMIT. So a stranger who
put a large enough number in a CONNECT became a contact having sent nothing.
#690 was the buyer naming the price; this was the buyer skipping the
payment.

Payment is no longer decided here at all. A stranger offering one falls
through to `default` (ask on careful) and pays through ONBOARD_SUBMIT,
where the transfer is checked. One door, one check.

The tests pin the trust lists per test. They live wherever _project_co_dir()
points, which during a run is shared by the whole session -- measured at
/tmp/.co/contacts.txt -- and promote_to_contact is durable, so the first red
run of this file left its own stranger a contact for the green one.

* Two tests asserted the bypass; correct them with the measurement

test_payment_onboards and test_exact_payment_works asserted that a number
in the client's own request promotes it to contact. Nothing on that path
verifies a transfer. Demonstrated against a real host from a
freshly-generated identity with no balance:

    claimed payment: 999, transferred: nothing
    before -> {"type": "CONNECTED", "status": "new"}   contacts.txt: 1 entry
    after  -> {"type": "ONBOARD_REQUIRED", "methods": ["payment"],
               "payment_amount": 10.0}                    contacts.txt: absent

A stranger is not sent to a door that is not there (#697)

should_allow read the raw config to decide whether onboarding was on offer:

    onboard = self._config.get('onboard', {})
    if onboard and (onboard.get('invite_code') or onboard.get('payment')):
        return Decision(allow=False, reason="Onboard required")

    return self._llm_decide(client_id, request)

Both shipped values are unexpanded placeholders -- [$CO_INVITE_CODE] and
$CO_PAYMENT -- so both are truthy on an agent with neither set, and every
stranger was sent to onboard through nothing.

Two things wrong at once. The stranger was told to onboard while /info,
correctly since #671, published no way to. And _llm_decide never ran:
careful is the default trust level and `default: ask` evaluated by the LLM

Measured against a real host, default trust, no CO_INVITE_CODE, no

  before  {"type": "ERROR", "message": "forbidden: Onboard required"}
          host: [FAST_RULES] Returning None (needs LLM)   <- and then it did not

  after   {"type": "ERROR", "message": "forbidden: The client has a current
          level of 'stranger' and lacks an invite code or verified payment,
          so admission is not justified from identity and level alone."}

doors_that_open is the one rule. #561 fixed two places that decided this

This was the fifth.

A session belongs to whoever started it (#698)

* A session belongs to whoever started it

Measured before: two different identities, both whitelisted on one agent.

    A CONNECTED session=457204c5… status=new
    A -> "Remember this exactly: my codeword is PURPLE-OTTER-42."
    B CONNECTED session=457204c5… status=connected    <- B named A's id
    B -> "What codeword did I give you earlier?"
    B <- "PURPLE-OTTER-42."

The session id comes off the client's frame and nothing checked who it
belonged to. The owner was already recorded -- input_handler writes
session['requester'] from the signature-verified address every turn, and
requester is in SERVER_OWNED_SESSION_KEYS so a client carries it but does
not author it. Nothing read it back.

Three places had to be closed, found one at a time by re-running the
measurement rather than by reading:

  1. establish_connection merged the stored session
  2. the active registry attached the live turn, which streams its output
  3. input_handler looked the session up again on the INPUT that followed

Fixing 1 and 2 alone still leaked. B was correctly told status=new and the
host logged "belongs to another caller", and then its INPUT named the same
id and (3) handed over A's conversation anyway.

Owned by someone else is treated as not found -- a fresh session with that
id, indistinguishable from one that expired. Refusing would confirm it
exists. Nothing legitimate breaks: a session is one conversation with one
caller.

    after   B CONNECTED session=8d240fd0… status=new
            B <- "I don't have a codeword."

Closes #696.

* A squatter gets a different id, so the owner's session survives

Step 7 on my own fix, and it had introduced the next bug.

Treating a session owned by someone else as "not found" was not enough on
its own: the caller kept the id, their turn saved a record under it --
storage is append-only, last entry wins -- and the owner came back to an
empty conversation.

    A turn 1: session=1b7625e1…  -> OK.
    B squats on it (status=new)  -> Hello!
    A returns (status=connected) -> "I don't have a codeword from you."
    A LOST their conversation

Trading a disclosure for a destruction is not a trade. A caller who names
somebody else's session now gets a fresh id, reported in CONNECTED, so the
owner's record is never written to and the client knows which session it is
in.

    A turn 1: session=080d48a3…  -> OK.
    B squats on it (status=new)  -> Hello!
    A returns (status=connected) -> PURPLE-OTTER-42
    A KEPT their conversation

The live-session check moved up with it: a caller who does not own the id is
given a new one before the registry lookup, so there is one place that
decides this instead of two.

One bad command file no longer empties the menu (#700)

list_all() parsed every .md through _parse_file, which raises on a file
without frontmatter, so one typo lost every good command:

    .co/commands/good.md      valid
    .co/commands/broken.md    no frontmatter

    list_all()    -> ValueError: Command file .../broken.md missing YAML frontmatter
    load('good')  -> works

The good command was individually loadable. Only the listing died, so a user
saw no commands at all plus a traceback, for a file they may never have
opened.

A file that cannot be read is now skipped and named. Silence would be its
own bug -- #629 exists because a dropped entry is indistinguishable from one
that was never there -- so list_all(report=True) returns the reasons.

Checked, not caught, copying #629's shape:
_why_the_command_cannot_be_read asks the questions _parse_file would raise
on, so a genuine bug in the parser still surfaces instead of being swallowed
as "malformed". The single try/except is around yaml.safe_load, where the
alternative is writing a second YAML parser.

load() by name still raises: a command you asked for and cannot have is an
error, not something to skip past.

Not decided here: whether a command with no frontmatter should work the way
a SKILL.md with none does -- filename as name, whole file as prompt. The two
subsystems disagree about identical input, which #668 records; that is a
format decision and the menu losing everything is a bug either way.

Closes #668.

One corrupt eval file no longer disables co ai everywhere (#701)

Aaron measured this. The logger writes one eval per unique first input,
.co/evals/{slug}.yaml. Several co ai processes with the same opening line
derive the same slug and write the same file with no locking, and the
interleaved writes leave invalid YAML. Every later call then dies reading
it -- including calls from unrelated projects, because co ai uses the global
~/.co:

    could not find expected ':'
      in ".../.co/evals/5_slam_naturewill_jd_ros2_nav2_a_rrt_teb_mppi.yaml"

What made it expensive to diagnose: the failure is not in the run that
caused it, and co ai puts the error on stderr while writing nothing to
stdout, so a batch script reading stdout sees "the model returned nothing".
In Aaron's pipeline that was "extracted +0 people", exit code 0, green
logs.

Both halves fixed.

The write is atomic: dumped to a temp file in the same directory and moved
into place with os.replace, so a reader sees the old file or the new one and
never half of either. open(path, 'w') truncated first, which is what left
the wreckage.

A corrupt file is no longer fatal: it is renamed aside -- kept, because it
is the record of a run -- and a fresh one started, with a line on stderr
naming both. Same shape as #668 and #629: one bad file is a lost file, not a
reason the CLI stops working.

Closes #695.

Reading sessions needs an identity (#699)

* Reading sessions needs an identity

`curl http://agent/sessions` returned every conversation on the agent --
prompt, answer and full message history -- to anyone who could reach the
port. Measured on a real host, no signature, no identity, no key:

    GET /sessions -> {"sessions": [{"session_id": "9fd5d3fc-…",
                                    "prompt": "What codeword did I give you earlier?",
                                    "result": "PURPLE-OTTER-42",
                                    "session": {…every message…}}]}

POST /input immediately above it in the same dispatch went through
route_handlers["auth"]; these two never did. It is also where #696's attack
got its session ids.

A GET has no body to sign, so the signature travels in headers over
{method, path, timestamp}, canonicalised exactly as CONNECT and INPUT
already are and verified by the same _authenticate_signed -- same freshness
window, same blacklist, no second implementation of either. The payload is
rebuilt from the server's own method and path, so a signature made for one
path does not verify against another.

Scope comes from the owner #698 records: /sessions returns the caller's own,
/sessions/{id} returns one only if they own it. Sessions stored before an
owner existed stay readable, same rule as #698.

    unauthenticated curl     -> {"error": "unauthorized: 'from' field required"}
    signed as A              -> 1 session; result: PURPLE-OTTER-42.
    signed as B (new to it)  -> 0 sessions

The agent's own /docs page advertised the plain curl, which would now be a
documented call that always 401s.

Closes #683.

A captured CONNECT opens nothing twice, and nothing signed goes onto a LAN (#703)

EXEC carries no signature of its own -- the signature authenticates the
connection, and every command on it is trusted because of who opened it. So
a captured CONNECT replayed inside the five-minute window is not 'repeat
what the caller did', it is any whitelisted tool with any arguments, because
the attacker writes the EXEC frames. Measured in #649:

    1st (legitimate)                 -> ran 1 times
    2nd (CONNECT replayed verbatim)  -> ran 2 times
    3rd (replayed again)             -> ran 3 times

Two halves, neither a protocol change.

One signature opens one connection. The attack has to open one; without a
MITM position an attacker cannot inject into a live socket. Legitimate
clients build a fresh CONNECT each time, and the one place this codebase
re-establishes a connection already avoids replaying the frame.

Plaintext only to loopback. #643 made direct resolution work and a
self-hosted agent announces plain ws://, so on a LAN anyone who can watch
the traffic can capture a CONNECT. wss:// is preferred when offered, plain
ws:// is used only where there is no network to observe, and everything else
falls back to the relay.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: a LAN agent reached over plain http/ws is no longer
contacted directly -- that traffic goes through the relay now. Deployed
agents are https (1.5.3) and localhost is unaffected, so both cases direct
resolution was built for keep it.

Not done: signing each command (#649 option 3). That is the complete answer
and a protocol change.

Two test-side consequences, both real rather than cosmetic. The replay cache
is process-global -- it has to be, since the replay it refuses crosses
connections -- so conftest clears it per test; several files send a
hardcoded signature and the second test to use one would be refused for
reasons unrelated to itself. And #643's resolution tests now describe their
LAN and public hosts over TLS, because they are about ordering, not schemes.

Part of #649.

A stray .co above the working directory is a failure, not a wrong answer (#704)

* A stray .co above the working directory is a failure, not a wrong answer

_never_touch_the_real_home isolates HOME, so ~/.co is covered. This is the
other half: project_root() walks up from the working directory, and a stray
.co/ anywhere above it wins.

My own real-host runs left a /private/tmp/.co behind, and afterwards a unit
test unrelated to any of it failed:

    assert logger.log_file_path == Path('.co/logs/test-agent.log').resolve()
    E  assert PosixPath('/private/tmp/.co/logs/test-agent.log') == ...

standalone, so -p no:randomly does not hide it, and invisible on CI where
the machine is clean -- a local run disagreeing with CI for a reason nobody
can reproduce.

The escape, reproduced exactly:

    cwd          /private/tmp/probe_no_co   (no .co of its own)
    project_root /private/tmp               (the stray one wins)

The guard repoints nothing. Tests that chdir into their own project depend
on the walk-up finding it, and pinning the answer would break them. It only
refuses to let the walk-up land somewhere shared, so contamination is named
instead of silently changing what the code under test reads.

Verified by planting a test that chdirs under a stray project: the run ends
non-zero with the guard naming the directory.

It called project_root() in teardown, which calls Path.cwd(). A test whose

    tests/unit/test_relay.py::TestRelaySupervisorResilience::…

The agent log has a ceiling (#705)

.co/logs/{agent}.log was appended to forever -- no maxBytes, no rotation, no
cleanup. Measured in #638 on the deployed naturewill agent over 3.3 days:

    .co/logs/naturewill.log  1.46 MB  ->  ~0.44 MB/day  =  ~160 MB/year

and a working agent on a fifteen-minute schedule at ~1.3 KB/turn, ~44
MB/year. Neither fills the 1-2 GB VPS co server new provisions soon, which
is why that issue was filed rather than fixed -- but 1.6.0 is meant to run
for years unattended, and #637 capped the fast member of the same family.

Rotation, not truncation: at 10 MB the file becomes .log.1 and a fresh one
starts. History is what an operator opens the log for. One generation kept,
so the ceiling is two files.

On open, not from a background thread. These stay ordinary append-only text
files an operator can point logrotate at, and rotating underneath a running
writer loses the lines in flight.

Closes #638.

A running agent compacts its session log (#706)

compact() was called from host() and create_app() and nowhere else, both
startup. An agent left running never compacted -- the ordinary case for what
1.6.0 is for. Its docstring measures the cost: 17 MB for 222 sessions, ~7 MB
a day and 2.5 GB a year on a fifteen-minute schedule, with a dashboard that
reparses the lot each time it is opened. Measured on nw-e2e after ~15 hours:
494106 bytes, 73 lines.

Moving the call was not enough, which is why #625 was filed rather than
fixed. The existing guard reads the size, builds the replacement, reads the
size again and skips if it changed -- but between that second read and the
replace there is still a window, and an append landing in it is in the file
being thrown away. compact() says what that costs: 'A lost session record is
a turn that happened and left no trace.'

So appends and compaction now exclude each other, with the same cross-process
flock schedule.py uses. compact() takes it non-blocking and skips if a turn
is mid-write -- housekeeping, and the next tick compacts. save() waits,
because giving up and writing anyway is exactly the lost turn. That was the
first version here and its test stayed red.

Called from the schedule tick, which already runs every minute and is
already elected to one process per cluster (#687), rather than a second
timer that would add back what that fixed.

Closes #625.

A subscribed skill keeps its instructions and loses its permission grant (#708)

sub_commands.py states its own trust assumption: v1 trusts the relay, which
strips signer and signature, so nothing proves who wrote a fetched skill.

What makes that worth acting on is that a SKILL.md is not only instructions.
Its frontmatter carries a tools: list, and invoking the skill auto-approves
those patterns for the turn -- measured on a real agent:

    during the turn : ['Bash(git status)', 'read_file']

So a synced skill arrives asking for auto-approval from an unverified
source, is written verbatim, and is fanned out into ~/.claude, ~/.codex,
~/.openclaw, ~/.cursor and ~/.kiro. One co sub sync, five agents' skill
directories, four of them not ours.

tools: is now removed on sync. The instructions are what you subscribed to;
the grant is not, and the operator can add the patterns to their own
.co/host.yaml where the decision is theirs and visible. #654's option 2.

Option 1 too: co sub sync --help now says the content is unverified and
where it lands. The warning had been at lines 23-24 of a module docstring --
the person taking the risk was the one who could not see it.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: a subscribed skill that used to auto-approve
Bash(git status) now asks.

Option 3, verifying the publisher's signature, is the real answer and needs
the relay to stop stripping it.

Found while writing it: my first version listed the removed patterns in the
skill body. That body is the prompt an agent reads, and the list is a
decision the operator makes -- so it goes to the terminal at sync time, and
the body only says that something was removed.

Part of #654.

fix(browser): the clipboard keeps its characters on Windows (#584)

The humanize typing path pastes CJK runs through the OS clipboard, because a
real user pastes Chinese far more often than they hand-type it. On Windows it
piped UTF-8 into clip.exe:

    subprocess.run(["clip"], input=text.encode())

clip.exe decodes stdin with the console OEM code page — cp936 on Chinese
Windows, cp932 on Japanese — so 中文 landed on the clipboard as mojibake and
was pasted into the page wrong. Not a crash: the automation reported success
and typed the wrong characters.

Windows now goes through PowerShell with the text carried inside the command as
base64, which is ASCII whatever the console is set to, and decoded as UTF-8 on
the other side. Reading back pins [Console]::OutputEncoding for the same
reason. No code page is consulted in either direction. macOS and Linux are
unchanged; there the text goes on stdin, where UTF-8 is what these tools want.

#277 says the correct fix needs validation on a real Windows box. There are
Windows runners in CI, so the round-trip tests run there — put CJK on the
clipboard, read it back, and check the previous contents are restored. Skipped
elsewhere, which is honest about where they mean anything.

Carrying the text in the command buys a length limit, and that is the shape of
the bug being replaced: Windows caps a command line near 8191 characters and
base64 inflates by a third, so a long paste would be truncated into a fragment,
silently, only for long text. _paste already falls back to the IME path when
the clipboard route is unavailable, so a run that would overflow declines the
route rather than half-using it.

3134 unit tests pass. Closes #277.

Unreviewed AI-generated PRs are arriving, and the current template
actively rewards them. Every gate in it is a checkbox -- "I have tested
this code locally", "I have performed a self-review of my own code" -- and
an agent ticks all of them at zero cost. A checkbox cannot distinguish
someone who read the diff from someone who did not, so it filters nothing.

Replace the parts that can be faked cheaply with prose that cannot:

- Which model and which tool wrote it, named exactly rather than as "AI".
  Capability differs enough between models to change where a reviewer
  looks first. Never grounds for rejection; it calibrates review.
- What the author is least sure about, what they never ran, and what
  breaks first if it's wrong. "I'm not sure" is explicitly allowed --
  without that escape hatch people simply assert confidence instead, and
  the question stops working.
- Real pasted test output instead of a ticked "I tested it" box.
- Which files this touches and why each one has to change.

Also swaps "I have performed a self-review" for "I have read every line of
this diff and can defend each change", which is a claim someone has to be
willing to stand behind in review.

The scope question is doing separate work. The most common reason a
correct-looking PR gets closed here is not wrong code -- it is a change
that spans three subsystems at once, every hunk defensible and CI green,
leaving a design nobody owns. Asking up front makes that visible before
the review, not after it.

Does not touch .github/workflows/, so no workflow scope needed to merge.

docs(protocol): the trust gate answers CONNECT, and that was undocumented (#562)

The protocol reference described CONNECT as always answered by CONNECTED, and
never mentioned the onboard handshake at all. ONBOARD_SUBMIT appeared once, in a
console-log example; ONBOARD_REQUIRED and ONBOARD_SUCCESS appeared nowhere. So the
question direction was documented and the answer direction was not.

That gap has already cost us. A client was built to read the gate from `/info` —
anonymous, and therefore identical for an admin and a stranger, which put a code
prompt in front of people who hold the keys. A second attempt watched for a repeat
ONBOARD_REQUIRED to detect a refused code; refusals come back as ERROR, so that
code could never fire and a wrong code produced no feedback at all. Both are
things the reference should have said.

Adds:

- A "Trust Gate (onboarding)" flow under Protocol Flows, with the three things a
  client gets wrong: the answer arrives before the first message (so no message
  need be spent to discover the gate), a refusal is ERROR and not another
  ONBOARD_REQUIRED, and the stashed CONNECT is resumed by the server rather than
  replayed by the client — replaying it can exceed the five-minute signature
  window while a human hunts for their code.
- ONBOARD_SUBMIT, ONBOARD_REQUIRED, ONBOARD_SUCCESS and ADMIN_RESULT in the
  message reference, with field tables.
- The CONNECT response table now says CONNECTED is not its only possible reply,
  and that the decision is per-caller, made after the signature is verified.

Every claim was checked against a running agent rather than read off the source:
CONNECT answered by ONBOARD_REQUIRED carrying identity and methods and no session,
a wrong code answered by ERROR, a retry on the same socket succeeding, and
CONNECTED arriving on its own afterwards. 8/8.

The protocol doc says what CONNECT does now (#710)

#562 landed a real specification of the onboard handshake -- it had been
undocumented, and two client bugs came out of that. It was written before
this release changed three things underneath it, so it would have shipped
describing behaviour that no longer holds.

ONBOARD_REQUIRED is not sent merely because onboard methods are written in
the policy. The shipped one declares invite_code: [$CO_INVITE_CODE] and
payment: $CO_PAYMENT; with neither set nothing resolves, so a stranger gets
ERROR from the policy rather than an ONBOARD_REQUIRED leading nowhere
(#697).

A replayed CONNECT is refused -- one signature opens one connection (#703).
Worth stating in the spec rather than leaving a client to discover it,
because it is the one case where a byte-identical frame gets a different
answer.

And a session named by someone who does not own it returns a new session
with a new id, not theirs and not an error (#698, #706). The table listed
'not found' but not 'not yours'.

co server new asks for a key by name, so it can create a server again (#712)

Measured, trying to provision a machine for this release's end-to-end test:

    $ co server new rel160-e2e --yes
    No SSH key to install.
    The key is derived from your recovery phrase; without it the server would
    be created with no way in.

The phrase was there — co keys --ssh lists a derived key for every registered
server. The key was never asked for:

    def _ensure_ssh_key(name: str = None):
        if not name:
            return None

    handle_server_fix_key:  _ensure_ssh_key()      # no name
    handle_server_new:      _ensure_ssh_key()      # no name

Both take name and neither passed it, so both always took the failure
branch. co server new could not create a server at all, and co server
fix-key — which exists to recover a machine that will not take your key —
could not fix one.

#464 gave _ensure_ssh_key the parameter when the key became per-server
(#427). Three call sites, one updated.

Nothing caught it because the tests for these commands mock
_ensure_ssh_key itself: a fake that answers regardless of its arguments
cannot notice that the caller passes none. The new test reads the call
sites instead.

Verified against the real API: the command now gets past the key check and
reaches provisioning, where it failed on a GCE address quota and correctly
refunded.

A keyless project knows its own address, and can take payment (#719)

Two places in the trust layer loaded the agent's key straight from the project
directory. Neither co init nor co create writes one, so both came back empty.

Paid onboarding could never succeed. _verify_transfer_via_api loaded keys to
sign the oo-api request and returned False when there were none — before making
the call. Measured on main, in a keyless project:

    project_co_dir(): .../keyless/.co
    address.load(...): None
    => verify_payment returns False before any oo-api call

A stranger who really had transferred the money was refused, and the refusal is
indistinguishable from "you did not pay".

And the address to pay was not the agent's: get_self_address has the same shape,
so doors_that_open advertised either no payment door at all — nothing to send to
— or a stale one from address.json.

Both ask project_identity now: the project's own key, else the machine's, which
is what the host already serves under.

Deliberately not a per-project derived identity. An address is what an OpenOnion
account is keyed on — authenticate() signs with it and the backend issues the
token for that public key — so minting one per project would give every project
an empty balance. That was #715; Aaron stopped it and he was right.

co doctor had the same rule twice in one file: the keys row, and the
connectivity check picking a key to sign the backend probe with. They agreed by
luck, and nothing made them. The probe asks the resolver now. The row still
names a file, which is a different and worth-printing question — there is a test
that the file it names holds the identity it authenticates as.

A credential conflict says which value is used (#718)

* A credential conflict says which value is used

co status reported

    Gemini  GEMINI_API_KEY  conflict  process environment + <project>/.env

Both true, and one word short of the answer. An operator reads this panel
because something is using the wrong key, and the natural guess is that the
project's own .env wins, being the more specific of the two. It does not:
load_dotenv() does not override a variable already in the environment, so the
process environment wins. Measured:

    .env says: project-value | environment says: environment-value
    the value an agent would use: environment-value

The information was already there. _credential_sources returns its sources in
precedence order and the row preserves it, so the first one found is the winner
and nothing said so.

Marked rather than reordered or trimmed: where else a key is defined is the
other half of what the operator came for.

* The conflict test keeps its subject and takes the new source string

Its name says what it is for — reporting conflicting sources *without values* —
and the three no-leak assertions are that subject. The exact source string was
incidental, and now carries which of the two is used.

init and create say what they actually do with keys (#720)

Both headers claimed key generation:

    create.py:7   … uses address.generate() for Ed25519 keypair
    init.py:7     … uses address.generate() and address.save() for Ed25519 keypair

Neither file calls either function. Confirmed by running it: co create
demo-agent --yes leaves a .co/ with host.yaml, docs, admins.txt and logs, and no
keys/. The project reports the machine's address.

The generation those lines describe happens in ensure_global_config(), for
~/.co — the machine's identity, not the project's. A real thing, in the wrong
place.

It cost something. #642 states as fact that co create writes a project-local
keypair and scoped its problem to legacy co init projects on that basis. It is
not a legacy problem, and I read that premise as given for several rounds before
measuring it.

The test compares the header against the file's own calls rather than trusting
either, and pins the fact the headers got wrong — if these commands ever do write
a project key, it fails and asks for the header back.

The agent does not get to write the files that decide what it may do (#723)

* The agent does not get to write the files that decide what it may do

load_config_permissions() reads .co/host.yaml into session['permissions'], and
nothing treated that file as different from any other. With write allowed —
the configuration any coding agent has — the agent could write it:

    perms = {'write': {'allowed': True}, 'edit': {'allowed': True}}

    write  notes.md               -> (True, 'allowed')
    write  .co/host.yaml          -> (True, 'allowed')     <- its own whitelist
    write  .co/schedule.yaml      -> (True, 'allowed')

A prompt-injected turn writes itself Bash(*) and every later turn, in every
later session, is unrestricted. The gate is real and the thing it gates decided
its own rules.

Four files are refused however generously file writing was configured:
host.yaml, schedule.yaml, admins.txt and keys/. They decide what the agent may
do and who may command it. Everything else under .co/ stays writable —
dashboard.html *is* the Home page and the dashboard skill builds it, so a
blanket ban would break a feature to close a hole.

Paths are normalised first, so ../.co/host.yaml and an absolute path reach the
same answer. A check that only matches the tidy spelling is a check with a
published bypass.

For bash it is a speed bump and the code says so. It catches a control path
written literally; it does not catch `cd .co && echo x > host.yaml`, and nothing
word-shaped can — that would mean interpreting the shell. What bounds bash is
the operator's own whitelist, and Bash(*) has already granted everything. There
is a test asserting the bypass exists, so nobody mistakes the speed bump for a
boundary.

* Guard the path the agent's own turn takes, not only the other one

is_tool_permitted is not where the attack lands. check_approval — the
before_each_tool hook, which runs when the agent itself calls a tool — has its
own copy of the matching and never calls it. Its docstring calls them "same
matching the LLM approval flow uses in check_approval", which reads like a
guarantee and is a duplication.

So the guard I added covered network EXEC and left the agent's own turn — the
case this issue is about — exactly as it was. Measured, driving the real hook:

    write .co/host.yaml  ->  allowed

Both paths call one _refuse_control_file now.

The test that found it was wrong first, in a way worth recording.
check_approval(agent) takes only the agent; the call under consideration comes
from session['pending_tool']. My harness passed tool_name= and tool_args= as
keywords, which are not parameters, so every call raised TypeError, the except
read it as a refusal, and the two tests expecting a refusal passed for that
reason. Two green tests off a TypeError, in a file about false confidence.

A schedule entry can run a command, not only a prompt (#721)

From #709, measured on a real agent. A task whose whole job was running one
script logged, on several consecutive runs:

    [co] ✓ The agent successfully executed the `stats.py` script and updated ...

The output file's mtime never changed. Running the script by hand on the same
box, as the same user, updated it immediately. So the schedule reported success
for about a day while the dashboard served day-old numbers.

Structural rather than a one-off: `run` is a prompt executed through the same
path as POST /input, and there was no way to say "just execute this command".
Deterministic maintenance went through a model that can claim completion, and
the log line was that model's own account — nothing compared it against the
filesystem.

An entry may now say `exec:` instead of `run:`. The command runs and what is
recorded is its exit code, which nothing has an opinion about. On failure the
command's own stderr is kept: a non-zero exit with nothing to read is a mystery
at 3am, and the schedule state is where someone will look.

Both keys on one entry is a problem, not a default — two answers to "what does
this do" is a question, and picking one silently is how the wrong half runs.

Verified on a real host:

    command ran: YES
    stamp    status=done    reason=
    broken   status=failed  reason=exit 3: real-reason

Two things found reviewing my own change. An unnamed exec entry would have been
called "None", because the name falls back to `run`. And Home takes `run` for
each row, so an exec entry would have shown a scheduled task with a blank where
its work should be.

Closes #709.

Half the selectable models were billed from a made-up price

MODEL_REGISTRY offers 21 models. MODEL_PRICING and MODEL_CONTEXT_LIMITS held
11 of them, so the other 10 were costed from DEFAULT_PRICING, 1.00/3.00 — a
figure that is no real model's price.

The prefix fallback was supposed to cover this, and it widens in one direction
only: a queried name may be longer than a key. OpenAI and Gemini rows are
keyed on the bare family name and the world ships dated variants, so that is
the right direction for them. The Claude rows were stocked the other way — the
table held claude-sonnet-4-20250514 while the registry offers the bare alias
claude-sonnet-4 — and

    "claude-sonnet-4".startswith("claude-sonnet-4-20250514")  ->  False

One model, two spellings, two answers on identical token counts:

    claude-sonnet-4-20250514   1M in + 1M out   $18.00   correct
    claude-sonnet-4            1M in + 1M out   $ 4.00   fallback

The whole claude-opus-4-1 family read $4.00 against a true $90.00, and every
Claude alias reported a 128000 context window instead of 200000 — the side
that decides when auto-compaction fires.

Fixed by keying the Claude rows on the family, which the existing longest-first
prefix match then resolves in both directions. Opus 4 and 4.1 cost the same, so
one claude-opus-4 row covers the family and no entry shadows another.

Two old tests asserted a literal dated key was in the dict. That is not the
same question as whether the model gets priced, and asking it that way is how
this survived: the test and the table agreed with each other while neither
agreed with the registry. They now ask the lookup.

The new test asserts the invariant across MODEL_REGISTRY rather than a list of
names, so a model added tomorrow without a price fails here.

## The first version of this fix was wrong

It compared the registry against Google's ListModels endpoint, passed, and
missed a third of the problem: ListModels advertises both gemini-3-pro-preview
and gemini-2.0-flash while neither can complete a call. On the strength of that
green check I had added gemini-2.0-flash to the registry as a live replacement.

Listed is not callable. The network test now sends one real request per offered
model, which is the only thing that establishes a name works.

gemini-2.0-flash and gemini-3-pro-preview keep their MODEL_PRICING rows on
purpose: a price for a retired model costs nothing and lets an old session's
tokens still cost correctly. The registry is the list of what a user may pick,
and that is the one that has to be true.

Say what MODEL_REGISTRY actually is

My own commits in this branch described it as the list of models a user may
select. It is not. create_llm consults it, then falls through to inferring the
provider from the name's prefix:

    provider = MODEL_REGISTRY.get(model)
    if not provider:
        if model.startswith("gpt") or model.startswith(OPENAI_REASONING_PREFIXES):
        elif model.startswith("claude"):
        elif model.startswith("gemini"):
        else: raise ValueError

Measured: gpt-5, gpt-4o and claude-sonnet-4-5 are all absent from the table and
all route fine. Only a name with no recognisable prefix is refused.

So dropping the three retired Gemini entries blocks nobody — a user who asks for
gemini-3-pro-preview still reaches Google and still gets its 404. What the
registry is, is the curated list: the names this project vouches for, prices, and
prints to users. The functional fixes in this branch are the GeminiLLM class
default and the list the CLI advertises. The registry edit is us stopping
recommending a dead name, which is worth doing and is not the same claim.

Renames the test file accordingly and drops "routable"/"selectable" from the
assertions, which asserted the right invariant under the wrong name.

Filing wrong claims in comments as bugs all release (#717, #724, #726) and then

Answer a mistyped command once (#714)

    $ co skil
    No such command 'skil'. Did you mean 'skills'? Did you mean 'skills'?

Click builds the message with its own suggestion and Typer's resolve_command
appends a second to whatever Click produced. It happened at every level —
top-level, subcommand, and the nested `co outlook contact` group.

Turns Typer's layer off and keeps Click's, which is the one that would still be
there if Typer were dropped tomorrow.

All twelve groups had it, so the switch goes in one factory rather than at the
call sites: a fix applied twelve times is a fix the thirteenth group does not
get. The test walks the command tree recursively and asserts no group anywhere
still appends its own — which is what caught outlook_contact_app, a multi-line
construction the first pass missed.

    co skil            -> No such command 'skil'. Did you mean 'skills'?
    co depoly          -> No such command 'depoly'. Did you mean 'deploy'?
    co server lst      -> No such command 'lst'. Did you mean 'ls'?
    co outlook contat  -> No such command 'contat'. Did you mean 'contact'?

Checked by running the CLI as a process against this worktree, not only through
CliRunner: the first check I ran used the globally installed `co`, which is
1.5.11, and reported the fix had done nothing.

Fix the typo suggestion properly, and stop a colon from hiding a skill

## The typo fix I pushed last was wrong, and CI caught it

Turning Typer's `suggest_commands` off removed the doubling on typer 0.20 and
removed the *only* suggestion on 0.27:

    CI (typer 0.27.1):  No such command 'skil'.

The two clauses arrive by different routes. Click 8.4's NoSuchCommand keeps
`possibilities` and appends its clause when the message is rendered:

    def format_message(self):
        if not self.possibilities:
            return self.message
        return f"{self.message} {_format_possibilities(self.possibilities)}"

while Typer writes a copy into `.message` beforehand. On 0.27 Click gets no
possibilities, so Typer's copy is the only one there is.

So the text copy is dropped exactly when the exception will render one itself.
Verified by installing CI's typer and running the real CLI on both:

    typer 0.20  co skil / co server lst / co outlook contat  -> one clause each
    typer 0.27  co skil / co server lst / co outlook contat  -> one clause each
    both        co zzzzzz                                    -> no clause

An earlier version of the unit test reimplemented the production logic inside
itself, so it would have passed whatever the code did. It now stubs the layer
underneath and drives the real resolve_command.

## A colon in a description made a skill invisible to the model

`_parse_skill_content` returned `{}` on a YAMLError. The description is what the
model is given to decide whether a skill applies, so the skill was listed with
nothing about when to use it and was never chosen. skills.py already described
this outcome, in the comment explaining why `co doctor` reports these files — the
detection was built and the swallowing was left.

Eight skills installed on this machine were in that state, every one written by the
coding agent that produced them, which loads them all. The cause is an unquoted colon in a value:

    description: …from a local Markdown draft: prepare or generate a cover…

YAML stays the authority. A file it rejects now gives up its `name` and
`description` only — deliberately not `tools:`, which is fed to
_grant_skill_permissions. test_one_reader_for_skill_frontmatter recorded the rule
as "neither invents a reading of a file that has a syntax error in it", and
guessing a permission from a line split would break it. A broken file still
grants exactly nothing, and `co doctor` still reports it.

Two existing tests asserted `frontmatter == {}`. Both now state the narrower
contract they were protecting.

## Bare `co` said "Commands:" while omitting eight of them

ai, announce, call, reset, server, setup, skills and sub are all real and none
appeared. `co --help` is generated and does list all 24, so nothing was promised
that does not exist — the heading was just claiming to be the register. It says
"Common commands:" and points at `co --help`. Which of the eight belong on a new
user's first screen is a product call, left alone. A test locks the invariant
that every name on that screen is a command you can run.

A dead browser is no longer reported as open (#711)

Reproduced against the running daemon while doing the release e2e. Every
command, not one, and no recovery:

    $ co browser go_to https://chat.openonion.ai
    TargetClosedError: BrowserContext.new_page: Target page, context or browser
    has been closed
    $ co browser go_to https://chat.openonion.ai      # again, and again
    TargetClosedError: BrowserContext.new_page: ...

Meanwhile `co browser status` said `Browser: open`. Both read
_context_is_alive(), which asked the wrong question:

    # Alive = the context still answers protocol calls. Zero open pages is
    # still alive (a page opens on demand), so listing pages IS the check.
    list(self.browser.pages)

`pages` is a local list, not a protocol call. So the serve loop never exited,
the endpoint stayed bound, and the daemon went on accepting commands it could
not run. `open_browser` has a teardown-and-relaunch path, but per-command
dispatch reaches `_ensure_page`, which guards `if not self.browser` and whether
the *page* is closed — never the context.

Only a round-trip can answer it. Measured with the browser process killed,
which is how it goes in the field:

    is_closed()      ->  False   a flag set by close(), and close() never ran
    len(ctx.pages)   ->  1       the local list still holds the dead tab
    ctx.cookies()    ->  TargetClosedError
    ctx.new_page()   ->  TargetClosedError   <- what the user hits

is_closed() stays as a sufficient negative — if it says closed, it is — and
cookies() is the authority.

My first version of this used is_closed() alone. It passed a test built on a
politely closed context and then failed the same real replay it was meant to
fix, because a killed browser reports False. That is the second time on this
issue that a local attribute was mistaken for asking the browser: the attempt
before mine checked `context.browser`, which is None for
launch_persistent_context, and its unit tests passed only because a MagicMock
carried an attribute the real object does not. So the tests here open a real
browser through the real driver and kill it with SIGKILL.

Verified end to end, same sequence before and after:

    before    kill browser -> status "open"      -> every command TargetClosedError
    after     kill browser -> status "not open"  -> next command navigates

and the release e2e it was blocking now runs: chat.openonion.ai loads and

doctor: say how much disk co has taken

`co ai` writes one eval per distinct first prompt plus a directory of runs for
it. Runs inside an eval are capped — KEEP_RUNS_PER_EVAL = 20, trimmed after
every write — but the number of evals is capped by nothing, so a one-off prompt
leaves its directory for good. On the machine this was found on:

    ~/.co/evals   857 evals, 858 run directories, 217 MB

and neither `co doctor` nor `co status` mentioned it. The largest thing co
writes was the one thing the diagnostic did not report.

A note, not a problem row, and not a deletion — which evals are worth keeping is
the user's call, and not being able to see the size is what stops them making
it. Quiet below 20 MB, because a line printed every run is a line nobody reads.
Verified on the real directory, and the problem count stayed at 8.

faster for non-Latin prompts: they used to collide into default.yaml, which
bounded the count by accident.

a bound that a test asserts and the field does not have. It is not: copying the
367-run directory and calling _trim_old_runs on the copy took it to 20, keeping
the newest. Those runs predate the cap, and the next run of that eval trims
them. The cap works; only directories never used again keep their history.

Reading an agent's logs no longer needs the key that pays for its models (#670)

/admin/logs and /admin/sessions authenticated with Bearer OPENONION_API_KEY —
the key `co auth` obtains, `co create` writes into the project's .env, and every
co/* call sends to oo.openonion.ai. So letting anyone read an agent's activity
meant handing over the credential that spends its money.

/superadmin/* take a signed request and check admins.txt, with GETs signing via

families go through one _admin_signature, so the check guarding the trust routes
cannot drift from the check guarding the logs. That is the failure shape this
release has hit most often.

drop the key.

The payload is still {timestamp} alone, so a signature is not bound to the route
it authorises — an unspent one can be spent on a route the signer did not choose.

with x-co-* headers, and its comment is about exactly this hazard:

    One canonicalisation, one freshness window, one blacklist check -- a second
    implementation of any of those is how the halves of a gate drift apart

Binding the payload changes what every existing client must sign, which is a
coordinated change with a compatibility window, not a line in a bug-fix branch.

First run on a HOME that does not exist ended in a traceback

Reproduced while probing something else, with HOME pointing at a directory I had
not created:

    global_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/…/fakehome/.co'

`exist_ok=True` creates one level, and `~/.co` is the first thing this project
puts under HOME — so with HOME absent there is no parent to create it in, and a
FIRST RUN ends in rich's traceback renderer instead of a message. This project is
deliberate about not doing that elsewhere (`send()` catches every setup
RuntimeError so typer's pretty exceptions never print frame locals), and a first
run is the worst place for it: the reader has nothing else to go on.

An absent HOME is not exotic — containers and sandboxes hand over one that has
not been created, and this repo ships a Dockerfile.

`parents=True` in the two places that create `~/.co` itself: ensure_global_config
and the reset path. It cannot do less than exist_ok alone did, and the test pins
that it stays idempotent.

Scope: the other fourteen bare `mkdir(exist_ok=True)` calls are ordering-guarded,
not broken — they sit under the cwd (a project's `.co`, whose parent is where you
are standing) or under `~/.co` after auth has already created it.

Verified on a real non-existent HOME: the three directories are created and key
generation is reached, no traceback.

Found via a pyflakes sweep for dead assignments, which is also what turned up
`is_html` in the previous commit. The other two live findings from that sweep are
in #733: `co init` discards `authenticate()`'s result, and

    $ co call --out /tmp/notimage.png 0xcf1619cb… uptime

    exit=0

    ls: cannot access '/tmp/notimage.png': No such file or directory

The flag is documented as image-specific and that part is honest:

    --out PATH   save an image result (screenshot) to PATH; else ./screenshot.png

What it did not say is what happens when the result is text, and the answer was
that the option is dropped without a word. `co call --out result.txt <addr> co
status` reads like "save the output to a file" to anyone who has not read that
line, and they got no file and no explanation.

module's own contract; exit stays 0 because the call succeeded and only the save
did not apply; and the text is still not written to the path, since putting it in
a .png would be worse than not writing.

exit 0.

Keep tests/unit runnable: move the browser test out, cap every test

`tests/unit/test_a_dead_context_is_not_reported_open.py` starts Playwright and
launches real Chrome, then locates that browser with `pgrep` and kills it.
`tests/TEST_ORGANIZATION.md` defines `tests/unit/` as "fast, deps mocked" and
`tests/e2e/` as "real protocol, real I/O", so it moves.

It also hangs. Two runs of `pytest tests/unit` on a developer machine stopped at
2% and never returned — killed after 25 minutes — both at the same test. A third
run passed in 34 seconds, so it is intermittent, which is worse: there is
nothing to reproduce and nothing to bisect.

That is what the timeout is for. `pytest.ini` has carried

    # Test timeout (if pytest-timeout is installed)
    # timeout = 300

since before the dependency was installable. Adding pytest-timeout to the dev
extra turns those two lines on.

Without it a hung test and a slow test are the same event: no output, no
failure, nothing to grep, and the natural reading is that your own change broke
something. With it, one test fails with a traceback naming itself and the other
several hundred still report.

300s is far above anything here — CI runs the whole suite in about seven
minutes — so it only fires on something genuinely stopped. A test that needs
longer says so with @pytest.mark.timeout(N).

browser: choose the engine from the attested tier, and never withhold one (#782)

* browser: choose the engine from the attested tier, and never withhold one

The decision half of openonion/connectonion#511: free drives patchright, pro
drives the onion browser. A pure function, no network, so the rule that matters
is testable directly —

    nothing here may stop a browser from starting

A default install drives system Chrome through patchright today with no licence
call anywhere on that path. Measured on a clean Ubuntu box, not assumed: a fresh
venv installs co 1.6.0 and patchright 1.61.2, `co browser --headless go_to`
navigates, and the process that serves it is /opt/google/chrome/chrome. So the
free path cannot currently be blocked by billing, an expired attestation or an
oo-api outage, and tiering must not hand a free user a new way to fail.

Every branch therefore ends in an engine. What varies is which, and whether
there is one line worth saying:

    no attestation      patchright, silent   (offline, or no account — not a sale)
    tier=free           patchright, "unlocks at $10.00"
    pro, not active     patchright, "balance empty"
    pro, binary absent  patchright, "not installed yet"
    pro, present        onion, silent

The "binary absent" branch exists because onionwright is not a dependency of
connectonion, so a paying customer's first launch has nothing on disk to run. A
pro attestation with no binary must not leave them worse off than a free user.

A malformed payload reads as no licence, deliberately: guessing pro would try to
launch something that may not exist, guessing free just works.

Adds resolve() on top of choose(): ask whether the paid package is installed
and whether a licence is cached, then apply the policy.

The design decision worth stating: **the presence of the onionwright package is
itself the free/paid signal.** _cached_attestation() opens with
`from onionwright.licence import ...`, so on a default install it raises
ImportError before a token is read or a socket opened. A free machine touches
the network exactly as often as it did before tiering existed — never — and
that falls out of the structure rather than out of remembering to guard it.

Reading the cache rather than refreshing is also deliberate. A browser command
is not where anyone should discover oo-api is slow; the refresh belongs to the
licence client's own 12-hour half-life schedule, not to `co browser go_to`.

Both lookups are injected and both are wrapped, so every way of failing to
establish a licence — no package, expired token, unreadable disk, oo-api down —

safe — to the free engine — which is why 44 green tests missed them.

1. _onion_path() called launcher.installed_path(), which does not exist in

2. _cached_attestation() was a NotImplementedError stub, so a machine that had
   paid, held a valid cached attestation and had the binary still resolved to

Every test injects both lookups, so neither default was ever executed. The
parametrised sweep asserts an engine always comes out — true, and still true
with both defaults broken, because broken defaults produce the free engine. I
proved the property I wrote the tests for, not the one that matters: that a
paying customer gets what they paid for.

That is the same shape as the two defects this change exists to fix.
/license/download computed an attestation and ignored it; attest() accepted a
tier and never checked it. Code that looks like it is doing the work.

So: the guessed API is gone, both defaults now name what is actually missing
(cache path, pinned server key, Chromium revision — none of which connectonion
holds yet), and test_the_paid_path_is_not_wired_up_yet asserts the gap out loud.

writing it as a test instead of a comment.

fix(syno): send the upload sid in the query, and let it survive a stale session (#808)

Closes #794. `co syno put` failed on every path with 'SID not found' (DSM 119)
while ls, get and share worked on the same session.

Two causes, both from upload being the one call that does not go through
_request():

1. It passed `_sid` as a multipart form field. `_call()` and `download()` both
   put it in the query string, and SYNO.FileStation.Upload only reads it there.
   One inconsistency, one broken command.

2. 119 is already in STALE_SESSION, but only _request() acts on that set, and
   upload posts multipart so it cannot use _request(). The command most likely
   to meet a dead session — a long upload — was the only one that could not
   recover from one.

Closes half of #800. `Outlook.send()` takes attachments and `Gmail.send()` did

The message becomes MIMEMultipart only when there is something to attach. Always

produces for no reason, and a single-part multipart renders differently in some

recipient sees and what their client uses to decide how to open it.

The CLI precheck mirrors Outlook's: a missing path costs a message, not a
traceback after megabytes have been base64-encoded. The limit deliberately is
not shared -- Gmail takes 25MB where Graph stops at 3MB, so borrowing Outlook's
number would refuse mail Gmail accepts. There is a test for exactly that: a 5MB
file, over Graph's limit and under Gmail's, must send.

Scheduling and contacts stay unbuilt and are described in #800 rather than
half-done: the Gmail API has no scheduled send at all (it is a web-client
feature), and contacts need the People API, which is a new OAuth scope that
forces every connected user back through consent.

Keep tests/unit runnable: move the browser test out, cap every test

`tests/unit/test_a_dead_context_is_not_reported_open.py` starts Playwright and
launches real Chrome, then locates that browser with `pgrep` and kills it.
`tests/TEST_ORGANIZATION.md` defines `tests/unit/` as "fast, deps mocked" and
`tests/e2e/` as "real protocol, real I/O", so it moves.

It also hangs. Two runs of `pytest tests/unit` on a developer machine stopped at
2% and never returned — killed after 25 minutes — both at the same test. A third
run passed in 34 seconds, so it is intermittent, which is worse: there is
nothing to reproduce and nothing to bisect.

That is what the timeout is for. `pytest.ini` has carried

    # Test timeout (if pytest-timeout is installed)
    # timeout = 300

since before the dependency was installable. Adding pytest-timeout to the dev
extra turns those two lines on.

Without it a hung test and a slow test are the same event: no output, no
failure, nothing to grep, and the natural reading is that your own change broke
something. With it, one test fails with a traceback naming itself and the other
several hundred still report.

300s is far above anything here — CI runs the whole suite in about seven
minutes — so it only fires on something genuinely stopped. A test that needs
longer says so with @pytest.mark.timeout(N).

Refs #850

Stop the project walk at the repository and at $HOME

`project_root()` looked for the nearest `.co/` above the working directory with
no upper bound, so nothing told it when it had left the project. This module's
docstring already records the shape of the resulting bugs:

    Two of those bugs failed open: a project configured `trust: strict` ran as
    `careful`, and an address on the blocklist read back as a stranger.

It calls the cause a "stray `.co/`". On any ordinary machine there is always
one: `~/.co` is the *global* config directory and sits directly above every
directory the user owns. Measured before this change:

    ~/Desktop   ->  /Users/me       ($HOME, via the global ~/.co)
    /tmp        ->  /private/tmp    (a stray any user on the box can create)

So `co` run anywhere under $HOME outside a project believed it was in a project
rooted at $HOME and read the machine's own config — trust lists included — as
that project's. Silent, and it fails open.

Two boundaries, both meaning "the project cannot be above here": a directory
holding `.git` (a `.co/` reached by climbing out of the checkout belongs to
something else — `.git` is a file in a worktree, so `.exists()`, not
`.is_dir()`), and `$HOME` itself, whose `.co/` is never a project's own.

The global `~/.co` stays reachable where it is genuinely global:
`project_identity()` falls back to `address.load(Path.home() / CO_DIR)` by name
and is untouched. The bug was never that `~/.co` gets read — it is that it got
read as one particular project's configuration by whoever stood in the wrong
directory.

Behaviour on the two paths that already worked is unchanged: a subdirectory
still finds its project, and a directory with no project above it still falls
back to itself.

Closes #846

ci: install pytest-timeout wherever pytest runs

pytest.ini sets `timeout` and the suite runs under --strict-config, so a
runner without the plugin exits on an unknown ini option before collecting
anything. The test job and the windows-browser job both install their test
dependencies by explicit list rather than from the dev extra, so both need it

Route the browser agent's key through the account check

`resolve_api_key()` was a second implementation of `load_api_key()` — read the
environment, else `~/.co/keys.env` — missing the one thing that matters on this
path: `_token_for_this_account()`, which checks the token belongs to the account
whose key this machine holds.

It matters here more than most places. `co browser do` and `click` bill a model
call to whatever the token says, and `daemon.py:642` resolves the key once at
daemon startup — so a wrong token is not one wrong command, it is every command
until the daemon restarts.

That is not hypothetical. `co browser click` reported insufficient credit on an
account with a healthy balance: a `.env` in the working directory named a
different agent, drained to $0.001, and the daemon had taken it at startup. The
error was accurate. It was about someone else's balance.

The fix is not a better copy of the lookup — it is to stop keeping a copy. The
"" contract callers depend on is preserved.

Add acp_agent: one ACP client tool for every ACP-speaking engine

Neither of the two priority engines speaks ACP natively — both route through
adapters maintained by the ACP org (@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp,
@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp), while Gemini CLI speaks it with
--experimental-acp. The protocol side is identical for all of them, so this
is one tool with an engine table, not a tool per engine: written once, it
gains every agent in the ACP registry, and `command=...` drives any other.

The engine's inner steps stream as the same native events codex.py already
ships — tool_call / tool_result with a stable tool_id — so @connectonion/react
renders the sub-agent's command runs and file edits live with no frontend
change. session/request_permission routes through the same operator approval
gate as every other tool.

Two decisions worth recording:

- Not the acp SDK's client side: that API is asyncio-based, and tools run as
  plain synchronous functions on the agent's worker thread with no event loop
  to join. JSON-RPC over pipes is small enough to speak directly — the same
  choice codex.py made for app-server. Promoted from prototypes/codex_acp/,
  which validated exactly this.

- A refusal never falls back to "the first option": on a malformed option
  list that could be the allow option. No allow/reject match answers with
  ACP's `cancelled` outcome, which needs no optionId and grants nothing.

engine_status() reports, per engine, whether the launcher is installed and
whether the underlying CLI looks authenticated (credential-file heuristic,
reported as such) — so the delegating agent picks a ready engine instead of
failing mid-task, and the UI can show login state.

codex.py and claude_code.py stay: direct app-server needs no npm dependency
and remains the default codex route. This adds breadth, not replacement.

The test's fake agent is a real subprocess speaking real newline-delimited
JSON-RPC — what the tests pin is the wire behaviour, which is the part that
would break against the real adapters.

Closes #900

Rework acp_agent on the typed acp SDK, pin adapters, move authority to the operator

Reworked in review (by a second session; recorded here for provenance):

- The official acp SDK's typed client replaces the hand-rolled JSON-RPC
  client. The original commit argued the SDK's asyncio surface did not fit a
  synchronous tool; wrapping the run in asyncio.run() inside the tool call
  resolves that cleanly, and the typed schema (ToolCallStart/Progress/Update,
  RequestPermissionResponse) replaces dict-shape guessing.

- Adapter versions are pinned (@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp@1.1.14,
  @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp@0.66.0) — closing the adapter-drift
  risk the PR itself named.

- command= and approval= move off the model-facing tool signature onto the
  operator-constructed ACPAgent instance. The model can pick a named,
  exact-version engine; it can no longer compose an arbitrary argv or weaken
  its own approval mode. The module-level acp_agent() remains the simple
  default (manual approval, named engines only).

- argv is validated as a sequence, never parsed from a shell string.

Add find-selling-points skill, and the first run's findings (#939)

* Add find-selling-points skill

The failure mode when writing marketing copy is not running out of ideas.
It is that plausible sentences about software are easy to generate and
wrong most of the time. This skill makes a claim expensive to assert and
cheap to check: every point ends in file:line or gets deleted, and every
candidate goes through a step whose job is to kill it.

It also bans, on sight, the things we keep reaching for and should not:
framework comparisons, line counts, developer ergonomics as the headline,
and any sentence that survives find-and-replacing our name with a
competitor's.

The falsification step carries a table of claims that actually shipped on
our own public sites and were false — MIT instead of Apache-2.0, an
end-to-end encryption claim with no payload encryption behind it, migration
tools that do not exist, a dummy-data trust mechanism that does not exist,
and an invented 75% statistic. Every one was written by someone confident
and helpful. The table is there so the bar stays where it is.

Output goes to docs/SELLING_POINTS.md, dated per run, recording what was
cut and why — that half stops the same false claim being rediscovered and
shipped again next quarter.

No packaging change needed; connectonion/**/*.md already ships.

* Record the first run of find-selling-points

Thirteen claims survived, ten were cut. The cut list is the half that
matters: four of the cuts are things that look shipped and are not.

cli/co_ai/commands/__init__.py defines /init /help /cost /compact /tasks
/export /sessions /new /resume /undo /redo, and BUILTIN_COMMANDS is
imported nowhere at runtime — the slash commands that actually work are
skill names. cli/co_ai/sessions.py and its SQLite store are only reachable
from those unwired commands. cli/co_ai/agents/registry.py duplicates the
explore and plan subagents but the running agent never imports it. Email is
not a wired tool on the co ai agent, only a CLI path.

Anyone writing copy from a directory listing would have claimed all four.

The strongest surviving point was not in any of our marketing: co ai hosts
the agent and opens chat.openonion.ai against your own machine, so one
command produces a working chat UI, a dashboard, and a shareable address.
Nothing on any of our sites said that.

fix: a deployed agent runs on its own account, not its author's

co init copies AGENT_ADDRESS, AGENT_EMAIL, IS_EMAIL_ACTIVE and
OPENONION_API_KEY from ~/.co/keys.env into a project .env on purpose — a
project under development should run as its author with no second setup step.
co deploy --to then wrote that file to /etc/connectonion/<agent>.env verbatim.

The server has its own key, so those four lines describe someone else, and two
are not inert: AGENT_EMAIL overrides the mailbox address.load() derives from
the agent's own address, and OPENONION_API_KEY decides which account every
model call is billed to. The agent ran as itself and paid as its author with
nothing reporting an error, and the spend cannot be split back out afterwards
because usage_logs carries no column naming the machine that made the call.

The deploy now withholds the identity keys and substitutes the agent's own,
authenticated from the key it already derived in order to install it. The
mailbox comes from the auth response rather than being computed locally: the
backend routes the mail, and the address[:10] fallback has not always agreed
with what it issues.

--own-identity mints the key on the machine, so the operator cannot sign as
that agent. No account is written and the deploy says so, naming co auth in
/srv/<agent>. An agent with no account fails visibly on its first model call;
an agent quietly spending its author's credits does not fail at all.

The key set is named once in env_inheritance.py and read by both commands —
propagating it is the point in one and a bug in the other, so they must not
each keep a copy.

test_deploy_env_is_secret asserted OPENONION_API_KEY survived _env_for_server;
that assertion was incidental to what it tests (only AGENT_CONFIG_PATH is
rewritten), so it now uses an application key, which still does pass through.

next-step tip (with a tip test that scores the tip by what a fresh, text-only
model does with it), and every failure is a fix-it guide (--help enumerated
and diffed against the skill, every exit code provoked at least once).
