co email failures exit 1 instead of 0 (#1012) (#1016)

Every failure path in email_commands printed an error and returned
normally, so the process exited 0 and 'co email send ... && next' ran
next after a failed send. co gmail and co outlook exit 1 in the same
situations -- two sibling command groups disagreed about what a failure
is.

A legitimately empty listing still exits 0: an empty inbox is an answer.
Asking for a specific email that does not exist is a failure -- the
command did not deliver what was asked.

Red-first: the three failure-path tests fail on unmodified main (exit 0,
no exception), pass here; the two no-raise tests pin unchanged behavior
on both sides. Process-level check: 'co email inbox' with no credentials
now exits 1.

send_email: choose which owned address to send as (#1007) (#1017)

The backend (oo-api#150, live in production) accepts an optional
from_address and verifies it belongs to the caller. The client half:
send_email() gains from_address, the CLI gains --from, and an omitted
choice leaves the payload byte-identical so every existing caller keeps
the server-derived default.

Red-first: test fails on main with TypeError (unexpected keyword),
passes here. Live check against production: --from with an unowned
address is refused with 'rental@mail.openonion.ai is not one of this
account's email addresses' and nothing is sent.

Add PRODUCT.md — the foundation the public pages get written from (#1013)

Writing marketing from an impression of the codebase kept failing the same
way. Four false claims shipped publicly this year — MIT instead of
Apache-2.0, end-to-end encryption that does not exist, migration tools that
do not exist, an invented 75% statistic — and a landing page rebuild quietly
dropped eleven of fifteen real capabilities because they were awkward to fit.
Same cause both times: nothing said what the product is.

Three parallel inventories over the plugin system, the network and trust
layer, the templates, every built-in tool, and the front end. Organised by
what a reader wants to know rather than by directory, because that is what a
page gets written from. Every entry states what someone can do, whether it is
on by default, and the limit they would feel misled by.

Things nobody had written down: co copy vendors 16 tools, 13 plugins and 10
TUI components into your own project; co create copies the entire docs tree
into .co/docs/ for vibe coding; auto_debug_exception hands a debug agent the
live crashed frame to execute code in; Codex already runs as a subprocess
over native JSON-RPC; there are nine model providers, not three; the address
IS the public key, with no hash.

Things that stop us saying something:
- oo-chat has NO LICENSE and package.json says private:true, while its README
  calls it an open-source web chat client. We cannot claim an open-source
  front end until that repo has a licence.
- The --to flag on co deploy does not exist. Cloud only; self-hosting means
  running host() yourself.
- The relay server is not in this repo, so self-hosting the relay is not real
  without reimplementing the protocol.
- No agent-to-agent tool ships wired.
- co ai's effective default model is co/gemini-3.6-flash, from the CLI option.
  The co/claude-opus-4-5 in ai_commands.py is a Python default the CLI always
  overrides. I reported the opposite before checking which one wins.
- web-research ships a search_web that returns fake results, and the custom
  template falls back to a stub that only echoes its input.

And one security finding that is not a marketing note: payment onboarding
verifies transfers on the WebSocket path, but the fast-rule path promotes
anyone whose self-declared payment field meets the number.

cli: co transfer, co email addresses, and tips that survive piping (#1023)

Three gaps found by applying the cli-skill-design methodology (#1008):

- co transfer <address> <amount> + co transfer list [--sent|--received]
  expose the live credit-transfer API (POST/GET /api/v1/transfers).
  Sending is irreversible, so the command states what will happen and
  requires --yes or an interactive confirm; a declined confirm exits 1
  before anything is posted. Success prints the resulting balance
  (GET /api/v1/tokens/balance) and names the next step. (#1018)

- co email addresses lists every address the account owns and marks the
  default sender; the ownership 403 on co email send --from now ends
  with 'See your addresses: co email addresses'. An empty list is an
  answer (exit 0) with a pointer to co email name <name>. (#1019)

- Next-step tips now survive piping in gmail/outlook/gdrive listings
  (the is_terminal guard hid them from exactly the AI callers who need
  them); the idempotency retry hint restates the full send command; the
  stale-number messages name the step after the refresh; co email send
  success points at co email sent. (#1011)

Every PR ships its dev-blog post, enforced by CI (#1020)

* Every PR ships its dev-blog post, enforced by CI

A credit-transfer API ran in production for months while no CLI, help
text, or doc mentioned it -- for every user and AI the feature did not
exist. Docs written after the fact lose the race every time, so the
requirement moves into the merge path: a PR must add or update a file
under docs/blog/ or the blog-gate check fails. Maintainers waive it
with the no-blog label for genuinely trivial changes.

The PR template's Design Journal section had a 'Not applicable'
checkbox, which made the requirement a suggestion; replaced with the
enforced contract. This commit carries the first post through its own
gate.

* The blog gate reads the post: a changelog wearing prose fails

Existence was never the point -- a post nobody wants to read keeps the
docs site technically current and actually dead. The gate now runs the
post through a story rubric (problem someone hit, a turn, a lesson;
llm_do on co/gemini-2.5-flash) and fails with the model's one concrete
fix when it reads as a feature list.

Verified both directions before shipping: the policy post passes
(STORY), a bullet-list changelog fails (NOT_STORY) with an actionable
reason. Fork PRs carry no secret, so they get the existence check only.

fix(outlook): support attachments on replies

Add repeatable --attach/-a to `co outlook reply` and an attachments
argument to Outlook.reply(), reusing send()'s validation, 3MB ceiling,
MIME detection, and base64 encoding. Files ride on Graph's reply action,
so replies stay threaded — including scheduled ones.

Keep send_at third positional in Outlook.reply() and `at` third
positional in handle_outlook_reply(), with attachments keyword-only.
Placing attachments before them would make a pre-existing caller's
timestamp be read as attachment paths: a string is iterable, so
reply(id, body, "2026-07-06T15:30:00Z") failed with "Attachment not
found: 2" and the scheduled reply never went out. Regression tests pin
the legacy positional call and assert both parameter lists.

Refs #847.

llm: every provider client carries explicit network bounds (#1116)

A scheduled run froze mid-iteration with the upstream socket in CLOSE_WAIT —
the server had closed its side and the client sat in a read nothing bounded.
No error, no exit, killed by hand after 15 minutes.

One helper, _network_bounds(), and no provider client is constructed on
implicit SDK defaults again: connect 20s, read 600s (long generations
legitimately send nothing for minutes — not cut off), bounded retries
(2 default; OpenOnionLLM keeps its deliberate 5). A stalled upstream now
ends in the existing typed LLMConnectionError within a documented bound of
(1 + retries) x 600s.

The inventory test constructs every LLM subclass and checks the bounds by
value — the connect number doubles as the tripwire, since the SDK's implicit
default is 5s. It caught OpenRouterLLM missing the bounds during this very

fix(remote-browser): map the hostname before deciding on it

An adversarial review of this module found the special-use hostname list
was bypassable by appending one character:

  http://metadata.google.internal。/   -> allowed
  http://localhost。/                  -> allowed

U+3002 (and U+FF0E, U+FF61) map to ASCII '.' under UTS-46, which a browser
applies before anything else. This module applied it seventh: after the
double-dot check, the trailing-dot strip, and the IPv4-form parser, and
before the special-name lookup. So the code deciding 'is this localhost?'
and the code producing the string 'localhost.' sat on opposite sides of
the mapping. metadata.google.internal. is the exact FQDN GCE resolves to
169.254.169.254; the address tables cannot catch a split-horizon name,
which is what the suffix list exists for.

The same ordering lost IP literals: http://127。0。0。1/ returned
literal=None, so a destination the browser dials numerically was handed
to a resolver whose answer the caller can influence.

Second finding, same shape: classify_address materialized deny_networks
with tuple() and then recursed into IPv4-mapped/NAT64/6to4 addresses
passing the original, now-exhausted iterable. An operator deny range was
bypassable by wrapping the address in ::ffff:.

Fixes: run uts46_remap first for every non-IPv6 host, then every existing
check reads the string the browser reads; materialize deny_networks once
and pass the frozen tuple down every recursion.

The 20 new tests were verified red against the unpatched module first.
Vectors gained the Unicode-dot and fullwidth-digit authorities the file
had none of. 7,043 unit tests pass; ruff clean.

fix(egress-gateway): rewrite the response head, stream the body, budget pre-auth sockets

An adversarial review of this gateway found no way to reach an unapproved
socket — resolve/classify/pin/dial, the request parser, and the auth path
all held under 26 smuggling probes, DNS rebinding on a new connection,
mixed answer sets, and every alternate address form. Three real defects
were on the paths it did not protect.

1. The upstream response was relayed byte-for-byte. The gateway serves one
   request per connection and then stops reading, but an origin replying
   'Connection: keep-alive' told the client otherwise — with a second
   response the origin had queued already sitting in the client's receive
   buffer. Chromium pools plain-HTTP proxy sockets by proxy server, not by
   origin. The response head is now rewritten: hop-by-hop headers dropped,
   'Connection: close' appended. (The docs claimed this was already done;
   it was only done on the request sent upstream.)

2. Content-Length sized a readexactly(). One connection declaring 64 MiB
   grew RSS by 227 MB before forwarding anything, times the connection
   cap. The body now streams in 64 KiB chunks; a declaration larger than
   the transfer limit is refused outright.

3. Admission counted connections before reading them, so sockets that sent
   nothing held slots for the whole header timeout: four silent TCP
   connections made an authenticated CONNECT return 429 on a four-slot
   gateway, renewably. Pending sockets now have their own budget and take
   a served slot only once the credential is proven.

Also: password out of ProxyEndpoint's repr, so no traceback or debug dump
can publish it; an unexpected resolver exception answers DNS_FAILED
instead of closing silently; a fragment reports INVALID rather than
SCHEME_DENIED.

Six new tests, all verified red first. Also corrected
test_overload_is_rejected_without_read_resolve_or_dial, which encoded the
pre-auth admission it now must not have. 7,062 unit tests pass; ruff clean.

Review also flagged that test_numeric_dialer_never_calls_getaddrinfo passes
on a dialer that resolves by name (asyncio short-circuits the numeric
string before the patched resolver). The property is enforced elsewhere;
the test that reads like the guard is not one. Tracked separately.

fix(native-egress): make the preflight able to pass, and able to fail

Adversarial review found this preflight could never succeed against the
real stack, while every test was green.

1. The .invalid witness required status 502. The gateway answers 403:
   its destination policy denies .invalid by name before DNS is consulted,
   so the DNS-failure path the witness expected is unreachable for that
   host. Verified against a real gateway.

2. The gateway sends refusals with Content-Length: 0, and Chromium will
   not commit a bodyless 4xx/5xx main-frame navigation - it reports
   ERR_HTTP_RESPONSE_CODE_FAILURE, so page.goto raises rather than
   returning the status. Measured on Chrome 151: 403/502 with an empty
   body raise, with a body they return the status. Both probes therefore
   raised and collapsed to EGRESS_PREFLIGHT_FAILED. Fail-closed, but the
   private browser could never start.

   Refusals now carry a one-line body holding the stable code.

3. The witness is now the X-ConnectOnion-Error header rather than a bare
   status, since a 403 from anything the browser could reach satisfied the
   old check; the status is still required to be 403, because a 407 also
   carries the header and means the credential never arrived.

4. The subresource probes could not fail. They run inside a bounded race
   that swallows their own errors, so a probe that silently did nothing
   left exactly the zero-socket reading a correctly proxied one leaves -
   replacing the whole function with a no-op kept the preflight passing.
   EgressGateway now counts decided requests, and the preflight requires
   that count to move. This also removes the dependence on a ~1.6s window
   in which a late leak was invisible.

The tests could not see any of it: FakePage returns a response object
where Chromium raises and hard-codes the status the gateway never sends,
so the suite verified the fake. No test ran this preflight against a real
browser. tests/e2e/test_native_egress_preflight_real_driver.py now does,
in both directions.

Each guarantee verified by breaking it: removing the positive control
reddens the neutered-probe test, removing the header check reddens the
foreign-403 test, and restoring the empty error body reddens the
real-driver test. Against the real stack the preflight now passes with
all seven probes reaching the gateway, and still fails when <-loopback>
is replaced by a real loopback bypass.

main for the merged #1303/#1305 fixes.

fix(paid): one idempotency key per session, not per attempt

Adversarial review of the money path found the paid client generated a
fresh idempotency key inside every launch attempt:

    f"connectonion-start:{uuid.uuid4()}"

The server mints the licence inside launch_async, so a launch that fails
after that point - a transient RPC error, a driver that will not start,
an egress preflight that cannot prove the boundary - has already been
charged. The next co browser command retries with a new key and buys
another 15-minute interval. Three consecutive failed opens produced three
distinct keys and three charges. On a machine where the launch can never
succeed, that bills $0.025 per command, forever, while every command
fails.

The key is now minted once per logical session and reused across retries,
and cleared on a deliberate teardown so a real close starts a new interval.
Both directions have tests, verified red against the old code.

feat(proxy): share this computer's connection with a remote browser

A browser on a server reaches the internet from a data-centre address.
This is the other half of #991: lend it yours and pages see your address.

    browser on the host  --> your computer --> the internet (your address)

    co proxy share to 0xHOST
    co remote-browser 0xHOST start --proxy shared

The share is not a forwarder. It is the same machinery as the host's own
egress gateway - same parser, same authentication, same destination
policy, same limits - bound to a reachable address instead of loopback.
That is deliberate: point a server's browser at your laptop without it and
you have lent your network, not your connection. Your router's admin page,
localhost, the NAS all answer on your LAN, and a page the remote caller
controls can ask for any of them. Asking the share for 192.168.0.1 returns
403 DESTINATION_ADDRESS_DENIED.

The host still resolves the hostname, classifies every address the lookup
returns, and pins one numeric address. Only the last hop moves: it asks the
share for that same numeric address, never the hostname. Forwarding the
name would let the share resolve it a second time and land somewhere the
host never approved - the same time-of-check/time-of-use gap that made
DD-056 put the boundary at the socket.

Verified across two real machines: a Google Cloud server running the paid
Chromium 151 downloaded through the signed release channel, egressing
through a laptop in Sydney. The server's own address is 34.21.243.229; the
site saw 129.94.43.159.

fix(proxy): serve the share instead of reporting it and exiting

co proxy share printed 'sharing this computer's connection at
http://192.168.0.39:53131' and returned. The share is a socket owned by
that process, so it closed the moment the shell got its prompt back:
connecting to the address it had just advertised answered
ConnectionRefusedError, while co proxy status kept reporting the share as
live.

An in-process test did not catch it - the listening socket survives inside
one interpreter, so the check passed while the real command was broken.
Running it as a subprocess and connecting after it exited is the same
measurement taken where it protects something.

The command now serves until stopped (--ttl for a timer, & to background
it), handles SIGTERM as well as Ctrl-C since a supervisor sends the
former, and removes its registry entry on the way out so nothing later
reports a share that nothing serves.

advertises, then terminates it and asserts the registry is clean.

Two follow-ups from the adversarial review (#1323), neither exploitable the

The frozen-table test compared the tables to themselves, which proves two

fix(daemon): bind before preparing the private runtime

A daemon that lost the singleton race deleted the winner's proxy
credential. serve_async prepared the runtime — start gateway, write
proxy-auth.json — before _bind took the lock. The credential path derives
from the shared profile, so a loser wrote the shared file with its own
password, then lost the lock, exited, and its finally: _shutdown_async
removed it — the winner's live credential. The owning daemon then answered
407 on every command with nothing logged and the loser already gone.

Swapping the two lines fixes it: _bind first, so a loser exits at the lock
before it has written or started anything, and _prepare_runtime runs only
for the winner.

Regression test holds the lock as the winner would, writes a credential,
runs a second daemon's serve_async, and asserts it exits 0 with the
winner's bytes intact. Reinstating the old order reddens it.

This is #1326 problem 1. Problem 2 (a preflight failure leaves the gateway
up) is fail-closed and a lifecycle-design question; it stays open on the
issue rather than being rushed in here.

34 tests pass; ruff clean.

* feat(proxy): PROXY_STREAM wire format and host-side proxy channel

A laptop share now rides the laptop's own outbound WebSocket. This adds the
frame schema (PROXY_ATTACH / PROXY_ATTACHED / PROXY_STREAM with resolve,

[1.7] Backport the replay-ledger self-heal (#1420)

* fix(auth): rebuild a replay ledger deleted under a running host

A hosted agent refused every signed call for 2h45m -- 213 consecutive
`replay protection unavailable` errors -- after a deploy replaced
`.co/replay.sqlite3` while the process was running.

The store is only validated in `__init__`, but the file it points at
outlives no guarantee: an rsync over `.co/` that does not protect the
ledger deletes it and leaves an empty file at the same path. Every later
`already_used()` then opens that schemaless database and raises
`no such table: used_signatures`, forever, because init ran hours ago and
never runs again.

Recover where the fault is actually found. On a missing-table error,
rebuild the schema once and retry the claim; a second failure still fails
closed. Scoped deliberately narrowly -- `database is locked`, I/O errors
and real corruption keep failing closed, because those ledgers are still
authoritative and rebuilding would discard signatures already spent.

Rebuilding forgets prior signatures, so a captured one can be replayed
until it expires. That is bounded by SIGNATURE_EXPIRY_SECONDS and strictly
better than the alternative, which is an agent that answers nothing at all
while `/health` still returns 200.

Note a zero-byte ledger alone is harmless: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`
succeeds against an empty file, so construction repairs it. The outage
needed the file to be swapped *after* a healthy start.

proxy: signed grants and delegations, verified at the presenter (#1036)

The authorisation half of the 1.8 proxy capability: P signs a grant, D signs
a delegation in advance, B presents both. Nobody signs at request time, which
is the whole point — the 3am schedule runs with every human asleep.

A direct grant is the same object with holder == presenter and no delegation.
Verification binds to the party PRESENTING the credential, never the party
that opened the connection — in the reverse tunnel P dials B, so binding to

fix(remote-browser): map the hostname before deciding on it

An adversarial review of this module found the special-use hostname list
was bypassable by appending one character:

  http://metadata.google.internal。/   -> allowed
  http://localhost。/                  -> allowed

U+3002 (and U+FF0E, U+FF61) map to ASCII '.' under UTS-46, which a browser
applies before anything else. This module applied it seventh: after the
double-dot check, the trailing-dot strip, and the IPv4-form parser, and
before the special-name lookup. So the code deciding 'is this localhost?'
and the code producing the string 'localhost.' sat on opposite sides of
the mapping. metadata.google.internal. is the exact FQDN GCE resolves to
169.254.169.254; the address tables cannot catch a split-horizon name,
which is what the suffix list exists for.

The same ordering lost IP literals: http://127。0。0。1/ returned
literal=None, so a destination the browser dials numerically was handed
to a resolver whose answer the caller can influence.

Second finding, same shape: classify_address materialized deny_networks
with tuple() and then recursed into IPv4-mapped/NAT64/6to4 addresses
passing the original, now-exhausted iterable. An operator deny range was
bypassable by wrapping the address in ::ffff:.

Fixes: run uts46_remap first for every non-IPv6 host, then every existing
check reads the string the browser reads; materialize deny_networks once
and pass the frozen tuple down every recursion.

The 20 new tests were verified red against the unpatched module first.
Vectors gained the Unicode-dot and fullwidth-digit authorities the file
had none of. 7,043 unit tests pass; ruff clean.

fix(egress-gateway): rewrite the response head, stream the body, budget pre-auth sockets

An adversarial review of this gateway found no way to reach an unapproved
socket — resolve/classify/pin/dial, the request parser, and the auth path
all held under 26 smuggling probes, DNS rebinding on a new connection,
mixed answer sets, and every alternate address form. Three real defects
were on the paths it did not protect.

1. The upstream response was relayed byte-for-byte. The gateway serves one
   request per connection and then stops reading, but an origin replying
   'Connection: keep-alive' told the client otherwise — with a second
   response the origin had queued already sitting in the client's receive
   buffer. Chromium pools plain-HTTP proxy sockets by proxy server, not by
   origin. The response head is now rewritten: hop-by-hop headers dropped,
   'Connection: close' appended. (The docs claimed this was already done;
   it was only done on the request sent upstream.)

2. Content-Length sized a readexactly(). One connection declaring 64 MiB
   grew RSS by 227 MB before forwarding anything, times the connection
   cap. The body now streams in 64 KiB chunks; a declaration larger than
   the transfer limit is refused outright.

3. Admission counted connections before reading them, so sockets that sent
   nothing held slots for the whole header timeout: four silent TCP
   connections made an authenticated CONNECT return 429 on a four-slot
   gateway, renewably. Pending sockets now have their own budget and take
   a served slot only once the credential is proven.

Also: password out of ProxyEndpoint's repr, so no traceback or debug dump
can publish it; an unexpected resolver exception answers DNS_FAILED
instead of closing silently; a fragment reports INVALID rather than
SCHEME_DENIED.

test_overload_is_rejected_without_read_resolve_or_dial, which encoded the
pre-auth admission it now must not have. 7,062 unit tests pass; ruff clean.

feat(proxy): share this computer's connection with a remote browser

A browser on a server reaches the internet from a data-centre address.
This is the other half of #991: lend it yours and pages see your address.

    browser on the host  --> your computer --> the internet (your address)

    co proxy share to 0xHOST
    co remote-browser 0xHOST start --proxy shared

The share is not a forwarder. It is the same machinery as the host's own
egress gateway - same parser, same authentication, same destination
policy, same limits - bound to a reachable address instead of loopback.
That is deliberate: point a server's browser at your laptop without it and
you have lent your network, not your connection. Your router's admin page,
localhost, the NAS all answer on your LAN, and a page the remote caller
controls can ask for any of them. Asking the share for 192.168.0.1 returns
403 DESTINATION_ADDRESS_DENIED.

The host still resolves the hostname, classifies every address the lookup
returns, and pins one numeric address. Only the last hop moves: it asks the
share for that same numeric address, never the hostname. Forwarding the
name would let the share resolve it a second time and land somewhere the
host never approved - the same time-of-check/time-of-use gap that made
DD-056 put the boundary at the socket.

Chromium 151 downloaded through the signed release channel, egressing
through a laptop in Sydney. The server's own address is 34.21.243.229; the
site saw 129.94.43.159.

fix(daemon): bind before preparing the private runtime

A daemon that lost the singleton race deleted the winner's proxy
credential. serve_async prepared the runtime — start gateway, write
proxy-auth.json — before _bind took the lock. The credential path derives
from the shared profile, so a loser wrote the shared file with its own
password, then lost the lock, exited, and its finally: _shutdown_async
removed it — the winner's live credential. The owning daemon then answered
407 on every command with nothing logged and the loser already gone.

Swapping the two lines fixes it: _bind first, so a loser exits at the lock
before it has written or started anything, and _prepare_runtime runs only
for the winner.

Regression test holds the lock as the winner would, writes a credential,
runs a second daemon's serve_async, and asserts it exits 0 with the
winner's bytes intact. Reinstating the old order reddens it.

This is #1326 problem 1. Problem 2 (a preflight failure leaves the gateway
up) is fail-closed and a lifecycle-design question; it stays open on the
issue rather than being rushed in here.

34 tests pass; ruff clean.

* feat(proxy): PROXY_STREAM wire format and host-side proxy channel

A laptop share now rides the laptop's own outbound WebSocket. This adds the
frame schema (PROXY_ATTACH / PROXY_ATTACHED / PROXY_STREAM with resolve,
connect, data, eof, close, error ops), and ProxyChannel: the host end that
multiplexes streams over one channel and backs an EgressGateway on loopback
with a channel Resolver/Dialer. EgressGateway gains public resolve_destination

registers a ProxyChannel keyed by the laptop's address; the session finally
detaches it. RemoteBrowserService looks the caller up in that registry for

none. The start request no longer carries a share endpoint.

attaches with a fresh grant (default 24h, --ttl), serves the host's resolve

reconnects with backoff. --bind is gone; status shows attached/reconnecting
and diagnose tells apart no share, a dead process and one not yet attached.

network: seal direct sockets end to end — a host needs a port, not a certificate (#1393)

* network: seal direct sockets end to end, so a host needs a port and not a certificate

A signed CONNECT captured on a plaintext link could be replayed within its
window (#649), so direct connections were limited to TLS or loopback and every
self-hosted agent needed a domain, a certificate and Caddy. The Melbourne
rental host announced http://34.129.161.131:8001 and the 1.8.0b1 laptop

The direct socket now opens with SEAL/SEALED_OK: one-time X25519 keys signed
by both Ed25519 identities (the address already is the key), then every frame
travels in a NaCl Box with a per-direction counter. A captured frame is
unreadable and a replayed one does not open. The relay is not involved and is
unchanged. An older host that cannot seal is used bare only over TLS or
loopback, or by a client with no keys; otherwise the client moves on.

* email: read and filter every mailbox an account can reach, and pick a default

An account can own several addresses and be granted read access to another
account's, but the CLI could not tell them apart or ask for one:

- `co email inbox` merged every readable address into one list and never said
  which address a message arrived at
- there was no way to narrow to a single mailbox
- `is_default` existed in the database and was displayed by `co email
  addresses`; nothing could change it

Adds `co email inbox --address`, a To column that appears only when the page
actually spans more than one mailbox, and `co email default <address>`.

get_emails() refuses a backend that ignored the address parameter rather than
silently returning every address, the same guard the offset parameter already
had. An old backend answering with the whole mailbox when one was requested is
the exact failure the filter exists to prevent.

Why this matters, from a real incident on 2026-09-05: a job application went
out carrying the wrong one of two addresses. The employer's reply was delivered
and stored correctly, and could not be found — successful delivery generates no
bounce, so nothing anywhere reported a problem. The mail was simply in a list
that did not say which mailbox anything belonged to.

Needs the matching oo-api change: `to` on each received message, and the
`address` query parameter on GET /api/v1/email/received.

fix(outlook): scheduled replies become a deferred reply draft, not a reply action (#1417)

#1221 moved Outlook.send(send_at=...) off sendMail because the one-shot
endpoint delivered at once and left a deferred copy behind (#1198). reply()
still used POST /me/messages/{id}/reply with the same property inside
`message`. The reply action is create-and-send in one step, and Graph lists
neither it nor sendMail among the requests that can carry an extended
property, so a scheduled reply had the same shape as the bug just fixed.

Scheduled replies now follow the documented draft lifecycle:

  POST  /me/messages/{id}/createReply      draft, threading kept
  POST  /me/messages/{draft}/attachments   one per file (PATCH takes none)
  PATCH /me/messages/{draft}               0x3FEF + 0x000F deferred-send times
  POST  /me/messages/{draft}/send          submit that exact draft

The scheduled branch requires Mail.ReadWrite before any request, as send()
does. Immediate replies are unchanged. docs/cli/outlook.md no longer claims
scheduling works with Mail.Send alone.

Verified live on a real mailbox by the #1221 author: body intact, attachment
on both copies, nothing delivered before the due time, one copy each after
it in the original conversation, and a cancelled reply that never went out.

docs: explain agent identity, and add an agent-identity skill

An agent has one identity and two things that look like it: the keypair in
.co/keys/agent.key, the account inside OPENONION_API_KEY, and the AGENT_ADDRESS
line in .env. Nothing keeps them in agreement and drift is silent, so the same
question keeps getting answered from whichever one was nearest.

docs/agent-identity.md writes down what is authoritative and what is only a
record: AGENT_ADDRESS never sets the address (address.load() reads the keypair
and takes only AGENT_EMAIL/IS_EMAIL_ACTIVE from the environment), billing
follows the JWT rather than the keypair, and an identity is derived from the
operator's phrase plus the agent *name* — so deploying one name twice gives two
machines the same key by design, not by leak.

The skill is the procedure that falls out of it: read the address from /info
before publishing it, decode the token to find the payer, derive from the name
to tell 'minted its own identity' from 'wrong key', and fix the project .env as
well as the server copy since _sync_env rewrites the latter every deploy.

co copy agent-identity needs the SKILLS registry entry — without it the bundle
ships but the command cannot find it.

Stop the session-registry cleanup thread with the app it belongs to

`create_app()` started a `while True: time.sleep(60)` daemon thread that
nothing could stop, so every construction of the app leaked one for the life
of the process. In the test suite four modules left 39 behind. Later in the
same run `tests/unit/test_scroll.py` patched `time.sleep` to a no-op for the
whole process, every leaked thread turned into a busy loop, and on Linux the
main thread starved until the 300s timeout fired at the setup of whichever
scroll test came next. Seven red runs on main between Aug 21 and Sep 2 were
this one hang, blamed on a file that had nothing to do with it (#1246).

The cleanup job is now a thread with a stop Event that waits instead of
sleeping, and it is started by the app's lifespan and stopped by it, so a
bare create_app() starts nothing. The scroll tests patch the scroll module's
own view of `time` rather than the global.

Also in this change: the auto-debug test that hung main today (2026-09-08)
mocked only the console, so the excepthook built a real debug Agent and the
unmocked `agent.input()` went to the network with the key "test-key". It now
asserts the fallback-frame behaviour it was named for, offline.

Fail any test that reaches the network or leaves a thread running

Two autouse guards in tests/conftest.py, each written after the thing it
forbids cost a day:

- _no_network refuses any socket that leaves the machine and points the
  backend URL at a dead loopback port. The connect raises
  ConnectionRefusedError at once, so nothing hangs, and the test fails in
  teardown naming the host even when the code under test swallowed the
  error. It found 57 tests reaching production on every run through the
  default URL: `co init`, `co doctor`, host startup, passing only because
  the fallback for a 401 to "test-key" looks like the fallback for no
  backend at all. Tests that are about URL resolution itself request the
  new `default_backend_url` fixture.

- _no_leaked_threads fails a test, by thread name, that leaves one running.
  It found the registry-cleanup leak behind #1246, and that the legacy
  BrowserAutomation never retired its worker thread even on close(): the
  worker exited only when the cyclic GC freed the instance, which is not a
  time. close() now retires it and the next call starts a fresh one. The
  one process-wide thread that is meant to outlive tests, the async-tools
  event loop, is allowed by name.

Also in the same file: FORCE_COLOR and friends are stripped before
connectonion is imported (module-level Rich consoles read them once), so a
shell that forces colour no longer turns 43 text assertions red locally
while CI stays green; sys.excepthook is restored after each test; the
root conftest no longer loads the developer's .env for offline runs; and
the eight fixtures nothing used, the unused --relay-url options, and the
three per-folder conftests that only repeated the folder-marker policy are
gone.

One test configuration, one way to run it, one minute

pytest.ini is the only configuration. The `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` block
in pyproject was dead (pytest.ini always won) and disagreed with it on the
asyncio mode, the marker set and the default selection; tox.ini pointed at
tests/integration, which does not exist, and stopped at 3.12. Both are gone.
tests/cli/ moves under tests/e2e/cli/ where the docs said it was; the
stray tests/.co/ from a `co init` run at 1.6.6 and the Gemini debug script
go where they belong.

pytest-xdist joins the dev extra and `make test` runs the offline suite
across every core: 68s here against 222s serial, with an identical result
set. Single-file runs stay in-process so -s and breakpoints work.

What a failure looks like also changes: `-ra` lists every non-pass outcome
(the old `-rs` listed only skips, so a quiet run ended with no record of
what failed), the per-test timeout drops from 300s to 60s so a hang is
named within a minute instead of five, and xfail is strict.

The Makefile, CONTRIBUTING, tests/README.md, TEST_ORGANIZATION.md and
CLAUDE.md now describe the same commands, and tests/README.md lists every
rule the suite holds a test to and how to opt out of it.

CI runs the suite in parallel, bounded, with a coverage floor

The test job runs `pytest -n auto` (about a minute instead of six per
interpreter), carries a 15 minute job timeout as the backstop for a hang
outside any test, and injects no provider secrets: tests/conftest.py now
refuses any connection that leaves the machine, so a credential in this
process could only ever be misused. Coverage is measured on 3.12 with a
floor of 78%, today's number; the xml report is uploaded as an artifact.
Raise the floor as coverage rises, never lower it to make a PR pass.

fix(listen): do not retry Feishu's monthly quota error

99991403 is the tenant's monthly API cap (10,000 counted calls on the
free edition across every self-built app), not a per-minute limit;
retrying it three times with backoff only delays the same answer. Fail
at once with what it is and where to look. Document what this tool
spends: receiving over the long connection and the tenant token are
not counted; bot/v3/info once per listen start and each reply are.

fix(listen): start the stale clock at the claim, notice a dead listener, add done

rename() keeps a queue file's delivery-time mtime, so a message delivered
two hours ago and taken a minute ago was stale at once and the sweep
handed it out a second time. The claim now resets the mtime.

receive() started a background listener and then waited forever for
files if that listener died within a second (no SDK, bad credentials).
ensure_listener() now reports an immediate exit and receive/serve exit 1
pointing at the log.

A consumer that takes a message and chooses not to answer had no way to
say so; the message came back every hour. `co feishu done ID` forgets it.

fix(listen): review findings on the mailbox and the Feishu provider

- /bot/v3/info puts bot at the top level beside code and msg; _data()
  now accepts both shapes, so check() no longer reports 'no bot' for a
  correctly configured app and mention matching learns our open_id.
- The reply uuid now hashes the text, so a retry still dedupes on the
  Feishu side while reply --again with new text actually posts.
- done() clears new/ as well as cur/ and matches the whole id, so a reply
  made from ls does not leave the message queued, and Telegram's 123.55
  cannot delete -123.55.
- hold_lock() takes the lock with O_EXCL; ensure_listener() waits for the
  child to hold it or exit, and reports a listener that won the race
  instead of a spurious failure.
- The claim, the stale sweep and the sweep thread tolerate a file that
  another process finished between listing and rename.
- receive and serve re-check the listener every minute while waiting.
- A raw payload the SDK cannot marshal is logged, not dropped silently.
- One iso_utc() in mailbox.py for every timestamp.

listen: a refusal is one sentence and exit 1, a bad event is one log line, not a retry storm

Review of the Feishu/Lark listener before its first live run, with wrong
credentials on purpose. Three things it did wrong, each pinned by a test
that failed on the unpatched code for the defect's own reason:

- `co lark listen` with an invalid app_id printed a forty-line traceback
  ending in the SDK's ClientException. handle_listen now catches it, prints
  the platform's sentence and the log path, and exits 1; the lock is
  released either way.
- After bot/v3/info had already answered "refused the credentials", run()
  dialled the WebSocket with the same pair, and the SDK's auto-reconnect
  turned one clear refusal into a `connect failed` line every two minutes
  forever. A RuntimeError from bot_info (Feishu answered and said no) now
  stops before the dial; any other exception (no answer at all) still
  proceeds, because the long connection may get through.
- The SDK wraps our event handler and answers HTTP 500 when it raises, and
  Feishu treats 500 as "not delivered, send it again" for hours. A payload
  to_message cannot read is now one `event not understood` log line and a
  normal return. deliver() is deliberately left to raise: on a full disk the
  redelivery is what saves the message.

Also: error messages say "Lark" when the domain is Lark, so a `co lark` user
is not sent to the Feishu console; the parent no longer keeps the listener's
log handle open after Popen; the top-level help lists `lark` beside `feishu`.

listen: the kernel holds the lock, a redelivery is the recovery, serve keeps what it could not answer

Second review pass, ten findings, each pinned by a test that failed on the
unpatched code for the defect's own reason.

- deliver() dropped Feishu's redelivery as a duplicate whenever the log
  line had been written but the queue file had not, which is exactly the
  crash the log-first order exists to survive. An id in the log is now a
  duplicate only while the message is queued, taken, or answered; otherwise
  the queue file is recreated and the log left alone.
- The listener lock was a pid in an O_EXCL file. The file existed empty for
  an instant before the pid landed, so a concurrent starter read "" and
  unlinked the winner's lock: two listeners. After a reboot a reused pid
  was a phantom nothing cleared. Reuses transport.acquire_singleton_lock,
  an flock the kernel drops on death; the pid in the file is for `check`.
- serve called done() after every outcome, so a failed command or a refused
  reply consumed the question. Only a sent reply or explicit silence
  (exit 0, empty stdout) finishes a message; the rest stays taken and
  returns in an hour. A command that cannot run is refused (exit 2) before
  any message is claimed.
- Junk in new/ (.DS_Store, a zero-byte file from a full disk) raised out of
  receive, serve and ls, and done() could not remove it. Only
  <ms>-<id> names are ours; a queue file that does not parse is moved to
  bad/ with a log line. lookup() skips a log line with no chat.
- run() re-raised every RuntimeError from bot_info as a refusal, including
  a 502 page or a rate limit on that call. Only CredentialsRefused, raised
  where Feishu rejects the app_id/secret pair, stops before the dial.
- ensure_listener spawned a child that loaded ~/.co/keys.env on its own,
  so a CO_<PROVIDER>_HOME there or a parent --env-file sent it to another
  directory. The child gets the directory pinned and the env file forwarded.
- A cached tenant token that Feishu rejects (rotated secret) is dropped and
  the request retried once with a fresh one.
- Mention placeholders are substituted longest key first, so @_user_1 no
  longer eats @_user_10.
- reply --again sends a fresh reply uuid; the same key with the same text
  was silently swallowed by Feishu while the CLI printed an id.
- listen asks for the SDK before taking the lock and exits 3 with the pip
  line; a listener that died at once has its last log lines printed on
  stderr, unwrapped, instead of "see the log".

one lane per conversation, and a lease instead of a guess (#1478)

The directory could be consumed, but only by hand: receive, do something,
reply. `serve` did it in a loop of one. Anything that wanted to answer several
people at once, or to remember what a person said a minute ago, had to write
the loop again.

Inbox.serve(handler) is that loop. One lane per conversation, which is Kafka's
partition-by-key and Erlang's process-per-session: strictly ordered where a
human would notice, parallel where they would not. A pool was the obvious
alternative and it answers two messages from the same person at once, in the
wrong order.

The handler owns the outcome, and that is the whole contract: returning means
the message is finished, however it was finished — an answer sent, or a
decision to stay silent — and raising means it is not, so it waits in cur/ for
the sweep. Which is why one loop can drive a subprocess, an Agent or a Host
without knowing which it has.

Two things the loop needs and the directory did not have:

A lease. The stale window used to be a guess about how long an answer takes,
and a handler slower than the guess had its message taken away mid-sentence and
answered twice by whoever got it next. renew() touches the file while the
handler runs, so the window measures silence rather than work, and the sweep
only reclaims from consumers that really died.

A count. A message that crashes whoever takes it used to come back every hour
forever. attempts() counts handouts in attempts.jsonl — durably, because the
point of counting is to survive the crash that caused the retry — and the loop
gives up on the fourth, completing it with a line saying so.

`co feishu serve` keeps its one-at-a-time behaviour: commands written for it
have always run alone and some are not safe to run twice at once. --workers
opts in. It gains the lease and the give-up rule either way.

channels are configured in host.yaml, and co ai answers them (#1478)

Two halves of the same decision.

The configuration half: which channels an agent listens to belongs in
~/.co/host.yaml, beside `name` and `trust`, and not on the command line. With
several channels a flag-driven design only grows longer, while one file shows
every channel at a glance — and `co ai` with no flags at all is the normal way
to start. --listen replaces the list for one run and --no-listen empties it;
neither changes how a channel is configured, so a channel named on the command
line still takes its options from the file.

    listen:
      feishu:
        chats: [oc_a1b2]     # empty or absent = every group the bot is in
        mention_only: true   # a group needs an @; a direct message is already one

An unknown channel name, or a host.yaml that does not parse, stops the start
and says so. Starting with no channels looks exactly like starting with them,
right up until somebody wonders why the bot is ignoring them. It is checked
before the model key is, so a typo is answered by the typo.

The consumer half: co ai answers those channels. DD-063 left every decision
about what a message may do to "whatever consumes the directory", and then
nothing consumed it. This is the first consumer — a message becomes a turn, the
turn's answer becomes a reply, an empty answer is silence rather than an empty
message, and a turn that raises leaves its message for the sweep so a model
outage costs a delay and not an unanswered question.

One session per chat, and per thread where the platform has threads, so a
follow-up remembers the question it follows and two threads of one group do not
read as non-sequiturs to each other. Turns are taken one at a time: an Agent's
session lives on the object, so two threads calling input() would interleave
two conversations into one history. Parallel answering needs an Agent each,
which is a cost worth measuring before it is spent.

Trust is open, as decided for 1.8.5: anyone who can address the bot can command
it, which for a self-built application means the company and the groups the bot
was invited to. The sender is recorded as `feishu:<sender>` on every session
anyway, so the allowlist in #1479 starts with data instead of a migration.

Connecting a bot took eleven steps and step four decided whether anyone
finished: create the app in the console, add three scopes whose names have to
be exactly right, subscribe to one event, then copy a password into a file. A
missing scope is not an error at setup time. It is an error an hour later, in a
log, when someone @-mentions the bot and nothing happens.

`co auth feishu` is a QR code in the terminal. Scan it, approve, and the
application exists — in your own tenant, owned by you — with its credentials in
~/.co/keys.env. No console, no copy, no paste.

We had concluded this was impossible, and the conclusion was built on a name.
`application/v6` returns no app_secret and needs a token you cannot have without
one, which is true; the official CLI does it anyway, and a string in its binary
reads `larksuite_cli_app/probe`, which looked like the private back door that
explained it. The CLI is MIT licensed. That endpoint is a telemetry ping whose
result the code discards, and the real flow is forty lines above it: OAuth 2.0's
device authorization grant pointed at app creation, with no client identity in
the request at all. It is platform-documented and wrapped by all three official
SDKs, including the Python one this project already depends on.

So this is lark_oapi.register_app plus a QR renderer. qrcode was already a
dependency; lark-oapi stays optional and a missing one exits 3 with the pip
command, the same shape `co feishu listen` uses.

`co env set FEISHU_APP_SECRET` now refuses and names this command, the way the
Google and Microsoft records do. The reason is different and worth saying: those
are refused so a single field cannot describe a different account than the rest;
this one is refused because a hand-typed app secret came from somewhere the
command cannot check, and there is now a command that can.

make runs a named verification target, not anything a Makefile says

An adversarial sweep of the shipped policy before publishing — twenty-six
bypass attempts — refused twenty-five. The twenty-sixth was `make install`,
and it was allowed in 1.8.4 too, along with bare `make` and
`make -C /etc all`, under "focused test, lint, or build command". `cargo` is
limited to test/check/clippy/build, `go` to test, and the package runners to
targets naming test/lint/build/check/typecheck. `make` was the one left open.

`make` now needs a named target from a verification set, with no `-C`, `-f`
or `--makefile` pointing it at another directory or another program. `make
test` runs; `make install`, bare `make`, `make -C /etc all` and `make test
install` ask.

This does not pretend to stop an agent from running its own code. The focused
category is an execution surface by design — anything that may write a test
and run it may run what the test runs. What the narrowing keeps out is the
commands in that category which are not verification at all, and `make
install` writing outside the workspace is the clearest of them.

An explicit grant is an approval already given

The owner asked the question I should have asked first: if the user's command
explicitly allows it, or a skill allows it, shouldn't it just run — isn't
auto-approval the user having said yes?

Measured on 1.8.4, it was not. Nine grants written by hand into a project's
own .co/host.yaml — Bash(curl *), Bash(rm -rf build), Bash(git push *),
Bash(co deploy), Bash(cat .env), send_email and three more. Unattended, eight
of nine refused. With a person present they did not auto-approve either: the
dialog opened every time for a call the operator had already written down.
And a skill that declares Bash(mkdir *) got nothing at all — the identical
grant ran as source: config and was refused as source: skill.

When the policy says "ask a human", check_approval discarded every grant that
did not come from a human in this session, because a broad Bash(co *) must not
imply co deploy. The concern is real; the correction was aimed at the grant's
source when the thing that differs is its breadth. And the code could not tell
an operator's grant from a shipped default anyway, because all 78 template
entries also declare source: config — which is why Bash(co *) needed a
hardcoded exception naming co status and co browser. The general rule was
unwritable because the information it needs was not recorded.

The template's entries are now stamped `template` at load time. An explicit
grant — operator host.yaml, skill `tools:` frontmatter, human session approval
— allows the call for any effect class, attended or not, and the policy
decides it once so no dialog opens for something already permitted. A wildcard
is honoured only for the effect its own text classifies to, so Bash(git *)
does not carry git push while Bash(git push *) does. The hardcoded `co`
exception is gone, replaced by classifying that multiplexer's strong verbs as
what they are: co email send is an external effect, co transfer a payment, co
server an external effect, co keys a credential, co auth and co reset ask.

One bug came out of building it. Checking a pipe segment by handing its text
back to the chain checker re-parses, and segment text arrives with its quotes
already removed, so `awk BEGIN{system("x")}` failed to parse and the broad
except turned that into "no grant". Noticed because a granted
`awk '{print $1}'` was allowed while a granted `awk 'BEGIN{system(...)}'` was
denied and I could not explain the difference. The denial was the safe answer,
which is what made it dangerous: a swallowed parse error refuses whatever it
cannot read, including grants the operator did write, and it looks like
security working. `segment_permitted` matches without re-parsing.

host.yaml, `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://example.com` runs
unattended, audit line "policy operator-configured", and returns 200.

Release 1.8.5a1: an explicit grant is an approval already given (#1481)

Every refusal says why, how to allow it, and think again before you retry

The human-rejection paths in this plugin have carried structured
<system-reminder> guidance for a long time. The policy's own refusals carried
a sentence naming a policy — "command is outside the focused verification
allowlist" — and an agent reading that has nothing to do with it but try
again. Trying again is guaranteed to fail, because the decision is
deterministic, so the iteration budget drains and the run ends with nothing
done and no explanation anyone can act on. That is what happened at 28 of 300
iterations.

Every refusal the policy makes now carries three parts: why, in plain words
and per effect class; how to allow it next time, naming the line and both
places it can go; and a re-think prompt that says what to try instead of this
call and not to retry it or reach for a different spelling of it.

Part 2 is the useful half. A credential refusal says you almost never need a
secret's contents. A `sed`/`awk` refusal says `head`, `cut` and
`read_file(limit=, offset=)` do the reading job without a grant. A publication
refusal says to prepare the change and stop.

The suggested grant is verified against the real grant path before it is
printed, in the same order the real path asks — control-file gate first, then
the grant check. Two of my own suggestions were lies before that: `Bash(cat *)`
cannot allow `cat /etc/shadow`, because a wildcard is honoured only for the
effect its own text names; and no pattern at all can allow `echo x >
../outside.txt`, because the parser strips redirects out of the text patterns
match against. Those now say THERE IS NO GRANT FOR THIS instead of naming a
line that would not work — a remedy that does not work is worse than none,
because it gets widened until something does.

A test pastes the suggested pattern for sixteen refused calls and asserts the
identical call then runs. That test is what found both lies.

Verified on a real unattended run: asked to read /etc/hosts, the agent made
one attempt, received the reminder, did not retry, and told the user why.

[1.8.5] A command runs unless a rule holds it back (#1485)

* a command runs unless a rule holds it back (#1481, #1447)

instead — thirty read-only command names where there had been eleven — and the
maintainer asked the question that undid it: if the default were allow, what
would the list be for.

Nothing. They are alternatives, not layers. Enumerating what may run is a list
somebody has to extend for every tool anyone installs, and the way you learn it
needs extending is that an unattended job dies at two in the morning.

Neither of the tools on the maintainer's machine works that way. Claude Code's
allow, ask and deny lists are all empty. Codex has no command list at all. Both
constrain by boundary and by a reviewer. A name is not a capability.

Nor was the list buying what it looked like. It excluded `awk` and `sed` with a
careful paragraph — they take a program, and an awk BEGIN block that calls
system() reads like an inspection — while allowing `make`, `cargo` and `npm`,
whose config files are arbitrary execution. The argument was right and pointed
at the wrong list.

So an ordinary command runs, and three rules the old list had been enforcing by
omission are now written down:

- A command whose argument is a program asks: bash, sh, python, node, ruby,
  perl, awk, sed, and `uv run python -c`, which is `python -c` wearing a coat.
  Found because the flip allowed a heredoc into bash.
- A command that sends something to somebody asks: send, reply, post, publish,
  deploy, push, transfer, pay. Found because the flip allowed `co email send`.
  Local damage and outward visibility are different axes; the old list had
  conflated them by accident, refusing `co email send` for being unrecognised
  rather than for being an email.
- A command that writes or deletes through its arguments gets the workspace
  check: tee, cp, mv, ln, chmod, dd, and find with -delete or -exec.

Everything denied before is still denied, and the rules now name categories of
consequence instead of programs. The dangerous verbs are a small set that
changes slowly; the safe commands are unbounded and change on every install.

Also #1447: a planning tool is recognised by what owns the call. TodoList
registers add, start, complete, update, list, remove and clear, so matching
names is wrong in both directions — `remove` is a deletion and `list` is a read
for every other tool. `todo_list` sat in WORKFLOW_TOOLS and was never a tool
name, so 438 `add` calls were refused in six days.

The job test from the previous fix pinned which steps needed an operator grant
and promised to fail loudly on a policy change. It did, in the other direction:
making a directory and running the binary the job had just built now need
nothing. Needing a standing broad CLI grant to run `mkdir` was the shape of the
problem, not a boundary worth keeping. It now asserts the job needs no grant.

* a filter does not need a grant of its own (#1488)

An operator writes `Bash(co browser *)` in host.yaml, and the command runs.
Pipe it into `head -40` and it is refused, because the chain checker treated
"no pattern matched this segment" as "this segment is not permitted" — so the
grant was defeated by the filter it was piped through. `head` is permitted
alone and refused one character later, as `| head`.

The chain checker now asks the single-command classifier about a segment
nobody granted. If that segment would have run on its own, it does not need a
grant here either. The segment the policy holds back still does: the question
is answered by the same classifier, so `&& co email send` is no more permitted
inside a chain than outside one.

The lenient reading is opt-in, and only the approval paths ask for it. The
plain question this function answers — does a pattern cover every segment — is
also what decides whether one pattern is broader than another, and conflating
the two made `git status` look granted by a pattern that never mentions it.
With the flag on, an answer of "permitted" also requires that some segment was
actually granted, so a chain nobody wrote a grant for is never reported as an
operator decision.

Also reconciles with what landed on main while this branch was open:

- `ping`, `nc`, `telnet`, `dig`, `traceroute` and the rest join the external
  commands. The old unknown-command fallback was refusing them by accident;
  with the default flipped, "nobody listed it" stops being a reason.
- `co` classifies by subcommand before the generic outward rule, so `co
  transfer` keeps the precise `payment` verdict main gives it and the generic
  rule stays the fallback for every other command.
- The refusal labels for `sed`, `awk`, `make install`, `python3 -c` and `ping`
  become the category rather than "unrecognised". The suggested grant is
  unchanged: none of these classes is in _SUGGEST_EXACTLY, so a refusal still
  offers the `Bash(verb *)` form that the test pastes back and re-runs.

Measured, with no grants at all, on the calls a LinkedIn round makes: 12 of 17
refused before, 4 of 13 now, and three of those four are `python3 -c`,
`co email send` and `rm -rf build`.

authorize the bot you already have (#1478) (#1498)

`co auth feishu` creates an application, which is the right default and the
wrong one for the case that comes up most: the bot is already in the group,
with its permissions granted and its name known to everyone there. A new
application is in no group at all, so using it means inviting it everywhere
again.

--app-id names an existing one. The SDK passes it to the confirmation page as
clientID, so the page authorizes that application rather than making another,
and the poll returns its credentials. Its groups and permissions are untouched.

Where the id comes from, if lark-cli is installed: its config.json records one
per application in plain text, and `co auth feishu` now lists them. It reads
only the ids.

The secret beside them is deliberately not read. lark-cli keeps it in the OS
keychain — the config holds `{"source": "keychain", "id": "appsecret:cli_…"}` —
and copying a keychain entry into a plaintext env file is a downgrade wearing
the word "import". Scanning gets the same credential with the platform's
consent instead of the operating system's, and works on a machine that never
had lark-cli. Moving our own secrets the other way, into the keychain, is
#1497.

An id that is not one is refused before the scan starts, because the failure
otherwise is a page that cannot work and a QR that expires while you wait.

connectonion/useful_skills/co-inbox/SKILL.md, written to the cli-skill-design
order: the routing table first, because picking the wrong command is the
expensive mistake; the 80% as copy-pasteable lines; then the gotchas that make
an agent report something false if it does not know them; errors last.

The gotchas are the part worth having. Taking a message is a claim and claims
expire, so a script that takes one and then sleeps loses it. `done` is not
optional — a message you decided to ignore stays claimed until it expires and
then comes back. A reply happens once. Two consumers never get the same
message, so running two is how you scale rather than a mistake.

It also says what the surface does not do: it decides nothing about who may
command an agent, and as of 1.8.5b1 it does not guarantee delivery across a
reconnect, because that gate has not passed. An agent cannot tell aspiration
from fact and pays for the difference with a failed run.

The test diffs the skill against `--help` both ways, which is the check the
methodology asks for and the one nobody runs by hand twice. It also pins the
three things a reader relies on: the read-the-output rule, an exit-code table
whose right column is a command rather than an adjective, and the sentence
about the gate. Verified now: nine verbs in the CLI, the same nine in the
skill, nothing invented in either direction.

`wait` takes seconds, so a millisecond argument must say so (#1509) (#1511)

`co browser wait 2500` meant 41 minutes, not 2.5 seconds, and it bought that
hold on the tab's operation lock before anyone could find out. Every later
command on that tab queued behind it and died at the client's 120s ceiling,
while `status` kept answering and other tabs kept working — so the round's
health probe found nothing to restart and the failure read as a wedged daemon.
Three unattended LinkedIn rounds died this way on 2026-09-12; the 18:00 round
spent 14 minutes on seven timeouts to post one comment.

The guessable part is the unit: every other settle knob in this codebase is
named in milliseconds (`wait_ms`, `timeout_ms`, `--wait_ms=2500`), so 2500 reads
as 2.5s to the caller and means 2500s here. Cap `wait` at 60s and refuse past it
BEFORE the tab lock is acquired, naming the seconds value the caller almost
certainly meant and pointing at the conditions that exist for longer settles.

Both spellings of the verb get the guard: the async core the daemon runs, and
the pre-asyncio implementation still shipped as the verb-contract oracle. A
limit the two disagree about is not a limit.

a pinned daemon must never refuse the command it tells you to run (#1510, #1501) (#1512)

The engine pin gated every request, including the ones that neither drive nor
create a page. So a daemon someone had once started with --engine wtf refused
`tab ls`, `status` and `close` — and the refusal's own remedy was
`co browser close`, refused by the same guard. Following the instruction
literally looped forever; only `co browser --engine onion close` worked, which
the message never mentioned. The browser was gone, the daemon unusable, and the
printed instructions could not get you out.

Three changes, in order of how much they matter:

`auto` is no preference, not a conflicting one. The guard read a bare command as
a demand for a different engine and refused it; now only a NAMED engine that
differs conflicts. That is what #1501 asked for, and it is why every bare
command failed against a warm paid daemon.

The exception is money, and it is narrow: a *running* paid session is consent
already given — while it is up, `auto` rides it and nothing further is charged.
Once it has ended, serving `auto` would silently open a new billing interval, so
that one case still asks.

Verbs that touch no page — close, closetab, status, engine_status, help,
`tab ls`, `tab close` — are answered whatever the pin says. `tab open` is
deliberately not among them: it allocates a page, and on a paid pin that spends.

Both refusals now name only commands this daemon would actually accept in this
state, and name the engine a person types (`wtf`) rather than the wire spelling
(`onion`). The property is tested directly: every `co browser ...` a refusal
prints is dispatched back at the daemon and must be admitted. That test caught
the first draft of the paid-relaunch message offering `--engine system`, which
the pin refuses — the same circle, reintroduced.

Also from #1510, the two cheap halves of the rest:

- PaidSessionEndedError said "browser_exited" and nothing else. Its tabs died
  with it, so the next command failed on a missing tab instead, reading as a
  second unrelated fault. It now names the way back.
- Nothing said which engine was about to bill. A session-starting verb on the
  paid engine prints one line before the command is sent. The Airbnb round that
  filed this spent 40 minutes on the paid engine, then finished the same work on
  the free one with the logins intact.

Not fixed here: the tab registry still dies with the browser, and there is no
auto-reconnect. That needs reconnect semantics, not a message — filed separately.

`install-onion` says pip refused by policy, not that pip exited 1 (#1516) (#1517)

* `install-onion` says pip refused by policy, not that pip exited 1 (#1509 follow-up)

Measured on the Intel acceptance Mac with `co` installed into Homebrew's
python@3.13:

    Could not install Onionwright: pip could not install Onionwright (exit 1).

pip's own text above it said `externally-managed-environment` — PEP 668, a
policy the OS applies to its own interpreter, which every Homebrew and system
Python applies too. But the line a reader ends on, and the only line an agent
parses, named an exit code. So the next move looks like "the download is
broken" when it is "this interpreter does not accept writes without an explicit
override", and nothing said which override or where.

pip's output is now captured, so a refusal-by-policy can be told apart from a
real failure, and it is printed back either way — the upstream text is the
evidence and is never summarised away. On a policy refusal the message names
the interpreter being decided about and both routes out:

  co browser install-onion --break-system-packages
  python3 -m venv ~/.co/venv && ~/.co/venv/bin/pip install --pre connectonion

Neither is chosen for the caller. The flag overrides a guard somebody put there
on purpose, so it is opt-in, named after pip's own, and the failure message is
the only place it is advertised. It is also not re-offered when it was already
used — repeating a flag that just failed is a loop.

An ordinary failure still reads as one: no flag is offered where it cannot help.

Verified on the machine that produced the original message: the refusal now
explains itself, and the command it prints installs Onionwright 0.0.14

* Asking for the paid engine fetches the client it runs on

The route to the paid browser was three commands, and you learned the second by
failing:

  co browser --engine wtf tab open work
  → onionwright_missing: Run `co browser install-onion`
  → Could not install Onionwright: this Python is externally managed...
  → co browser install-onion --break-system-packages

Every error there is well written. But the first one asked the caller to decide
nothing: the paid engine cannot run without its client, and there is no
configuration in which you want one and not the other. An error that offers no
choice is not an error, it is a missing step — and a good remedy for an
unnecessary question is easy to mistake for good documentation.

An explicit --engine wtf now fetches it. What must not widen is the rule
onionwright_install.py opens with: importing ConnectOnion, or selecting the
system browser, never mutates a Python environment. Neither is what happens
here; --engine wtf is a typed request for a commercial product on an
authenticated account.

Four of the six tests exist only to hold that line: auto installs nothing,
system installs nothing, `--engine wtf help` installs nothing, and a present
client is not reinstalled. A failed fetch reports and does not send the
command, so a paid command never reaches a daemon that cannot serve it.

--break-system-packages stays opt-in one layer down. Spending money, overwriting
something, or overriding a guard someone set on purpose are the steps that
should stay manual; this was not one of them.

* Reach a tab the site opened for itself

A click on target="_blank", a "view invoice" button, a payment popup: the work
moves to a page no session registered. `tab ls` lists the sessions we created,
so that page appeared nowhere, and every `-t` command kept running in the page
the agent was already on. There was no verb that could even see it.

`switch_page <index>` points the targeted session at one of them.

deciding which *session* a bare command meant, and targeting stays per command
with -t. This chooses which page a session drives. The removed-verb message now
says so, because "switch" names both things and answering only the one we
deleted sent people away from the one they wanted.

- "nobody drives this page" is a sentinel, not None. None is already the main
  tab's session key, so conflating them would have offered the shared main tab
  to a second agent as free.
- `tab ls` counts unclaimed pages and names `list_pages`. Nobody reads the help
  for a verb they do not know exists, and the board is where they look.

Verified on a real browser, not only against fakes: load a page, click a
target="_blank" link, and the popup is listed as unclaimed, switched into,
read (the payload is there), and switched back out of. The first probe used

Break the Lark auth deadlock: an honest link, a door for a console credential, and a secret that is not plain text (#1539)

Three commits that break one deadlock.

`co auth lark` could not create an application on a data-residency tenant,
and said nothing true about why: the launcher at open.larksuite.com strips
`user_code` and renders "Link expired" while the poller answers
`authorization_pending` in the same second. The command also quoted the
SDK's fallback of 600 as the TTL; the server returns 3600. The TTL now
comes from the server every time, the warning says what "Link expired"
really means, and it names `--app-id` as something that also fails —
tested, not assumed.

`co env set LARK_APP_SECRET` then refused the hand-typed value and pointed
back at `co auth lark`. Two correct rules pointing at each other, with no
way out. `--from-console` opens the door, and only for FEISHU_/LARK_ app
credentials — on any other key it is an error, not a no-op.

That means people now paste an app secret into a plain-text file, so
`co env set --secret` encrypts it instead. lark-cli, the reference
implementation, keeps an AES-256 master key in the OS keychain; we cannot,
because an agent under launchd or over ssh has no login keychain at all
(the wall openonion/browser#137 hit). We do not need one: derive.py already
turns a secret into a tree of keys, so the encryption key is derived at a
path and thrown away, and slip13_path's index already means rotation.

The root is .co/keys/agent.key, not recovery.txt. The phrase file is
optional — writing the twelve words down and deleting it is the correct
thing to do with a recovery phrase — so rooting there would have meant that
doing the right thing with your backup silently made every stored secret
unopenable. Nothing is given up, because agent.key is itself
derive_path(seed, slip13_path(ACCOUNT_URI)): the twelve words still reach
every secret, one link further along.

39 new tests, all verified red first. Verified on real files: recovery.txt
moved aside, `co env get` still returned the value, restored byte-identical.

CodeQL flags `print(get_secret(...))` in `co env get` and not the three
prints above it that reveal OAuth tokens and API keys the same way. It is
the command's contract — `export X=$(co env get X)` — and the reasoning is
written at the call site rather than suppressed.

Closes #1537. Unblocks #1462.

Release ConnectOnion 1.8.5b9 (#1540)

Release ConnectOnion 1.8.5b9

An app secret can be stored encrypted. `co env set --secret` writes ciphertext
under a key derived at a SLIP-0013 path and kept nowhere, and `co env rotate`
moves it to the next index.

b8's notes said this was #1497, targeted 2.x, and added the evidence that
unattended paths — launchd, SSH, `co deploy --to` servers — have no reachable
keychain at all. That second fact is what made the first solvable earlier, by
not needing a keychain. lark-cli generates an AES-256 master key and stores it
because it has no other secret to start from; derive.py already turns a secret
into a tree of keys, so the encryption key is derived at a path and thrown away.
Nothing to store, nothing to be blocked by a sandbox or a denied prompt, and
slip13_path's index already means rotation.

The root is .co/keys/agent.key, not recovery.txt. The phrase file is optional —
writing the twelve words down and deleting it is the correct thing to do with a
recovery phrase — so rooting there would have meant that doing the right thing
with your backup silently orphaned every stored secret. Nothing is given up,
because agent.key is itself derive_path(seed, slip13_path(ACCOUNT_URI)): the
words still reach every secret, one link further along.

Alongside it, `co env set --from-console` accepts the one app credential a
person can legitimately type, for tenants where `co auth lark` cannot create an
application at all — the two rules had been pointing at each other. And
`co auth lark` reports the server's real link lifetime, having quoted the SDK's
fallback of 600 against a server that returns 3600, and explains the "Link
expired" page some data-residency tenants render over a code that is still
alive (#1537).

Retrieval stays plaintext by design: `co env get` is the substitution form and
`co env show` is the browsing command that redacts. What encryption removes is a
secret sitting at rest in a file people cat in a screen share.

* a missing bot scope is one link away, not a console visit (#1544)

`co lark listen` recovers a connection gap by reading group history, which
needs the bot scope im:message.group_msg. An application created by
`co auth` did not have it, and neither did one set up by hand from our own
documented steps — so history recovery could never run for anyone, which is
what kept #1462's gate 3 open.

lark-cli solves this without going near the Developer Console, and says how
in cmd/event/console_url.go (MIT, larksuite/cli):

    {open-host}/page/launcher?clientID=<appID>&addons=<base64url(gzip(json))>

with its own comment as the contract — "The bot-specific scan-to-enable link
adds the scopes to the app manifest, after which the tenant token carries
them."

Three details are load-bearing, and the first attempt got all three wrong,
which is why it produced a page that said "App updated" and granted nothing:
the path is /page/launcher and not the /page/cli that registration uses; the
parameter is clientID carrying the app's own id, with no user_code; and both
scope sides are arrays, because the spec reads a missing side as empty.

So `co <provider> check` now turns the platform's own "need scope: X" into
that link, and says plainly that this one is sensitive — it lets the app read
every message in the groups it is in. Anything that is not a missing scope
keeps the log as its next step; a link that grants nothing would waste a
click and teach the reader nothing, so building one raises instead.

`co auth` also declares the whole set at registration now, so a new
application arrives able to do the work rather than able to receive and then
fail at the first recovery.

Google's events API defaults sendUpdates to 'none' and we never passed it, so
`co gcalendar meet --attendees someone@example.com` created the event, printed
a Meet link, and told the attendee nothing. It cost a live client meeting on
2026-09-15, whose guest said it plainly: "Didn't get an email invite but
anyway there is a Google Meet link there".

The same gap sat on update and delete, which is worse than never inviting
anyone: somebody who *was* invited is never told the meeting moved or was
cancelled, so they hold the old slot and arrive at nothing. Those two pass
'all' unconditionally, because the people to tell are the ones already on the
event and neither call knows who they are.

Create passes 'all' when there is somebody to tell and 'none' otherwise.
Asking Google to mail an empty list is a pointless round trip, and always
saying "everyone" makes "who was notified" unanswerable.

Which is the other half of this. "Event created" read identically whether
three people were invited or nobody was, so the silent failure looked exactly
like a success — which is how it survived until an attendee mentioned it. The
confirmation now names them:
