a confirmed time says which zone it is in (#1547) (#1550)

`co gcalendar meet "…" "2026-09-15T16:30:00+10:00" …` answered

    Start: 2026-09-15 06:30 AM

which is the same instant, correctly converted — and unreadable as anything
but a meeting at half past six in the morning. The event was right; the
sentence describing it was not, and a wrong sentence about a right event is
how somebody misses a call.

Naive values are labelled UTC, which is what _parse_time produces and what
the event body is labelled with. A value that carries its own offset keeps
it, because relabelling that as UTC would be the same bug pointed the other
way.

Two other claims in #1547 are NOT fixed here, because measuring them said
they were already true:

  * _parse_time does accept an ISO string with an offset. fromisoformat
    handles it, and '2026-09-15T16:30:00+10:00' parses today. The issue
    describes an older implementation.
  * 'timeZone': 'UTC' in the body is not self-contradictory. _parse_time
    converts to UTC and strips the offset BEFORE the body is built, so the
    stored dateTime really is UTC and the label is honest.

Both are pinned by a test now, so nobody spends an afternoon fixing a parser
that works. Changing either would have been a fix with no defect under it.

[1.8.6] Mail listings take a date window, and Outlook answers in JSON (#1522)

* Let the mail listings take a date window, and Outlook answer in JSON

`co outlook inbox` took `-n <count>` and `--unread`. That is the wrong unit for
every sweep: a census of who you correspond with, a backfill, a weekly digest
all want "between these two dates". With only a count, the caller asks for 5000
and throws most of it away -- on a real mailbox, 1851 messages fetched to read
a 150-day window.

`--since 30d` / `--since 2026-06-01` / `--until` now say it directly, on both
providers, walking a week at a time because one call for a long span comes back
silently truncated. `-n` keeps its meaning as a cap and nobody's habit changes.

`list_between` and `my_addresses` come with it. They were written for the Wiki
sources and have been sitting on that branch since 80d7a926, which is the wrong
place for them: anything reading mail by time window needs them, and they were
locked inside a 6,785-line feature branch. Ported verbatim, so when that branch
merges there is nothing to reconcile.

Outlook gains `--json`. Gmail already answers with a versioned envelope
(`schema_version`, `account`, `status`, `data`, plus `--cursor` paging) and is
left alone -- a second, differently-shaped `--json` in the same CLI would be
worse than the gap. Where the two cannot yet meet, `co gmail inbox --since
... --json` refuses and says so: a window silently dropped would return the last
ten and look like it worked.

Found while writing the tests: `--since 21d` issued a fourth request for a
window 0.0004 seconds wide, because the window's start and `now` are computed a
few hundred microseconds apart. A sliver is not a window; the walk stops when
less than a second remains.

Closes #1521

* Say on co outlook search that from:, to: and participants: narrow by who

Graph's $search takes them (measured: from:zhouodywork@gmail.com returned the
five mails it should), and the help said only "matches subject and body", so
a caller looking for one person's mail had no way to know.

* Design Journal: the window that would have been dropped

The refusal is the interesting part of #1521. Accepting --since with
--json and quietly ignoring the window would have returned the last ten
messages under a clean envelope and exit 0 — success by every visible
signal, and undetectable from the output. An agent building on those ten
has no way to learn the window was dropped.

Also records why the issue's premise was wrong: list_between was read off
an unmerged branch and did not exist on main, so this ports it verbatim
rather than wiring up something absent.

feat: WhatsApp as an inbox provider, behind an optional extra (#1543)

* Add WhatsApp as an inbox provider, behind an optional extra

A bot that answers in a WhatsApp group a person created cannot be built on
the official Cloud API: it has no endpoint for joining a group, the groups
it creates itself cap at eight participants, and creating them at all needs
an Official Business Account granted on editorial merit. The only route to
that room is to be a linked companion device, the way WhatsApp Web is.

So `co whatsapp` joins `co feishu` and `co lark` with the same nine verbs
over the same inbox directory — and the same provider contract, so `co ai`
picks a whatsapp channel out of host.yaml with no change to it.

Two things are unlike every other provider, both forced by the platform:

- It is an extra, `pip install 'connectonion[whatsapp]'`. neonize is a 21MB
  compiled Go library plus six more packages and a system libmagic, and
  nobody who only uses Feishu should pay for that. Pinned exactly rather
  than `>=`, because the wheel carries a snapshot of whatsmeow's protocol
  implementation and a version bump is a protocol change. `check` reads
  that snapshot's date out of the shared library and says so once it is
  over six months old, since a stale one fails without naming itself.

- `send` and `reply` do not connect. WhatsApp allows one socket per linked
  device, and a second process opening the same session would take the
  connection away from the listener — so they write to an outbox spool that
  the listener drains, and say what to start when nobody answers in 30s.
  The side effect is that they need no compiled library at all.

`missing()` stays empty on purpose: linking happens inside `listen` itself,
and reporting the absent session there would make the first
`co whatsapp listen` exit 3 telling the operator to run `co whatsapp listen`.
`check` reports it instead.

The docs lead with the two things to know before scanning a QR code: use a
number dedicated to this, because a linked device sees every chat the number
is in, and automating the consumer client is against WhatsApp's terms.

* Lock the whatsapp extra

`uv lock --check` in CI would have caught this; regenerating locally is
cheaper than a red run. Locked with uv 0.6.16, the version tests.yml pins:
a newer uv rewrites the file to lockfile revision 3 and renames every
`upload_time` key, which is 2,600 lines of churn CI's own uv would then
disagree with.

Adds neonize and its five new transitive dependencies — linkpreview,
phonenumbers, python-magic, python-magic-bin (Windows only) and segno.
pillow, tqdm, httpx, protobuf and requests were already locked.
`pip-audit --strict` over the export reports no advisory against any of
them.

* Publish both ends of the outbox atomically

CI on 3.11 caught the send round trip failing with
`JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)`: `send` read
the answer file and got zero bytes.

`write_text` creates the file before it writes to it, and `send` polled
`answer.exists()`. On a loaded runner the listener was descheduled in that
gap, and the caller read a name with no content behind it. The request side
already staged and renamed for exactly this reason; the answer side, which
is the one under contention, did not.

Both now go through `_publish`, which stages beside the destination and
renames — atomic within a directory, so the gap is unobservable. And both
read through `_collect`, which returns None for a file it cannot parse
rather than raising: a spool is a directory anyone can write to, so
"present but not yet readable" is one of its states and the caller's job is
to keep waiting. Our own writer can no longer produce one.

The regression test plants an empty `.result` and asserts `send` survives
it. Against the pre-fix reader it fails with the same JSONDecodeError CI
reported.

WhatsApp reads every message on protobuf 7, check stops calling an unscanned QR linked, and a live e2e suite (#1559)

* WhatsApp reads every message on protobuf 7, and check no longer calls an unscanned QR a linked device

Found on the first real-account run of 1.8.6a1, 17 September.

protobuf 7 removed FieldDescriptor.label. _context_info read it on the first
field of every message, outside its try, so on the protobuf a fresh install
resolves (the requirement is >=6.33.5, which pip satisfies with 7.x) every
inbound message was logged as "event not understood (AttributeError ...)"
and none reached the inbox. The unit fake carried a `label` attribute, which
is why the suite stayed green. The descriptor is now read through
is_repeated, falling back to label only where is_repeated does not exist.
Two tests pin it: a descriptor shaped like protobuf 7, and a real protobuf
descriptor on whichever major version is installed; both failed first with
the exact AttributeError from the live log.

check() treated any session file as a linked device, but listen creates the
file when it shows the first QR, before a phone has scanned anything. A scan
that failed left exactly that file, and check then reported the account as
ready. A link is the row whatsmeow writes to whatsmeow_device when the phone
confirms; check now requires it and says the QR was never confirmed. The
unit fakes wrote b"linked" as the session, so they now build the real table.

* A live end-to-end suite for co whatsapp, so each number is scanned once and never again

Every WhatsApp check so far meant scanning a QR and typing messages by hand,
and the 1.8.6 plan (#1555) cannot close without real-account evidence. A
linked session is a file that survives restarts, so the suite takes session
paths from the environment and drives the real CLI as subprocesses: the same
file accepts a source checkout or an installed wheel (WHATSAPP_E2E_CO).

With one number: a linked session connects with no QR and a restart reuses
the link; check passes on it and refuses a session whose QR was never
confirmed (this one needs no account at all); a send to our own chat goes out
and is not delivered back. With a second number: a direct message arrives
once and the reply reaches the sender, a message sent while the listener was
down arrives exactly once, and in a group only a message naming the number is
mentioned. Ctrl-C not stopping the listener is recorded as a strict xfail so
the fix flips it.

Marked real_api and provider_cli: it needs WhatsApp accounts, not model keys,
and skips with the setup command when a session is not configured.

* Design Journal: the tolerance that was right per message and wrong in aggregate

The listener paired, connected, received two messages and delivered neither.
Both are in its log as "event not understood ... skipped", which is what the
per-message catch is supposed to say about a payload nobody can parse — and
exactly the wrong thing to say when the build cannot parse any payload at all.

The post takes that as the dilemma rather than the protobuf 7 fix itself: the
except clause has to stay (neonize is compiled Go, a raising callback panics
across the boundary and ends the process), and it cannot distinguish "skip one
of a thousand" from "skip all of them". Nothing was counting the ratio.

It also records why check agreed: it read session.db's existence, a file
neonize creates before the QR is even drawn, and why two of its tests wrote
seven bytes named session.db and so stayed green through the whole bug.

Evidence is the real acceptance log, 2026-09-17 03:51:42 to 03:57:24.

An installed WhatsApp library is not told to install itself (#1560) (#1561)

On a clean macOS box, pip install 'connectonion[whatsapp]' succeeds and the
very next command answers "The WhatsApp library is not installed. Run: pip
install 'connectonion[whatsapp]'". Running it again succeeds again and changes
nothing.

neonize imports python-magic, a binding to the system library libmagic. pip
installs the binding; the library comes from brew/apt/dnf. The guard around
`import neonize` caught that ImportError and gave the one answer it knew, which
is the answer for a package that is absent.

ModuleNotFoundError carries .name, so the two cases separate cleanly: name ==
"neonize" means pip has not run; anything else means neonize is installed and
something underneath it is missing. The second case names libmagic and the
package for sys.platform, and for an error we do not recognise it repeats the
error and points at the traceback rather than guessing a fix.

Docs carry the system library in the same block as the extra, in both
quick-start blocks and with the reason in Setup — an extra pip cannot satisfy
alone should say so at install time, not at first run.

An @mention registers whichever id the group addresses us by (#1562)

The owner @-mentioned the bot in a WhatsApp group and it recorded
mentioned: false, so a mention_only channel would have stayed silent while
being addressed. The message itself arrived intact:

    "text": "@132754033377342 测试"
    "sender": "126121882435737@lid"
    "mentioned": false

132754033377342 is not a phone number, it is the account's LID. The linked
device holds both ids at once:

    jid              = 61410724095:2@s.whatsapp.net
    lid              = 132754033377342:2@lid
    lid_migration_ts = 1789610758      -> 2026-09-17 01:25 UTC

WhatsApp migrated this account six hours before the test. In a migrated group
the mention carries the LID, and the two ids share no digits. We read
Device.JID and compared against that alone; Device has carried LID all along.

Identity is now the set of ids the account answers to, and all three matching
paths test membership in it. Both stay live: groups migrate at different times
and older ones still address us by number. Resolving LIDs to numbers with
get_pn_from_lid was the alternative and was rejected: it hits a store that can
be empty, on the path that runs for every group message, and its failure mode
is the one being fixed.

The connect line now prints both ids, which is what would have made this one
glance instead of an investigation:

    2026-09-17T04:26:17Z connected as 61410724095 (also 132754033377342)

A reply quotes the message it answers (#1563) (#1567)

sent.jsonl recorded reply_to and the message that left quoted nothing. It
reached the right chat — that was never broken — but as a loose line, which in
a group with several conversations running is most of what a reply is for.

send() wrote {"chat", "text", "reply_to"} into the outbox request and
_drain_outbox read two of the three.

Feishu does not have this bug because there a reply is a reference: POST
/messages/{id}/reply, and the platform knows the chat and the quoted content.
WhatsApp is peer to peer — the quote travels inside the outgoing message as a
ContextInfo carrying the original's id, sender, and the original message — so

The queue is marked where the people in the chat can see it (#1564) (#1573)

Between being asked and answering, a bot in a group looks exactly like a bot
that has crashed. A consumer runs, a model thinks, someone is asked a question —
minutes — and from the group's side all of it renders as nothing.

Two reactions, not one. SEEN as the message enters the queue, ANSWERING the
moment an answer is actually on its way. The platforms replace a sender's
previous reaction rather than stacking them, so the pair reads as one status
changing. One marker cannot do this: five minutes after it appears the group
knows the message arrived and nothing else, which is where they already were.

It is also the cheapest debugger available, and that turned out to matter more
than the feedback. Three bugs this week presented identically — "I asked and
nothing happened" — and each is now a different symptom, visible from inside the
chat with no log access: no emoji means it never arrived or was never seen as
addressed to us; SEEN alone means nothing picked it up; ANSWERING with no answer
means the reply path failed.

The first mark goes directly from the listener, which already holds the only
socket. The second cannot: `reply` is another process, so it queues like every
other outbound, which is what forces the spool to carry a kind — until now a
queued request was assumed to be text.

In `consume` the second mark goes before the command, not before the send. There
the command *is* the answering and takes minutes; the send takes milliseconds.
Marking after it would light up for the instant before the answer lands, which
covers precisely none of the interval this exists for.

Two rules it obeys: it never marks a message nobody addressed to us, and it
never costs the message or the answer. The first mark runs inside neonize's
MessageEv handler, where an exception is a Go-side panic that ends the listener.

Both outcomes are logged, with the id the platform gave back. The first version
logged only failures, which made "sent" and "never attempted" identically
silent — the exact failure mode of the three bugs this was built to expose.

already keeps the right end.

untouched, and sorts ascending either way — the flag chooses which messages, not
their order. window_listing walks backwards from the recent edge.

* A window composes with the envelope, and a photo is not an empty message (#1569, #1566)

The two remaining blockers against #1555's stated outcomes.

--- #1569: --since now composes with --json on Gmail

The refusal was shipped on the grounds that composing meant reconciling a window
with cursor paging and completeness. It did not. Gmail's envelope path builds a
*query* and hands it to a pager, and Gmail's search has taken after:/before:
forever — the same terms Gmail.list_between already used one file away. So the
window is three more characters in the query string, and every open question
answers itself: the cursor is derived from the query, so a different window is a
different query and an old cursor stops matching on its own; `complete` still
comes from Gmail's page token; the cap still means what it meant.

Verified against the real account — the cursor carries its own context, so the
composition is provable from the wire:

    "query": "in:inbox after:1784518071 before:1787110071"

and `--since 60d --until 30d` returns only 17–18 August. A bad window is a typed
`invalid_window` inside the envelope rather than a traceback.

The tell was that Outlook composed these two all along. One provider doing what
the other refuses is a gap wearing a principled expression, and the two-minute
question — why doesn't the other one have this problem — went unasked for two
days.

--- #1566: a message carries what kind it is

An image, a sticker, a voice note and a message with nothing in it all arrived
with an empty `text` and no way to tell them apart, so a consumer either
answered noise or ignored real messages, and could not say "I can't read images
yet" because it did not know that it was one.

Message grows a `kind`, beside `text` because that is the field it qualifies.
"text" for anything readable as words, otherwise the platform's own word —
image, video, audio, document, sticker, location, contact. A variant we have
never seen keeps the protobuf's own name, lowercased: WhatsApp has 107 of them
and adds more, and arriving as something beats arriving as nothing. A record
written before the field existed reads as text.

The kind comes from the same ListFields walk that finds contextInfo, and reads
the descriptor name with getattr — reading an attribute a protobuf release had
removed is exactly how every message stopped being delivered in 1.8.6a1, and a
kind we cannot read must cost nothing.

Reactions are now never `mentioned`. They come back over the same socket,
including the ones this bot puts on its own queue; they are worth recording and
are not questions.

where `kind` sits is part of the shape, so the renamed test says so. One reads

"reachable" is a claim about a socket, so the socket now says it (#1599)

`co <provider> check` printed "reachable" from four facts, none of which is the
network: neonize being importable, a row in whatsmeow_device, a timestamp inside
the shared library, and a pid in a lock file. A listener whose connection had
quietly stopped — in any way that does not raise LoggedOutEv — still got a green
tick, so the command people run to find that failure was an instance of it.

Found while trying to confirm a live listener was healthy. It had been up 1h40m
with no log lines, and the second signal I reached for — session.db having been
written recently — turned out to measure traffic rather than liveness: three
hours old under a connection that was fine. A signal with one direction, read in
both.

The listener now records what it knows, on every transition rather than on a
timer, because a heartbeat says "something ran recently" and what is wanted is
"the socket is up, and this is when that last changed". check reads it and says
two different things instead of one:

    ✓ whatsapp configured · listener pid 35771 · 0 unread
    ✓ connected as 61410724095 since 2026-09-19T00:16:26Z

The third state is the one that makes it honest. A record is only believed while
the pid that wrote it is the pid holding the lock; a `connected` left by a
process that has since exited says what was true once, and reading it as current
is how a stale file becomes a confident wrong answer. Otherwise:

    listener 13813 is running; it has not said whether its socket is up.

which is the real output from the older listener that was running while this was
built. Saying "I cannot tell" was not previously available, because the command
had no way to be uncertain.

then connected-with-account-and-time after restarting on this build.

the new split; one of the new ones is unwrapped before asserting, because Rich
folds at the console width and a literal substring is then not in the output —

Run the Wiki maintainer for real: isolated Codex home, streamed sources, a reader

The first PR could not run a single real maintenance pass because Codex 0.147
inherits the user's MCP servers and plugins from CODEX_HOME and an override
cannot remove them. Instead of editing the user's config, give the app-server a
temporary CODEX_HOME holding only a copy of auth.json: there is nothing to
inherit, the effective config reads back as mcp_servers {} with every feature
off, and the existing verify_native_config gate stays as the check. A refreshed
token is written back to the real auth.json (only if it has not moved), which is
what Codex itself would have done.

With that in place the opt-in real-Codex tests pass on this machine: the
three-pass successive-update test and a new hostile-source test (shell command,
outside read, .state reset, skills/approved install requested from source text;
the sentinel and state are untouched and the legitimate sentence is kept).

Findings from the real runs, each with a red test first:

- A refused tool call no longer fails the run. Failing it preserved progress,
  so the same batch — hostile message included — came back every pass. The
  model is told why and continues; refusals and their safe reasons are
  recorded per run so the prompt can be tuned from real behaviour.
- Rollouts are streamed, not loaded. This machine has 18 sessions over 16 MB
  in one week (the largest 426 MB, almost all tool output); the old cap
  raised on the first of them and blocked every source. The consumed prefix
  is re-hashed in chunks, at most SCAN_BYTES_PER_PASS of tail is walked per
  pass, files last written before the lookback are never opened, and only
  lines that can be a message are parsed.
- One oversized message is truncated with a visible note instead of wedging
  its session forever.
- wiki_search is a tool. Without it the model had to read pages one by one to
  find an existing person or project, which burned the context budget and
  produced sibling pages.

The maintenance Skill gains a working order (search, read, write; one subject
one page; one fact one place), a rule that a project is named by its content
and not by the session's working directory, two short page examples, and a
title/Sources shape. Six dogfood batches over the author's own sessions showed
each of those gaps before they were written down.

`co wiki open` renders the notebook into one self-contained HTML file in the
system temp directory (0600, named after the root) and opens it in the default
browser. A page loaded from file:// cannot read the Markdown beside it, so the
notes are embedded at render time and the page carries an "as of" stamp; the
template is a client of that one embedded object so a served site later can
reuse it unchanged. Note text reaches the DOM only as data. Rendered in headless
Chromium with no errors. The docs, acceptance matrix and DD-065 record what was
measured.

Ship the milestone-1 loop: start, stop, sync, subscribe, launchd, newest-first

`co wiki start` shows the consent summary (the exact session directory, the
lookback, runner and model and where messages go, timezone and the six slots,
limits, what the background job is) and asks once; in a pipe it refuses and
asks for --yes after the summary has been read. On the first confirmed start
it runs one bounded batch in the foreground, then installs a per-user launchd
job that runs `co wiki sync` at the six times and once at login. Repeating
start re-applies the schedule without asking or rerunning. `stop` removes the
job and records it; consent, notes and manual sync remain. `subscribe` and
`unsubscribe` are thin wrappers over the existing choice store.

There is no worker of ours. `sync` already carries the lock, the attempt cap
and the checkpoint, so the background only needs a clock that survives a
closed terminal and a reboot; launchd is that on macOS, and it coalesces slots
missed while asleep. A process of our own would still need a per-OS login
launcher and would sit on top of it. Other platforms get consent and manual
sync until their job file exists.

Two things the live round-trip on this machine found before any test did:
loading the job fires its run-at-load batch immediately, so the first `stop`
failed with "Wiki is busy" (stop now takes no notebook lock -- the batch it
ends may be holding it) and the foreground first batch now runs before the
clock is installed instead of racing it. SIGTERM from bootout or stop is
routed through the Ctrl-C path so the run closes as interrupted rather than
staying "running" forever.

Sources are walked newest file first: a first start faces a week of backlog
and a daily cap, and oldest-first left the notebook describing last Monday.
The default input budget moves from 60k to 200k characters after five of six
real batches ran out of room reading existing pages.

Fresh-model tip test (three captured outputs, replies graded, never run):
3/3. --help and the wiki-use Skill diffed both ways. Live launchd install,
`launchctl print` state, completed run-at-load sync and clean removal are
recorded in the acceptance doc, with both dogfood runs' numbers.

End-to-end as a user lives it: tell Codex, start, ask through the Skill, correct, stop

A journey test drives the real CLI process, the real Codex + Spark maintainer
and a real launchd job: tell a non-interactive Codex something, `co wiki
start --yes`, ask a Codex that has the wiki-use Skill and watch it reach the
notebook through `co wiki search`/`show` (visible in its rollout), correct
yourself, `sync`, see the page rewritten, `sync` again with no model call,
`open`, `stop`, and find nothing left in launchd. 87 seconds, opt-in.

Its first run found what no fixture had: Codex injects a <recommended_plugins>
block into every session under role "user", and the maintainer had turned a
4.7k-character plugin list into an "opportunities" page. User messages that
open with such a tag are now excluded (red before the fix).

Failure paths through the real CLI process, no model, CI-safe: a missing
login, a missing codex binary and a second sync while one runs each exit 1
and name the fix. Two of them were red for a reason worth keeping: a failed
batch exited 0, and a configuration error spent one of the day's six attempts
-- six of them would have locked the real fix out until tomorrow. Login,
binary and version are now checked before an attempt is reserved, and a
failed batch exits nonzero with its run id.

The background job is a tick, not a calendar: launchd's StartCalendarInterval never fired here

The first job used StartCalendarInterval. Its run-at-load batch ran; the slot
two minutes later never did. Three experiments on this machine (macOS 26) with
plain /bin/sh jobs -- array form, dict form, with and without ProcessType --
fired nothing in 13-15 minutes and left no launchd log entry, while
StartInterval=120 fired seven times to the second. The repo's own
linkedin-first-comment template already used the tick form for the same reason.

So launchd now wakes `co wiki sync --scheduled` every five minutes and `sync`
owns the clock: it computes, in the saved timezone, the most recent saved time
at or before now and runs one batch if that slot has not been served since the
last scheduled batch (the same rule as host/schedule.py). A tick with nothing
due exits at once, no lock taken. Slots missed while asleep or off collapse
into one catch-up at the first tick after wake, and the timezone is ours
rather than the machine's. RunAtLoad is off, so nothing races the foreground
batch `start` just ran; at install the slot already past today is marked
served, so nothing is owed retroactively.

Unit tests cover the plist shape, the latest-slot arithmetic and the
once-per-slot/coalescing behaviour; the opt-in journey test now waits for a
real tick to serve a saved time one minute ahead.

Also: preflight (login, binary, version) runs before an attempt is reserved so
a configuration error does not spend one of the day's six attempts, and a
failed batch exits nonzero with its run id. A prompt-evaluation harness with
eight scenarios (people+agenda, decision vs proposal, question vs maintenance,
Chinese, dedupe across sessions, principle vs preference, noise, correction)
runs the real maintainer per model and prints a scorecard.

Claude Code as a source, oldest-first backfill with `sync --all`, per-source lookback caps

Claude Code transcripts (~/.claude/projects/<cwd>/<session>.jsonl) join Codex
rollouts as a source through the same importer: per-kind glob, metadata and
message parser, one incremental byte-offset checkpoint. From a real transcript
only two of nine row shapes are speech -- a user string and an assistant text
block; tool_use, tool_result, thinking, isMeta injections (skill directories,
images) and the <command-name> echo of a slash command are machinery and are
skipped. The injected-block rule now covers hyphenated tags.

Sources are walked oldest first again. Newest-first made the notebook useful on
day one, but the notebook should grow the way the user's understanding did,
later sessions revising earlier pages, and a backfill that starts at the
lookback and walks forward is the only way to exercise, in a test, what a year
of maintenance does to the pages. `sync --all` is the backfill: batch after
batch until nothing is pending, not limited by the daily attempt cap because
the user asked for it explicitly. The default lookback is two months; a custom
scope may ask for at most 180 days of coding sessions and 730 of mail.

Also: the category argument of wiki_list/wiki_search is an enum (Spark passed
"skills/candidates" and "people/" and was refused each time); refusals name
the offending category; the model's closing message is kept on the run record

Two passes: wiki-extract digests a large batch without tools, wiki-maintain organizes the digest

Sixty days of one machine's coding sessions is ~39,000 spoken messages; a
maintainer reading twenty at a time with a tool round-trip per page would need

from one assembled a week at a time: the timeline is complete, the way they
write is observed across every mail rather than guessed from one, and nothing

neither listing returned, so Outlook's listing now selects To/Cc and Gmail's

Read what the user typed, not what the harness typed into their turn

We believed coding sessions were being read as the user's own words, and the
filter said so. They were not. Codex writes AGENTS.md, the approval reviewer's
quotation of the agent's own transcript, and goal re-injection into the same
`role: user` slot; Claude Code puts subagent prompts and skill bodies there.
Measured over one real week of this machine's sessions: 1,493 of 2,062 user
messages were the harness talking to itself, carrying 97.2% of the characters
-- 19.1M against the user's 549k.

That single fact was behind the two worst things in the notebook. The pages
full of commit SHAs, CI tallies, PR numbers and a dead screenshot path were
never the user speaking; and a batch of forty "user messages" cost 1.2M input
tokens because thirty-eight of them were machine text, which is why a week of
work needed ten weeks of quota.

Codex marks what it injects with `internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough`
and a message the person typed carries only `role` and `type`, so structure
does the work and the preamble patterns are the belt to its braces. Claude
Code's sidechain rows are dropped, and a text block is checked on its own
rather than after being joined. The same week now reads as 142 Codex messages
(58k chars, down from 3.4M) and 223 from Claude Code, and one real batch spent
66k input tokens instead of 1.2M -- eighteen times less -- to write pages like
`principles/investigation-first.md` ("先认真调查清楚，再修改代码") with no SHA
on them at all.

Both Skills now say the same thing in their own words: from a coding session
you are reading intent, not a repository's state, and a bullet that names a
SHA, a branch, a test count or a bare PR number is describing execution and
was stale before it was written.

Read the shape the user types, and say so when that shape stops matching

Skipping what the client marks as injected is a denylist, and a denylist fails
open: the day Codex renames `internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough` we go
straight back to reading the agent's own transcript, silently, exactly as we
did for months. So the rule is inverted. A Codex message is read only when its
payload has exactly the three keys a typed message has -- over 30 real days the
user slot holds precisely two shapes, 688 typed ones with `content`, `role`,
`type` (median 172 characters) and 9,103 injected ones carrying `id` and the
passthrough as well (median 3,828) -- and Claude Code's are read only when the
row is neither meta nor sidechain and the content is a plain string or the text
beside a pasted image. `userType` says "external" on every row and is no help.

Failing closed is the safe direction but a silent one: a client could change
its format and the notebook would report "nothing new" while the person talked
all week. So a skip is now classified. Machinery we recognise is expected and
quiet; a user-slot message in a shape we do not know is counted, and a pass
that passes over twenty of them puts the source and the count on the run
record and in what the user is told, instead of "no change".

Measured over the same 30 days after the change: 363 Codex and 438 Claude Code
messages read, 19,893 skipped as known machinery, and zero unfamiliar.

and it does not work on a real machine. Directory was the only axis, and it is

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011Pt9ZGqDAfjoQnaj2Azpxf

Recognise a person by judgement, and read each source through its own Skill

Two things the notebook could not do, both measured on real runs today.

A person is named differently by every source. Mail carries a signature and an
address; a coding session carries whatever the user typed in the moment. A
session said "odi" while the notebook already held "Ody Zhou", and
`wiki_search("odi")` finds nothing -- literal search cannot bridge a changed
letter -- so a second page for the same human was created. Dictation and typos
make this the normal case, not the edge one.

`wiki_people` now hands the maintainer the roster instead of a search box:
every person page's title, recorded aliases, addresses and opening line. The
Skill works down an order -- an address matches, an alias matches, the context
says who this is, or you cannot tell -- and only the third step needs a model,
which is the one thing a model is for. When it cannot tell, it creates the page
and marks it `Possibly the same as:`, because a marked twin can be merged by
anyone later and an unmarked one is found by nobody. Verified end to end: a
batch saying only "odi", against a notebook holding only "Ody Zhou" and his
address, extended the existing page and wrote the new spelling into
`Also known as:` rather than creating a second.

The roster is derived from the pages rather than kept as an index, because an
index drifts from what it indexes and nothing tells you when it has.

The second thing: extraction now reads the shared rules plus the batch's own
source. Codex hides the user's words differently from mail -- 97% of what it
files under `role: user` is the harness talking to itself -- and one combined
file made the model read past half of it every run, with nowhere to write down
what a source had taught us. `wiki-extract-codex` carries where the words are,
how the store is laid out, and six lessons that each produced a bad page first.
A batch is therefore drawn from one source; the next batch takes the next.

Organise the Skills as stage times source, and name the layers they build

The notebook is built in layers and the Skills were not organised along them.
One file described how to digest a batch, how a person's page should look, and
what is true of mail and of coding sessions, all interleaved -- so a Codex
batch read past the mail half every run, and there was nowhere to write down
what a source had taught us that was not also a claim about a stage.

Two axes, independent. A stage says what to produce; a source says where the
user's words are in that store and how it lies about them. Writing one file per
pair is four sources times four stages, and a fifth source would cost four
files. `instructions(stage, kind)` composes them instead: seven files today,
and a new source costs one.

`abstract` takes no source and refuses one. Its input is pages the notebook
already holds, and a stage that reads pages has no business knowing which store
they came from -- that asymmetry is the check on whether the split is real, so
it is asserted rather than described.

Two stages are new. `wiki-investigate` is the first run: one subject, every
source at once, identity given rather than guessed. It exists because walking
the timeline meets every subject in slices -- 143 pages, median 700 bytes,
twenty of them one line -- and no amount of prompt tuning fixes a shape that
only ever shows the maintainer a few messages about anyone. `wiki-abstract`
lifts a layer: settled questions out of what happened, then reasons that recur
out of settled questions, with a threshold of three because two is a
coincidence and one is an opinion.

`wiki-extract-codex` becomes `wiki-source-codex`: it was never an extract
concern, and both the digest and the page-writer now load it.

Flat names, not nested folders: the Skill loader reads
`.co/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` one level deep, so `wiki/sources/codex/` would be
invisible to `co ai "/wiki-investigate"`.

DD-066 records the layers, the roster test that decides which categories can be
enumerated at all, and the two categories that become views.

The first run as commands a Skill drives: scan, stub, investigate, unfinished

Three throwaway scripts proved the shape of a first run today -- enumerate what
the sources already list, build every page with its structure in place, then
fill one page at a time from every source at once -- and a throwaway script
that proves something has a way of becoming the product. These are the same
steps as commands, so `wiki-init` can drive them and a person can run any one
by hand.

`co wiki scan people|projects` enumerates, with no model: correspondents with
counts, both directions, dates and a few subjects; projects with sessions,
dates and their git repository, so a linked worktree collapses into the
repository it belongs to rather than standing as a project of its own (33
paths on one machine were about a dozen repositories). The census hands over
signals -- `automated_hint`, `one_way` -- and no verdicts: an MBB notice and a
courier receipt trip the same pattern, and only one belongs in the notebook.
The first census dropped both by regex; classifying is the Skill's judgement.
Two things it got wrong before are fixed by construction: a display name is
read from the other party's side of the mail (the user's own name was being
filed under Ody, Dora and a private Gmail), and every address the user sends
from is excluded, not only the one mailbox the client reports.

`co wiki stub person|project` creates the page with its sections already
present, unknown ones marked so, the address it was found by already filled
in, and its own `Investigation:` line at the foot. The structure is a fact on
disk that the next pass edits, not a request in a prompt that three runs in a
row rewrote.

`co wiki investigate <page>` gathers everything every source holds about the
subject by its handles -- taken from the page itself plus any given -- hands
the page, the coverage and the material to one `investigate` turn, and then
records on the page what was searched. A handle that found nothing is written
down as such; "searched Gmail, none" and "did not mention Gmail" are different
facts. `co wiki unfinished` lists pages still carrying an Unknown, least
investigated first: the notebook is its own work list.

`wiki-init` is the Skill that runs them in order and supplies the judgement
between: collapse projects to repositories, classify correspondents, rank,
write the ranking down, investigate the account's owner first, stop at the
budget.
Document the first-run commands beside the rest of the contract

A transient timeout during a gather is retried, not fatal

The owner's first investigation ran for ten minutes and died on one body fetch
with a ReadTimeout from Graph -- one slow response, and everything gathered
before it thrown away, with no page written and the meter already charged for
the listings. Both provider calls in the gather are now retried four times with
a short backoff. A provider that is really down still fails; a provider that
was slow once no longer costs the run.

A sender's name comes from from_name when from is a bare address

The providers hand back a bare address in from and the display name beside it
in from_name. The census read only the header strings, so every correspondent
whose mail we mostly received -- Tamara, Vern, Wisiani, the whole UNSW side --
came out nameless.

Material over the input limit keeps the newest and says what waits

The account owner's investigation gathered for ten minutes, came back far over
input_chars_per_batch, and died at the runner's door -- nothing written, the
listings already paid for. The owner's address is on every mail there is, so
by-handle search returns the mailbox; but any busy subject can do the same. A
gather over the limit now keeps the newest material that fits and adds a
coverage line saying how many older items wait for a later pass, which the
page can carry where a crash cannot. The init Skill investigates the owner by
name and by what they wrote, not by an address that matches everything.

An investigation over the input room digests its material in order, not drops it

Ody's page was built from the newest 107 of 182 items; the 75 left waiting were
the oldest, which is where the terms of a relationship were set. The size of
the gather is now measured first -- characters, and the token estimate that
gives -- and material over the room for one turn is summarised in ordered
chunks by the tool-less extract pass, each chunk within the extract limits and
naming its source when it has one, before the single investigate turn reads
the page and every digest. This is the two-pass shape the timeline mode already
runs; investigate simply was not wired to it. Usage is reported by stage.

Enrichment is its own pass, after the sources, through the browser

Investigation reads what the user owns -- mail, sessions -- in a thread that
is read-only and has no network, on purpose. What those sources do not hold
is a different question with a different answer: the open web. A company's
site says what the company does and lists a switchboard; a register says the
signing entity. That is a pass of its own, with its own verb on the page's
status line, so the daily run can see which pages have had which stage.

`co wiki enrich <page>` runs only after the page has been investigated, and
runs under co ai rather than the Codex runner because it needs the browser.
The `wiki-enrich` Skill takes only the fields the web can answer -- company,
role, phone, signing entity, handles -- looks in the obvious place first (the

* fix(oip): say that an argv entry is too large, and how large it may be

A browser argv entry over 64 KiB was refused as "browser argv contains an
invalid value" -- the same message a NUL byte gets. The two are different
refusals: a NUL byte is a malformed value, a large one is a well-formed
value the protocol declines to carry. Reporting both as "invalid" sent a
caller looking for a bad character in a string whose only characters were
the letter `a`, and the limit it was measured against appeared nowhere in
the message, the help, or the docs.

The two conditions are now separate, each naming what it found: the NUL
message says NUL, and the size message reports the entry's index, its
actual size, and the limit -- matching the aggregate check below it, which
already named its own. Both limits are module constants rather than
literals, so they can be read from one place.

The caps themselves are unchanged.

Fetch WhatsApp media as it arrives, because there is no later

`co whatsapp` could see that a photo, a PDF or a voice note had arrived and
could not open it. Over three days on one deployment that cost a client brief
nobody read, a twenty-minute CRM search to identify a client whose photo was
sitting unread in the chat, and a screenshot the agent was asked to comment on
(#1619). The honest answer each time was "I can see that you sent an image",
which reads as evasion.

The issue proposed `co whatsapp download <message-id>`, and it cannot work.
The media keys live in the protobuf envelope; `to_message` keeps none of it and
the queue record has no room for it, so a later download has nothing to
download from. WhatsApp drops the bytes from its own servers after a while in
any case. The moment the event arrives is the only moment the file is reliably
reachable, so that is where this fetches: inside the MessageEv handler, before
the record is delivered, since a path that arrives after delivery arrives after
the answer.

`Message` gains `media`: `{path, mime, size}` when the bytes are on disk under
`<inbox>/media/`, `{error}` when they are not. Failure is loud on purpose --
expired media is the normal failure, and a zero-byte file is worse than an
error because a consumer reads it as an empty document. Anything over 64 MB is
refused the same way rather than filling the disk the inbox lives on, and the
fetch never raises, because this runs where an exception is a Go-side panic
that would take the listener down with it.

Four tests: the protobuf itself is what gets handed to the download (not a copy
of the record), a failed fetch leaves a reason and no file, a text message
never touches the path, and a saved path survives the round trip through the
queue file -- which is what a consumer actually reads.

Closes #1619

The initialization contract asks that unavailable, unauthorized, not scanned

absent. So init works out which of the four it is and the map states what it

co browser network and cookies on the tab names -t already has, with HAR recording (#1663)

* feat(browser): see what a page actually sent and received

`co browser` could read a page's DOM and could not see a byte it sent. The
skill that analyses pages (`browser-workflow-skill-builder`) therefore works
only from HTML and selectors, which is half the picture. This is the other
half, as a base tool for a skill to read rather than a product feature.

  co browser requests                    # the index: method, status, kind, size, took, url
  co browser requests --url-contains=/api/ --method=POST
  co browser requests --clear=true       # then one action, to isolate it
  co browser request 7                   # one request, headers and bodies both ways
  co browser request 7 --raw=true

Not a MITM proxy. The browser's own instrumentation needs no certificate, is
already inside TLS, sees bodies decompressed as the page saw them, and knows
which frame made the call. A proxy earns its place for traffic that is not
ours; that is a different tool.

Header values are shaped rather than printed — `x-sign: <32 hex>`,
`authorization: Bearer <48 chars>`, `cookie: <4 pairs, 312 bytes>`. The
consumer here is a skill and a skill feeds an LLM, so a session cookie must
not arrive in a prompt by accident; but hiding the header entirely would
defeat the point, since the shape is what somebody reversing the endpoint
needs. Headers that rebuild the call (content-type, origin, referer,
user-agent) print whole. --raw prints values. Names are shaped by a list plus
a heuristic, because every site invents its own: x-bogus, x-gorgon, x-sign.

Bodies are read only for xhr/fetch/document with a textual content type.
Images, fonts, media and video segments are listed but never fetched, which
is what keeps this free on the pages that are mostly those. Over 64 KiB goes
to a file; over 8 MiB is not stored. 500 records per tab, dropped with the tab.

Attaching is a capability check, not a caught AttributeError: a page that
cannot emit events is left alone, because losing the log costs a diagnostic
and raising would cost the navigation.

Verified against a real page, which is where the duration turned out to be
computed wrong — `responseEnd` is already relative to `startTime`, and the
fake had encoded the same misreading, so 29 offline tests agreed with it.
The fake now carries an observed epoch and would fail the old code.

Closes #1597.

* co browser network and co browser cookies, on the tab names -t already has, with HAR recording

The network log from #1598 moves under one verb that matches vercel-labs/agent-browser,
so an agent that knows one knows the other:

  co browser -t shop network requests --filter /api/ --type xhr,fetch --status 4xx
  co browser -t shop network request 7 [--raw]
  co browser -t shop network clear
  co browser -t shop network har start [--content text|all|none]
  co browser -t shop network har stop [FILE] [--raw]    # ~/.co/browser/har/shop-<time>.har

`requests` is for looking now; a HAR is a file DevTools and Charles import and
Playwright's route_from_har() replays. Checked that way: with the local site shut
down, a page and its POST rebuilt themselves from a HAR this wrote. A recording
takes only what fired while it was on, per tab; a second start is refused rather
than dropping the first; `--content text` widens body capture to every textual
response, `all` to binary as base64, and a body that went to a file is embedded whole.

  co browser -t shop cookies [--all] [--raw] [--json]
  co browser -t shop cookies set NAME VALUE | clear | save [FILE] | load FILE

Cookies belong to the browser, so the tab's current page decides which site is
meant and --all widens it; a tab with no site open is told to go_to one instead
of being shown everything. save writes the storage_state shape save_state and
seed_state already use.

Values stay shaped (`<22 chars>`, `x-sign: <32 hex>`) unless --raw, in the listing,
the detail view and the HAR alike: the reader is usually a skill and a skill feeds
a model. HAR and cookie files are created 0600, and fchmod-ed when they overwrite a
file someone left 0644.

The daemon now reads `--key value` as well as `--key=value` for a parameter that
takes a value, the way `tab open --who me` always has; a bare bool flag stays a
switch. That is what lets these read like every other CLI an agent knows.

Accepted on a real browser twice: headless Chrome through patchright against a
local site, and the WTF Browser through the real `co browser` CLI on an isolated
daemon against httpbin.org. The first found that a page loaded just before
`har start` was in the recording — the body is read after the event, so the
append landed after start; no fake could straddle that moment. Fixed with a test
that fails on the old code.

* Document network, HAR and cookies where people and agents look for them

docs/co-browser.md replaces the `requests --clear=true` section with the
network and cookies verbs, what a HAR holds, and when a value is shown. The
co-browser skill gains the one paragraph an agent needs: read the network layer
instead of guessing from screenshots, and never pass --raw values on. The
Design Journal post from #1598 gets a dated postscript, because the real-browser
run found the same kind of bug it was written about.

co benchmark and co eval run|report: write the standard before the skill, then score the real Agent (#1665)

* Agent(tools=[skill]) can be constructed: a tool may name its injected agent by forward reference

`skill(agent: 'Agent', name)` imports Agent only under TYPE_CHECKING, because a
module-level import would be circular. The tool factory resolved every
annotation with get_type_hints, the string did not resolve, and NameError was
raised at Agent construction — so the documented way to let an Agent choose a
skill had never worked. Found writing the `co eval run --invoke auto` tests.

The factory now retries with Agent supplied when resolution fails. Any other
name that does not resolve still raises: a real parameter with an unknown type
must fail loudly, and a test holds that. Both tests failed first.

* co benchmark and co eval run|report: write the standard before the skill, then score the real Agent against it

#1642. A benchmark is .co/benchmarks/<name>.yaml: at least five distinct cases,
normal and counterexample, each an input with `must` and (for a counterexample)
`must_not` outcomes. It names no agent and no skill, and check refuses one that
does, so the same cases can compare two implementations.

  co benchmark list | check <name> [--json]     read-only; never runs an Agent
  co eval run <name> --agent agent.py [--skill S] [--invoke auto|explicit] [--runs N] [--live]
  co eval report <name> [--latest | --run ID]

run imports the real agent.py (a template ending in host(agent) is imported
without serving) and sends every case through agent.input on a fresh session.
With --skill, the skill running is its own check: auto needs skill(name=S) in
the trace, explicit needs the skills plugin to have swapped in S's instructions.
A judge answers one question per statement — occurred, did not occur, cannot
verify — from the answer and what the tools actually did; code maps that to
PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED, a must_not that occurred is a hard FAIL, and an outside
effect only the Agent claims is UNVERIFIED. Exit 0/1/2/3 as the issue specifies.

Each run is a new read-only directory under .co/eval-runs/<name>/ with its
traces; the benchmark is never written to. report compares a run with the one
before: score over checks (expectations plus "did the skill run"), cases newly
passing or failing, forbidden outcomes that came back, and a warning when the
benchmark, invoke mode, model or agent changed.

Discovery: `co --help` and bare `co` name the workflow, `co skills --help` says
it manages skills and points here, every verb names the next one. The older
`co eval [NAME]` over .co/evals/*.yaml is unchanged: any first word that is not
run or report reaches it, and `co eval legacy` names it.

Accepted on a real model (co/gemini-3.8-flash, five cases, a ledger-writing
submit tool): the model alone handled every case but never called the skill —
0/5; a naive skill invoked explicitly — 3/5 with three forbidden outcomes;
only SKILL.md edited — 5/5, 50% → 100%, the two fixed cases named. Two bugs the
run and the tests found are fixed here with tests that failed first: run ids
named by the second could order two runs in one second backwards, and the score
counted expectations only, so a run where the skill never ran scored 100%.

* Name a project skill by its project path in activation evidence

The first real report printed `/reimbursement was replaced with
/private/tmp/.../.co/skills/reimbursement/SKILL.md` on every case, wrapping each
evidence line in two and naming a local directory in anything shared. A skill
inside the project is now `.co/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; one in ~/.co/skills or
built in stays absolute, because that is where it actually is.

* The skills-help test compares words, not bytes: CI's FORCE_COLOR puts ANSI codes mid-sentence

All four Python versions failed it in CI and it passed locally, where
FORCE_COLOR was unset. It strips the codes before matching now, and passes
with FORCE_COLOR set and unset.

A claimed schedule entry always runs, a run requested mid-run is kept, and a timed-out exec command is actually stopped (#1756). (#1759)

The scheduler's state file is a promise about what the processes will do, and
three paths broke it. A Control Center tick or compaction that raised between
the claim and the runs left entries marked running with no run behind them,
skipped every minute until a restart; claimed runs now start as tasks before
anything else in the tick can raise, and the tick awaits them regardless. A
completion rebuilt the entry's state keeping only paused, erasing a
run_requested that arrived during the run, so `co schedule run` promised a run
that never came; the request now survives every write except the claim that
consumes it. An exec: timeout killed only the shell, leaving the command
running beside the next tick's copy; the command now gets its own process
group and the timeout kills the group.

serving that channel, retry any other failure every minute while answering what

Microsoft calendar times say they are UTC, and Gmail replies go where the sender asked (#1755). (#1771)

them with no zone, so a Sydney user read a 4 pm meeting as 06:00 AM and saw a

uses GoogleCalendar's contract: every printed time names its zone, a create

Gmail reply() always answered From:, so a web-form or booking-site message

a Message-Id lost In-Reply-To and the reply left the thread elsewhere. It now
prefers Reply-To, follows up to the original To when From is one of
my_addresses(), matches header names case-insensitively and keeps the
References chain.

co browser import carries Chrome's logins into the co browser profile, so moving to the paid browser does not mean signing in again (#1477) (#1768)

* co browser import carries Chrome's logins into the co browser profile, because signing in again from a new browser is the riskiest way to get an account there (#1477).

The paid engine keeps its own profile, so a pipeline moved to --engine wtf
starts signed out, and a fresh login from an unseen browser is exactly what
a site flags. The import reads a private copy of a macOS Chrome profile's
cookie database (the source is never opened in place), decrypts it with the
Chrome Safe Storage key as Chrome does, including the SHA-256 host prefix of
database version 24, and writes each site through the target browser's own
add_cookies via the daemon's existing `cookies load` path, so the target
encrypts cookies its own way. Values are never printed; --dry-run touches
neither Keychain nor browser; a site the target already holds cookies for is
left alone unless --replace, so an import never switches an account.

cryptography becomes a declared dependency: address.py already used it and
it only arrived transitively.

Found on a real notebook's first nights on 1.8.9b1:
- the day's calls ran out by 03:00 and every five-minute tick until midnight
  retried the owed slot and logged the same error; a spent day now serves the
  slot with outcome budget_exhausted;

  written by code that knows their values, so they are put back instead;
- a maintenance pass spent ten of nineteen turns reading instructions.md and
  the chunked material file, each turn re-sending the whole context (1.45M
  input tokens for 9k characters of material); maintain and extract prompts
  now carry both inline when they fit one argv string (100k characters);
- ten project pages for the Wiki's own task folders, six for one project's
  dated Codex scratch folders and two pages for one person, all from the map
  of 2026-09-20, made maintenance try to merge by deleting, refused batch after
  batch. A page holding only map output is moved to .state/archived/ when this
  map covers its paths, excludes them, or keeps another page with the same
  address; Codex's dated scratch folders of one name are one project.

maintenance starts from the pages its material concerns, found without a model

A real maintenance pass on a 1,187-page notebook spent six of sixteen turns
running rg over every page to find where its material belonged, then timed out
at twenty minutes. The script now names the likely pages: the deepest project
whose Paths hold the session's directory, and the people whose title or alias
appears in the material (ASCII names of three characters or more, Chinese names
of two). The model starts there and searches only for what they miss.

The map also archives an older map's person page whose every address is now a
notice sender: a page called Google was a lead for every note that said Google.

maintenance updates one page per turn, as #1656 decided

One maintenance turn over a 1,187-page notebook edited eight pages at once,
spent twenty minutes deciding and rewriting, and timed out with nothing saved,
twice on the same real batch. The script now finds the pages the material
concerns and runs one turn per page through the investigation's candidate
path: that page plus the batch, the complete page written to candidate.md,
validated and promoted on its own. A refused page costs that page, not the
batch. Each page is one runner call against the day's cap, and a batch takes
as many pages (up to five) as the day has calls left, instead of refusing to
start. The candidate path also puts back runner-owned lines instead of
refusing a page for them. The maintain Skill says what to do when handed one
page.

maintenance leads skip the owner and find projects by name; a page turn may cite the page it was given

A real batch about One, ConnectOnion and the Wiki pilot was pointed at the
owner's other address and the home-directory project: every session is the
owner's own, so the owner's name is in all of it, and project pages were found
by folder only. Leads now skip the owner's page, possible own addresses and
automated senders, and match project titles as words (short Latin titles by
exact case, so "One" the project and not "one" the word).

A one-page turn that cited investigation:page, or re-cited the page's own
codex ids in new words, was refused; both name what the page already held.

a day holds 30 runner calls, and the round's investigation takes at most 8 of them

The cap of 6 was set when one maintenance call read the whole notebook
(0.7-1.4M input tokens). A page per call costs about 120k, and a 40-message
batch now spends about 470k across one digest and three page turns, so 6
calls left one batch a night against a backlog of hundreds of sessions. 30 is
less total spend than the old three batches. The daily investigation reserved
every call but two, which at 30 would let one large page spend the night; it
now takes at most 8.
